news.title: Abdul El-Sayed's Appeal to Michiganders After Haley Stevens' Sudden Switch
news.text: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday night that he understood some Detroit residents might have reservations about him based on their experiences with people who look like him, adding that he wanted to be judged on his character. Speaking with MS NOW in the hours after former Democratic rival Haley Stevens switched her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed said he felt he had been consistent in his message as he seeks to win Michigan's open, Democratic-held U.S. Senate seat. Democrats need to take back control of the chamber. El-Sayed has been a frequent target of Republican criticism, including attacks on his Muslim faith and attempts to portray his political views as extremist. "I know that for too many people in the city of Detroit, their interactions with people who look like me aren't very good," El-Sayed said. "They're being catcalled behind bulletproof glass in the gas station or a liquor store, watching kids get sold loosie cigarettes. "But I'm asking to be judged by the content of my character, not the color of my skin, and I hope that in the U.S. Senate, I can be somebody who brings communities together so that we can build together what we can't have alone." Stevens, who currently serves in the House of Representatives, insisted that her decision to endorse Rogers was "not anti-Muslim at all" as she spoke outside a Detroit church Sunday. She and El-Sayed have publicly differed in their view on Israel's military campaign in Gaza. Gaza health authorities say the campaign has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers' campaigns for comment via email outside of normal working hours Sunday. Michigan's Muslim Population: What to Know Michigan has one of the largest Muslim populations in the U.S., with an estimated 241,828 Muslim adherents, equivalent to about 2.4 percent of the state's population, according to the 2020 U.S. Religion Census. The U.S. Census does not ask Americans about their religion. The state's Muslim population, as well as its Arab American and Middle Eastern communities, are largely concentrated around Wayne County and the metro Detroit area, particularly in Dearborn, which became a focal point of the 2024 presidential election. The city's 2020 census data showed 54.5 percent of residents identifying as having Middle Eastern or North African ancestry. The communities grew over a significant period of time, including Arab migration to support Michigan's auto industry in the early 20th century, and later waves from Iraq, Yemen, and elsewhere in the Middle East. In 2020, President Joe Biden won Dearborn with 68.8 percent of the vote, compared with 29.9 percent for President Donald Trump. Trump's first administration had imposed travel restrictions on several predominantly Muslim countries, an issue that contributed to opposition among some Arab American voters. In 2022, Democrats won the Michigan governorship and control of both chambers of the state Legislature. In Dearborn, protests over LGBTQ+-themed school library books became a political flashpoint, with some conservative Muslim residents and Republicans calling for their removal. Democrats Rashida Tlaib and Alabas Farhat, who represented Dearborn in Congress and the state House, respectively, both won re-election. The 2024 election saw a major shift, with Trump winning across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, while former Vice President Kamala Harris won in Hamtramck. Opposition to the Biden administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza played a major role in the shift away from Democrats among Muslim voters, according to a 2024 exit poll by the Council on American-Islamic Relations. El-Sayed and other Muslim Americans running for or serving in elected offices have faced pushback for their views on Israel. The Democratic Senate candidate has described Israel's conduct in Gaza as a genocide and said he does not support U.S. military assistance to Israel. Some Jewish organizations and political opponents have criticized his positions on Israel, but El-Sayed has condemned antisemitism and Hamas, while arguing that criticism of Israel and its military campaign should not be equated with hostility toward Jewish people. El-Sayed's Response to Stevens' Switch Earlier Sunday, despite saying in recent days she was still backing El-Sayed, Stevens said she was switching her vote to Rogers, while still remaining a staunch Democrat. The move sparked criticism from several Democrats, as well as strategists and commentators. El-Sayed said he was not worried about Stevens and rather the other 9.9 million in the state who were not her. "Mike Rogers is going to be a vote for Donald Trump," he told MS NOW. "And if you don't believe me, just ask Donald Trump. He came here last Sunday and said that he is on the ballot. In fact, he is on the ballot in the form of Mike Rogers, and so I'm asking folks to say, what are your priorities? "If there are issues that we disagree on that are more important to you than protecting democracy, protecting the right to choose, protecting the right to a union, protecting health care, then so be it," El-Sayed said. "But if you believe in defending our democracy, defending health care, defending the insane attack on our policies, our politics, frankly, our democracy, then I hope that I can earn your support." Stevens appeared on CNN around an hour after El-Sayed's MS NOW appearance, with Anderson Cooper asking her if she believed her fellow Democrat was spreading hate or antisemitism, which she had said she could not stand alongside. "I think some of the actions have certainly been antisemitic, Anderson, but I am just sick of who he stands with," Stevens said. Trump praised Stevens' decision, telling reporters in Iowa he would like to see her join the GOP. He also took to Truth Social to praise the Congresswoman. "Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," Trump wrote. "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did. It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!" Stevens told CNN she wanted to see Democrats hold Trump accountable, with Cooper asking her if she wanted her party to win control of the Senate. "I absolutely do," she said. "I'm just casting my vote this one way." Cooper said she was not just casting her vote; she was "very publicly" casting it. Stevens was asked repeatedly what had changed between late Saturday, when she was reported to have said she was still supporting El-Sayed, and Sunday morning's announcement. She did not appear to answer the question, instead repeating El-Sayed had become "angrier and angrier." El-Sayed Remains Ahead in Final Polls To win control of the Senate, Democrats need to retain all their current seats, including the open Michigan seat, and flip at least four others, with eyes on Texas, Maine, Ohio, and Kansas. On Sunday, the final poll before Election Day from The New York Times/Siena was released, showing El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Rogers, at 53 percent compared to 42 percent among 1,011 likely voters conducted October 23-November 1. A previous poll, from YouGov, conducted October 26-29 among 2,093 voters, had El-Sayed with a 4-point lead of 51 percent to 47 percent. El-Sayed has largely been ahead in polling since early September, barring two polls affiliated with Republican sponsors. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steven Frank.
news.summary: The Democratic U.S. Senate candidate saw his polling take an 11-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers Sunday.
news.author: Dan Gooding

news.title: They voted for Trump last time. Now some are having second thoughts
news.text:
President Donald Trump was catapulted to the White House for a second term by a diverse, working-class coalition.

Many people in this powerful bloc, from gen Z men to Latinos and evangelical Christians, backed the president's America First agenda in 2024.

But two years into his second term, his approval ratings have plummeted and there are signs his support in these groups is crumbling.

While the president's personal brand is still considered strong among his MAGA base, Mr Trump's name will not appear on any ballots at the US midterm elections this week.

The ABC spoke to several voters from key demographics who backed Mr Trump last time, to see whether his Republican Party would get their support on Tuesday, or whether they had changed their minds.

Click on these labels to skip straight to their stories.

LatinosEvangelical ChristiansMAHA mumsBlack peopleFarmersVeteransYoung men

Donald Trump won Celia Salmerón's vote in 2024 with promises to bring down the cost of living.

Two years on, the 58-year-old hairdresser deeply regrets her choice.

"He promised to give us money. But he didn't give us anything. What he gave us this time was problems," she said.

"Ever since Trump came in, I have been bankrupt. I have lost everything; my house, my car. I can't pay my credit cards."

Celia, a permanent US resident who immigrated from El Salvador as a child, runs a modest salon in a working class Maryland neighbourhood home to a large Hispanic population.

Many of her clients are undocumented immigrants, some with pending asylum claims. Two weeks before the ABC's visit, an ICE operation saw a barber a few shops down from Celia's violently detained by agents.

Celia says the shopping complex where her salon is located was once bustling, but not anymore.

"It's as though the devil came here to the United States to govern. Because only the devil governs that way, with cruelty and evil," she said.

"If I had known this man was going to behave this way, I would not have voted for him. And I regret voting for him."

Mr Trump made significant gains among Latino voters in 2024, with multiple polls indicating his support increased from 32 per cent at the 2020 presidential election to 48 per cent four years later.

But there are indications of a massive reversal now, with a recent New York Times/Sienna poll giving Democrats a 30-point lead among the diverse voting bloc.

Evangelical Christians

When Donald Trump shared an AI-generated image of himself depicted as Jesus Christ in April, Jon Edwards was shocked. 

"That was a dumb thing to do … it was way out of line," the student minister said from a born-again Baptist church outside Atlanta, Georgia.

The president later deleted it, but the backlash had been begun, offending many Christians who form the bedrock of his Republican base.

The president has placed faith and religious freedom at the heart of his administration, even appointing a White House spiritual advisor, which is a move Jon has welcomed.

But the 31-year-old isn't convinced of the authenticity of Mr Trump's faith.

"He'll stand before God one day and have to give an answer to his claims … that's between the two of them," Jon said.

Religion has emerged as an increasingly prominent theme in the midterm elections, with a record number of faith leaders running as Democrats on federal and state offices.

Evangelical Christians have remained one of the president's most loyal supporters, although polling shows signs that support may be beginning to soften. 

While Jon has been uncomfortable with the aggressive tactics used by ICE, he remains broadly positive of the president's second crack at the White House and does not regret voting for him at the 2024 presidential election.

"There's a lot of the promises that he made on the trail that I'm seeing come to fruition," Jon said, pointing to his crackdown on transgenderism and immigration.

But the 31-year-old's vote is far from certain, having swung between Republican and Democratic candidates in the past.

This midterms, he's leaning towards Georgia's Democratic Senate candidate Jon Ossoff, whose campaign spoke to his values.

Tricia Busch has already battled cancer twice and undergone a stem cell transplant.

In the aftermath of her health crises, and the COVID-19 pandemic, she began paying close attention to America's health and environmental policies.

She threw her support behind the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement and its leader Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

He promised to rein in vaccines (something that has been criticised by a majority of medical experts) and remove toxic chemicals from the country's food system.

"I wish I would have never voted and never wasted my time with it," she said, adding she felt betrayed by Mr Trump's administration.

"We're still having all our food getting sprayed with chemicals," she said.

"Meanwhile, we are still being diagnosed with cancer at astronomical rates. It's a complete failure."

Tricia lives in Des Moines in deep red Iowa, a state at the heart of American agriculture.

For many in the MAHA movement, a vote for the president was effectively a vote for RFK Jr. Now many of those voters feel forgotten and furious.

The mother-of-two who runs a blog and told her readers she now feels like "a political orphan".

Despite that, she is backing Republican senate candidate Zach Lahn at the midterms this week, and hoping he "doesn't become one of Trump's puppets".

Black voters

Avery Toins had only ever voted Republican. Not anymore.

This midterms, he is backing the Democrats up and down the ballot.

According to multiple polls, Donald Trump nearly doubled his support among Black voters between the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, although most still backed his Democratic rival Kamala Harris.

Avery was among those who backed him, drawn to America First promises.

"He was meant to change the country for the better, Make America Great Again. That was the biggest lie ever told," he told the ABC.

"It was all just a scam to enrich himself and his cronies."

Avery runs a trucking company in Jackson, Mississippi, where rising gas prices and America's cost-of-living crisis have affected his business so badly, he's had to take out a loan.

"It's been rough. I've got 10 guys employed and they've got families to feed. I'm not seeing no relief in sight," he said.

"He undid everything that was already done. Instead of building off it, he just trashed everything. It just went to hell."

But Avery doesn't hope to be voting Democrat for long. Despite his disillusionment with the president, he still considers himself a lifelong conservative.

Fourth-generation farmer Scott Thomsen has voted for Donald Trump three times. But now he says enough is enough.

Speaking to the ABC as he harvests a field of corn on his Nebraska farm, Scott describes a tough year for farmers across the US.

He expected a bumper harvest but says diesel, fertiliser and equipment prices have surged during the president's second term.

The rising costs have left him worried about the future of the family business. His eldest son, one of his five children, hopes to take over the farm one day, a prospect that worries Scott.

"Our profit margin has been shrinking and we're seeing less and less of the pie every year," he said.

As a result of rising prices, a record number of farms have closed and the president's share of America's rural vote has shrunk, according to multiple polls.

Many farmers in the US have also complained about financial headwinds from the White House's tariff regime and trade wars.

Scott doesn't regret his support for Mr Trump, but wants to see him focus on decreasing the national debt and focusing on American issues.

Despite his financial frustrations, Scott plans on voting for candidates from Mr Trump's Republican Party in the midterms. 

After two deployments to Iraq, Dale King returned home to Ohio and opened a gym.

Now, with the US embroiled in another seemingly intractable war in the Middle East, he fears lessons from the past have been ignored, and another generation is being sent into a conflict without a clear endgame.

The former military officer is unconvinced by the rationale for starting the war.

"Where was the concrete credible intelligence shown to the American people that they were at the finish line of developing enough enriched material to make ballistic material?"

"We should have learned from my generation that we don't need to send another generation to another Middle East war for undefined outcomes."

To Dale, the parallels with Iraq are unmistakable.

"Enough is enough. It's time to cut bait and return home and figure out some sort of negotiated outcome," he said.

Dale is not sure who he will vote for in the midterms but is adamant he will not back any candidates in support of the Iran war.

Dale said he was never a committed supporter of Mr Trump's, but has previously voted for him. He was initially drawn to the fact Mr Trump styled himself as an anti-establishment candidate.

Now he says he feels "cheated".

Asked how optimistic he feels about his future, 29-year-old Nick Alverson responded: "How many swear words can I use?"

Nick, a college student, believes his generation has been priced out of home ownership while older Americans cash in.

Raised in the rust belt city of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, Nick is a registered independent.

He voted for the president with some scepticism in 2024, drawn to his persona as a political outsider and willingness to challenge conventions.

"He said the quiet part out loud," Nick said.

Men aged under 30 helped propel Mr Trump back into the White House two years ago, with polls showing more than half (56 per cent) of those who voted backed him.

But that support is eroding amid growing frustration over the economy, the war in Iran, and what some see as Mr Trump moving away from his America First priorities.

For Nick, the disillusionment runs deep.

"I'm sick to my stomach over it," he said. "Donald Trump turned his back on the average American. We have no business being in Iran."

Democrats have been eager to convert disillusioned Trump voters into their gain.

But Nick's disappointment hasn't pushed him towards the Democrats. Instead, he's decided not to vote "until there's a candidate that can affirm my values".
news.summary: President Donald Trump was catapulted to the White House for a second term by a diverse, working-class coalition, but two years on there is evidence to suggest it is all crumbling.
news.author: Phoebe Hosier

news.title: Early voting is over. Here's what the numbers can tell you before Tuesday — and what they can't
news.text:
HARRIS COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- Early voting is over, and Harris County did something it has never done in a midterm. More than a million people voted before Election Day even got here. That's 1,081,010 of us, nearly four in ten registered voters, and it's almost as many ballots as the county cast in the entire 2022 election, Election Day included.

Friday was the busiest day of the 12. It was the only one that topped the opening-day crowd. Fort Bend and Montgomery counties set their own records, and the statewide count had already passed 6.8 million before most counties posted their final day. Here's a number to sit with: that incomplete total is already more than 80% of every vote cast in 2018, the biggest midterm Texas has ever had.

So, the question. What does it mean? Last week we showed you that Texas polls have missed the final result by three to five points in each of the last three statewide elections. This week we have something the polls never had: a count of people who actually voted. It is tempting to read that count like a scoreboard. It isn't one. Here's what it can tell you about Tuesday, and what it can't.

PREVIOUS REPORT: Harris County broke early-voting records in 2018, too. Democrats still lost.

The surge is everywhere, not in one kind of neighborhood. We matched the county's early-vote rosters to the precinct-by-precinct results from 2022 and 2024, and the pattern is boring in the best way. In the neighborhoods that voted hardest for Ted Cruz in 2024, early voters alone already equal about two-thirds of everything those precincts cast in a presidential year. In the neighborhoods that voted hardest for Colin Allred, it's a little over 70%. Everyone else lands in between. Measured against the last midterm, the bluest precincts have already passed their entire 2022 turnout. The reddest aren't far behind.

Put another way: the mix of neighborhoods that showed up early looks a shade bluer than 2022 and almost identical to 2024. That's a real finding, and a modest one. A few points of difference between the bluest and reddest precincts is not a wave. It's a county where nearly everybody is voting more.

Early voting in Harris County has been a faithful preview of the county. In 2022, the people who voted early in the governor's race split 54–45 for Beto O'Rourke. The full county, once Election Day was counted, split 54–44. In 2024, early voters went 52–46 for Kamala Harris, and so did the county. Early voters here are not some separate electorate that shows up before the real one. They are most of the real one.

RELATED: What do the early voting numbers actually mean?

Turnout is up in every big county, blue and red. Compared with the same point in 2018, Harris County's early vote is up about a quarter. Dallas, Tarrant, and Bexar are all up by double digits. The suburbs, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Williamson, and Denton, are up even more, and Hidalgo County in the Valley is up nearly half. If you're looking for a corner of Texas that sat this one out, you will not find it.

What it won't tell you

Who those seven million people voted for. Texas doesn't register voters by party. The state's daily files record that you voted and where. That's it. Every chart you've seen this week that colors the early vote blue or red is an estimate built on something other than the ballots. Be careful what you read on the internet.

Whether early voters lean one way is the heart of the "blue early vote" idea, and the exit polls say it's wrong in Texas. AP VoteCast, the Associated Press survey of voters that ABC13 uses on election night, asks people when they voted. In each of the last three statewide elections, Democratic and Republican voters cast early ballots at nearly the same rate, within a point or three of each other. A record early vote is a record turnout. It is not a party's turnout.

Harris County is not Texas. We hold about one in seven of the state's registered voters. In 2022, O'Rourke carried Harris County by nearly 10 points and lost Texas by 11. In 2024, Allred carried it by 11 and lost by 8.5. Our early vote tells you a lot about us. It tells you very little about the six in seven Texans who live somewhere else, and that is where the last three statewide races were decided.

VoteCast also asks voters which party they identify with, and the answer is the whole ballgame. In 2018, the closest statewide race in a decade, Texans who voted identified Republican over Democrat by about eight points, and Cruz still won. In 2022 and 2024, the gap was closer to 20. For Tuesday to be close, the people who voted need to look more like 2018 than 2022. A turnout count can't confirm that, because a turnout count doesn't ask.

Election Day was about a third of the Texas vote in 2022 and under a fifth in 2024. Small, but not nothing. In Harris County, it has nudged the result both directions: a bit more Democratic in the 2022 governor's race and the 2024 Senate race, a bit less in the 2024 presidential. About 1.66 million registered voters here haven't voted yet. Some will on Tuesday, and the data can't tell you how many or which way.

VoteCast found that somewhere between one in 12 and one in 16 Texas voters made up their minds in the last few days, or later. That sounds small until you remember that nearly every poll of the Senate race this month has been inside the historical miss. In a race that polls as a tie or a two-point lead, the people who decide in the car on the way to vote are bigger than the margin.

The first numbers after 7 p.m. will be the early vote, and in Harris County that number has looked almost exactly like the final number two elections running. If our early vote lands near the roughly 54–44 split of the last governor's and Senate races, the county is doing what it does. The statewide question is different: whether the rest of Texas, reported county by county through the night, moves off its 2022 and 2024 pattern. That's the one number the early vote could never tell you. It's also the only one that decides the race.
news.summary: Early voting is over. Here's what the numbers can tell you before Tuesday, and what they can't.
news.author: Houston,Keaton Fox

news.title: The Midterms’ Two Defining Issues
news.text:
With the midterm elections just around the corner, Americans are gearing up to vote on an entirely different set of issues than in the 2024 general election. Rather than weighing the merits of a potential Kamala Harris administration, voters are now assessing the record of a second Trump term, defined by the rise of AI and military operations in Iran.

Around three weeks before the midterms, AP-NORC queried potential voters’ issue saliency. Economic concerns led at 85%, followed closely by cost-of-living concerns at 84%. Then came the Iran War at 64%, which ranked ahead of immigration and crime, the very issues that carried Donald Trump back to the White House in 2024.

Americans are often said not to vote on foreign policy, but survey findings suggest otherwise. Researchers David Karol and Edward Miguel found that Iraq casualties measurably depressed George W. Bush’s vote share in 2004; absent the war, they estimate Bush would have won 52.3% of the national vote and 366 electoral votes. Two years later, Pew called the Iraq War the central issue of the 2006 midterms, and the national exit poll showed voters who disapproved of the war breaking overwhelmingly for Democrats, who took back the House. This cycle, Fox News finds that six in ten voters oppose military action against Iran—and that those voters favor Democratic congressional candidates by 56 points.

Issue saliency changes with events and with what the president does, so the shift itself is no surprise. Nor have Democrats misread it. The war is unpopular, and their polling tells them so.
news.author: Beege Welborn

news.title: MICHIGAN MELTDOWN: Media Lost Their Minds Over Stevens Endorsement of Rogers
news.text:
The Elitist Media were shocked and stunned by news of U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) against Abdul el-Sayed for the United States Senate. The news triggered a veritable meltdown. 

This was not supposed to happen. In fact, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) went on NBC’s Meet the Press and assured host Kristen Welker and her viewers that Stevens was voting a straight Democrat ticket:

Rep. Jamie Raskin represents to @MeetThePress viewers that Haley Stevens is most assuredly voting the Democrat ticket. Stevens would then go on to make a joint appearance with fmr Rep. Mike Rogers at a Detroit church.JAMIE RASKIN: And Haley Stevens, she wants me to represent to… pic.twitter.com/fRd4yWL7H4— Jorge Bonilla (@BonillaJL) November 1, 2026

KRISTEN WELKER: Let's start with the dramatic developments out of Michigan. You have this last-minute interparty fighting between Abdul el-Sayed and his challenger in the primary, Haley Stevens. She has criticized his views on Israel. She's upset that he hasn't disavowed an ad that he had nothing to do with that she says was anti-semitic. Let me ask you, could this cost Democrats the seat in Michigan?JAMIE RASKIN: No. I spoke last night to Haley Stevens and I spoke to Abdul as well. And my wonderful friend Haley Stevens, she wants me to represent to you and everybody else I talked to that she is voting straight down the line on the Democratic ticket and she will be celebrating with Democrats across the country when we win on Tuesday night. And this is inside-the-Beltway- inside baseball imbroglio and so- I believe we will have a landslide in Michigan for lots of candidates like Callie Barr in the 1st District, like Sean McCann, there- I think Michigan’s going to be in great shape and the Democrats have really never been more unified or more focused because everybody understands the big picture here. Are we going to have progress under Democratic government or are we going to have continuing corruption under authoritarian chaos with Donald Trump and all of his MAGA followers? That's the big picture here. Haley gets it, Abdul gets it. And I think what we’re going to see on Tuesday night is a reflection of that.WELKER: All right, Well, we’ll watch and see how that one unfolds.

Welker didn’t show the slightest bit of journalistic curiosity. When did Stevens tell Raskin that she was voting for a straight ticket? We never know. Welker instead moved on to trying to get Raskin to downplay what is happening in Alaska. We did learn the truth a little later, though:

I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today. https://t.co/pQgfSBuhOJ— Haley Stevens (@HaleyforMI) November 1, 2026

And how did the Elitist Media handle this bombshell of a November Surprise? Pretty much as you would expect.

Here’s MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff lamenting that Mike Rogers has not sufficiently condemned Islamophobia:

MICHIGAN MELTDOWN: In the wake of Haley Stevens' endorsement of Mike Rogers in #MISEN, MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff laments Rogers' lack of denunciation of...Islamophobia.JACOB SOBOROFF: What you're watching right now is an Earth-shattering moment, I think it's fair to say in… pic.twitter.com/7fqeie3zdr— Jorge Bonilla (@BonillaJL) November 1, 2026

JACOB SOBOROFF: What you're watching right now is an Earth-shattering moment, I think it's fair to say in Democratic politics. The Democratic loser of the primary election in Michigan, Haley Stevens, who had said she would endorse Dr. Abdul el-Sayed, a Rhodes scholar, an epidemiologist who won the primary election in Michigan, has now withdrawn her support and has endorsed the Republican Mike Rogers in the election. After a back-and-forth feud over the course of the last several days between el-Sayed and Haley Stevens, Mike Rogers stepped to the podium and he invoked Jews. He invoked Jews in Michigan, talking about anti-semitism and fears that Jewish people in Michigan have- he did not mention, unless I missed it, the incredible amount of Islamophobia and bigotry that has been put forward in this race, including by him himself, using euphemisms and at some points, specific words like “terrorism” and “terrorist” in talking about Abdul el-Sayed, the candidate, the Democratic nominee for senate in the State of Michigan. And as they appear there together today after going to a service at a black church in Detroit, Michigan, a lot of questions for Haley Stevens to answer, of course.

Leave it to Soboroff to include a lamentation for the Rhodes Scholar el-Sayed, while never addressing the substance of that Drove Stevens to endorse Rogers. There were basic things that the nominee could’ve done to smooth things over. Among them: denouncing a recent vile anti-Israel ad, and denouncing the Muslim Brotherhood. But el-Sayed has steadfastly refused to do these things. Thus, all of the onus for preserving Democrat unity is on Stevens.

The media immediately sought to identify the purest, truest, victim of Stevens’ switch: the Democrats' chances of taking the Senate.

First question out of the chute from CNN: Are you concerned for the harm this could do to the Democratic Party? Way to establish the truest, purest victim of Stevens' endorsement of Rogers https://t.co/OP5AMeKueQ— Jorge Bonilla (@BonillaJL) November 1, 2026

Back to MS NOW, host Antonia Hylton gave Georgia Democrat Stacey Abrams several minutes to bash Stevens, but not before mentioning that she was “heartbroken” at the fact that the endorsement happened at a black church:

WATCH: MS NOW gives Stacey Abrams 4 minutes to bash Haley Stevens' decision to endorse Mike Rogers- host Antonia Hylton is "heartbroken" https://t.co/AkHj5qb1jy— Jorge Bonilla (@BonillaJL) November 1, 2026

There appears to be an early narrative congealing that accuses Stevens of endorsing Rogers out of personal spite, and in a manner that is exploitative to black people. Neither these critics nor their enablers in media address the fundamental issues that drove Stevens away: el-Sayed's refusal to address some of Stevens' fundamental concerns that put her on ice in the first place.

The media's reaction so far has been either to ignore lingering concerns about el-Sayed's adjacency to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hasan Piker and other islamists, or to accuse the people expressing these concerns of lingering Islamophobia, as Soboroff does.

When Liz Cheney broke from the Republican Party and came out in support of Kamala Harris, she was hailed as a profile in courage. At what point does Haley Stevens get similar treatment? Or is the standard (D)ifferent for her?

news.title: Everything you need to know about this week's US midterm elections
news.text:
Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.

Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:

More than 100 million people likely will cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle. Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities.

Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records.

Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.

Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.

Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.

Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.

Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.

The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.

Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.

Approval of Trump's performance is at an all-time low of 32%, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.

At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue it could point to a Democratic win in November.

There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.

However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.

Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce. In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation. 

Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats. The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.

Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.

This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies.

Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.

If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.

Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.

Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.

A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."

Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.

Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.

Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.

Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.

There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections. In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.

The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT), and then in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4). The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

When making calls, the Associated Press examines vote totals and estimates how many votes remain uncounted based on past voting patterns and early-vote data. The AP will call a race only when a trailing candidate cannot catch up.

In terms of who controls the House and Senate, how fast calls are made depends on how large the national swing is. A lopsided night can be decided within hours while a close one can take more than a week.

When Democrats won control of the House in 2018, the AP called it that night. But with a much narrower result in 2022, the AP did not call the chamber for Republicans until eight days after the vote, on Nov. 16.

The Senate can take the same amount of time, or longer. The AP called Senate control for Democrats in 2022 on Saturday, Nov. 12, when Nevada was decided.

news.title: Democrat infighting over Israel could hand Trump election victory
news.text:
“Are you a player in the Democrats’ civil war? We want to hear from you!” Politico’s editors wrote in a social media dispatch on Saturday.

The champagne bottles may still be unopened at Democratic Party headquarters where candidates anticipate victory in the US midterm elections on Tuesday night, but to the fury of party leaders, the party is already showing signs of tearing itself apart.

Ground zero for the Democratic Party civil war could be found this weekend in Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed, the epidemiologist who could become the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, found himself on the receiving end of opprobrium from one of his fellow party members.

Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who endorsed El-Sayed after losing to him earlier this year in Michigan’s Democratic Party primary, rounded on him over a third-party advertisement produced by the Rebellion Political Action Committee and funded by Cenk Uygur, the often-incendiary co-creator and host of ‘The Young Turks” online opinion network. 

The ad, which purports to support El-Sayed, claims that Michigan families are having to forgo groceries during America’s affordability crisis, because the Trump administration continues to send funds to Israel “for killing Palestinians”. 

“For days, Abdul’s only answer to the Rebellion PAC advertisement […] was that his campaign was ‘not affiliated’ with it”, thundered Stevens – a fervent backer of Israel and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). “A disclaimer is not a condemnation and everyone in my community knows it”, she wrote.

Democratic Party grandees and grassroots supporters of El-Sayed directed scorched-earth fury at Stevens, accusing her of betrayal on the eve of a possibly knife-edge race in Michigan that could determine which party ends up controlling the Senate.

On Saturday, El-Sayed told reporters: “That ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad”. He claimed that “most people don’t care about this intrigue stuff” and disclosed that he had told Stevens to stay away from his remaining campaign events.

Stevens later stunned observers by endorsing El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, on Sunday. “Abdul said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right,” she said. 

El-Sayed is no stranger to ferocious attacks from Republicans. In the past week, US President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr voiced overt racist assaults on his candidacy. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a fiercely loyal pro-Trump Republican, even warned that if the Democrats placed El-Sayed on the Senate Intelligence Committee, he might tip Islamic terrorists off to any secret plan to apprehend them.

El-Sayed has no record of supporting terrorists, is not a member of the Muslim Brotherhood and is not called “Abdul Ramadan” as Trump claimed on campaign stops last week.

Whatever the impact of the latest flap in Michigan, it is redolent of deep divisions within the Democratic Party over support for Israel. Former vice president Kamala Harris’s defeat in the 2024 presidential election has been blamed, in part, on her inability to explain how her policies towards the Middle East would differ from those of Joe Biden, the president she loyally served alongside.

Left-wing progressives and members of the Democratic Socialists of America argue that the US must cut all support and funding for Israel’s military. Centrists within the party maintain Biden’s repeated position that US support for Israel must be “ironclad”.

The party has struggled even to acknowledge the wedge nature of the issue, with an autopsy into Harris’s 2024 defeat released in May making not a single mention of Gaza. “Seriously?” asked an editorial in The Nation, a progressive magazine that bills itself as “the flagship of the left”. It argued that “too many Democrats still refuse to acknowledge how gravely the party was harmed by a failure to actively oppose genocide”.

There are also broader internal tensions that have long plagued Democratic Party politics.

In July 2016, furious supporters of Senator Bernie Sanders, the party’s veteran socialist gadfly, clashed with backers of Hillary Clinton at the party’s nominating convention in Philadelphia. To this day, left wingers claim Clinton’s nomination was rigged by centrists who still dominate the Democratic National Committee, the party’s central organising structure.

Governor Abigail Spanberger, the centrist now helming Virginia, has argued that she never wants to hear any Democrat claiming to be a “socialist” when they run for office.

After Democrats lost congressional seats in November 2020, she argued that a left-wing campaign to “defund the police” proved to be a disaster for the party. “We need to not ever use the words ‘socialist’ or ‘socialism’ ever again”, she told party grandees on a leaked call. “While people think it doesn’t matter, it does matter and we lost good members because of it”, she claimed.

That debate is unresolved, not least because of the triumph of so many DSA members in primary contests this year, and the election in New York City last November of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a DSA supporter who proudly backs the movement’s anti-war, pro-Palestinian and pro-worker agenda.

Analysts may not be wrong to anticipate internecine warfare among Democrats in the aftermath of Tuesday night’s results. For Trump, that may be one saving grace of an election that seems likely to deliver control of the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate into the hands of Democrats.

The President may relish the prospect of offering the American people a running commentary on the battle that Democrats will soon be waging against one another. Without a swift resolution, the damaging internal feud could further bedevil the party heading into the battle for the White House in 2028.
news.author: Simon Marks

news.title: 'This Week' Transcript 11-1-26: Vote 2026
news.text:
A rush transcript of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" airing on Sunday, November 1, 2026 on ABC News is below. This copy may not be in its final form, may be updated and may contain minor transcription errors. For previous show transcripts, visit the "This Week" transcript archive.

GEORGE STEPHANOPOULOS, ABC “THIS WEEK” ANCHOR: “THIS WEEK” with George Stephanopoulos starts right now.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

STEPHANOPOULOS: Final countdown.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We’re going to elect America First Republicans up and down the line.

BARACK OBAMA, FORMER U.S. PRESIDENT: We need to start bringing some accountability to this administration.

STEPHANOPOULOS: With two days to go, the Senate up for grabs.

SHERROD BROWN, (D) OHIO SENATE NOMINEE: These corporations, these billionaires may try to buy the election.

ASHLEY HINSON, (R) IOWA SENATE NOMINEE: This is about common sense versus crazy.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Could Texas turn blue?

JAMES TALARICO, (D) TEXAS SENATE NOMINEE: We are running against the embodiment of this corrupt system.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Martha Raddatz is there.

MARTHA RADDATZ, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: Did he make America great?

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: No, he made it worse.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Will Michigan turn red?

MIKE ROGERS, (R) MICHIGAN SENATE NOMINEE: You have Democrats coming out almost on a daily basis now saying I can’t vote for Abdul El-Sayed.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Jon Karl is there.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: A lot of people in this city are angry.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Well, your Jewish community is struggling.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: There’s a lot of hate being spewed.

STEPHANOPOULOS: And the surprising battlegrounds at the eleventh hour.

ANNIE ANDREWS, (D), SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE NOMINEE: I’m here because I deeply care about the people of South Carolina.

SEN. DARLINE GRAHAM, (R-SC) SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE NOMINEE: South Carolinians face a crystal clear choice between two very different candidates.

STEPHANOPOULOS: This morning, more than 50 million Americans have already voted. Our team is ready to break down the key races, the key issues and what to watch for as the results come in.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News, this is a special edition of “THIS WEEK VOTE 2026.” Here now, George Stephanopoulos.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Good morning and welcome to “THIS WEEK.”

Two days from the final votes in two years for the most consequential comeback in the history of American politics. Is the country poised for a backlash? With President Trump’s approval rating at an all-time low and Election Day gas prices approaching all-time highs, the Democrats appear to be on track for control of the House and the GOP Senate majority, which seemed rock solid at the start of this year, is now in play with seats in red states like Texas, North Carolina, even Kansas at risk.

But Democratic divisions, Republican money and razor-edge polling margins mean nothing is certain on this final weekend. President Trump’s campaign to cast doubt on the final outcome, backed by his Justice Department’s unprecedented moves to pressure election officials and litigate the counts, means that control of Congress may not be determined for days or even weeks.

And two days out, we are left with a question we never used to ask in American politics, will the losers accept the results?

This morning, our team of correspondents is fanned out across the country. We are in key swing states hearing from voters highlighting the issues driving the votes. And our roundtable is standing by with insights and analysis.

Senior political correspondent Rachel Scott starts us off with where things stand right now.

And, Rachel, tens of millions of Americans have already voted.

RACHEL SCOTT, ABC NEWS SENIOR POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT: Exactly, George. Two days to go and nearly 54 million Americans have already voted early in this midterm election. That number outpacing where we were for the midterm election just four years ago. And the unexpected battleground of Texas, Democrats starting to see some encouraging signs. More Democrats have turned out to vote this year than Republicans. And that number for Democrats also outpacing where they were four years ago.

But in a purple state like Michigan, a state where Democrats really have to have huge voter turnout here, you’ll see here they’re really not at the number that they were just four years ago for the 2022 midterm elections. They’re just a little bit below that. And Republicans averaging about the same, George.

STEPHANOPOULOS: And, Rachel, the Senate is going to be determined by a series of states which are really toss-ups right now.

SCOTT: They are. And this is going to be a challenge for Democrats. And I’m going to tell you why. Thirty-five seats up for grabs. Here in yellow, we have highlighted the toss-ups. We’ve also been really tracking the latest polls. And so, right now, as it stands, two days going in, Democrats likely to keep that seat there in Georgia. They’re likely to flip this seat in North Carolina. We know they’re making a play here for Maine. This is a state that Vice President Kamala Harris won. But the Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, really putting up a tough fight there. Even if they net these two seats right here, North Carolina and Maine, they still have to flip at least two seats that President Trump won by double digits. The question is, can they do it in a state like Kansas and a state like Texas? We also know they’re making a play for South Carolina and Mississippi as well.

Now, I said, that’s going to be a challenge. And here is why. So, we went and looked at all the states that President Trump won by double digits that are at play in this midterm election. You see it here, the margins. And then we looked at the last time they sent a Democrat to the Senate. So, in Ohio, President Trump won by 11 points. 2018 was the last time they sent a Democrat to the Senate. In Kansas, it’s been nearly a century. And so, yes, on one hand this is a good sign for Democrats that these races and these red states are so close, but they’re also going to have to defy some political odds here, George.

STEPHANOPOULOS: And the Democrats would also, of course, have to also hold on to Michigan, which they have right now.

Let’s go to the House right now. The question there is really the margin for the Democrats.

SCOTT: It really is because Democrats are only going to have to flip three seats in order to take control of the House. We did a little bit of homework for you, and we went back in history to see how past presidents have fared during their midterm election year. You’re going to see that here on the left.

I want you to pay attention to the number here in the middle. This is the approval rating for all of those presidents. And then how many seats they lost in the House.

One thing you’re going to notice, President Trump’s approval rating at 33 percent, that record low, much lower than his predecessors.

Come on down with me to 2006. President Bush, at the time, 40 percent approval rating, lost 30 seats in the House. He called that a thumping. 2010, you may remember Barack Obama, 50 percent approval rating, lost a whopping 63 seats in the House. Called that a shellacking. And then take a look at 2018. President Trump’s approval rating much higher than it is now, 40 percent back then, he lost 40 seats over in the House. That triggered that blue wave. Of course, the question mark here is only going to be answered on election night.

But here’s what I can tell you. We’ve been closely following all the House races all across the country. And since Labor Day, about 65 races have shifted towards Democrats. And in the final weeks of this campaign, and the key battleground states, at least 17 races have moved towards Democrats just in the final days of this campaign. Again, they only got a net three, George.

STEPHANOPOULOS: OK, Rachel, thanks very much.

Let’s go to Mary Bruce for the view from the White House right now.

And, Mary, the president’s going to make closing arguments in Kansas and Iowa today. That ends a remarkable string of rallies in red states.

MARY BRUCE, ABC NEWS CHIEF WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Yes, George, good morning.

By the end of the day, the president will have done 28 rallies just this month. He is, again, as you mentioned, in Iowa and Kansas today. And the president insists these rallies are having a big impact. The White House is dismissing much of the polling. But the reality is, he would not be spending so much time in these deep red states if he wasn’t worried.

And the president is putting himself front and center in these races. He is hoping his dominant presence in the party will help drive turnout and push Republicans in these competitive races over the finish line.

But behind the scenes, there is a sense of unease here at the White House. The president has been short-tempered, and he does have a lot at stake beyond just the control of Congress. The president wants to show that he still has command over his party, command over his base, and, of course, fend off enhanced investigations and oversight, George.

STEPHANOPOULOS: And, Mary, let’s talk about the president’s rhetoric at these rallies. He’s always been pretty freewheeling. But what we’ve seen this time around is more crude, more rambling and he’s had this fixation on men’s bodies.

BRUCE: Yes, George, it really has been something to watch. The president, in these speeches, they are quite lengthy and rambling. They usually go more than an hour, about 90 minutes. He goes off on these tangents. In fact, he -- more than once he has told the same story twice within the same speech. He always speaks at length about his White House construction projects. And you’re right, he has this fixation on bodies over and over again.

He has talked about Ohio Republican Jon Husted’s physique, and he’s also ramping up his personal Islamophobic attacks against other candidates and lawmakers. And it’s sparking another round of questions about the 80-year-old’s fitness, a point which the president is quite sensitive about. He often talks about his high IQ in these remarks.

But, George, all of this is time that the president is spending not talking about the issues that are top of mind for voters, the economy, the rising cost of living, the war with Iran. And it is yet another reason we will be watching closely on Tuesday to see just what impact these rallies have really had, George.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Mary Bruce, thanks.

Now to Texas, one of the surprise Senate battlegrounds. It’s already the most expensive non-presidential race on record. No state has gotten more visits from Trump. State officials redrew the congressional maps to give Republicans an edge, but high prices and a backlash against the president’s immigration tactics is fueling anger among Latino voters, which could shift the state towards Democrats for the first time in decades.

Martha Raddatz was on the scene this week.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

MARTHA RADDATZ, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR (voice over): It is here in ruby red Texas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in 38 years, where there are signs that this time around Democrats’ hopes could be realized.

JAMES TALARICO, (D) TEXAS SENATE NOMINEE: We are the underdogs. It's David versus Goliath. It’s the powers that be versus the powers that ought to be.

RADDATZ (voice over): Thirty-seven-year-old Democratic nominee, state representative, James Talarico is locked in a tight race with Texas Attorney General, Republican, Ken Paxton.

KEN PAXTON, (R) TEXAS SENATE NOMINEE: Mr. President, I am so grateful to have you here in Texas.

RADDATZ (voice over): President Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024, but he’s now playing defense.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: On November 3rd we’ve got to win.

RADDATZ (voice over): Early vote in the Lone Star State surging. More than seven million people cast their ballots before it ended Friday.

RADDATZ: But it is here in the Rio Grande Valley, just north of the Mexican border, where

Hispanics caused a political earthquake in 2024. For the first time in modern history, Hispanics by majority voted Republican.

RADDATZ (voice-over): McAllen, like much of the Rio Grande Valley, is more than 90 percent Hispanic. Mayor Javier Villalobos, a Republican, acknowledges the Trump administration's deportation tactics in particular have angered his constituents.

MAYOR JAVIER VILLALOBOS, (R) MCALLEN, TEXAS: The president, when he secured the border, everybody was happy about it. When he started deporting bad people with the worst of the worst, everybody was happy about it. But when we start affecting our economy by getting people that are good and productive and deporting them, sometimes without opportunity, that's what's a little more difficult. And that's something that the Hispanic community is taking a look at.

RADDATZ: And they're taking a look at it, and are Republicans going to have a rougher time this time, you think?

VILLALOBOS: I don't think we'll go back to the way it was last presidential, but I don't think -- I think this area is still going to be competitive.

RADDATZ (voice-over): The immigration crackdown has had major economic impacts here as well.

Ronnie Cavazos chairs the South Texas Builders Association and runs his own construction firm just north of McAllen. He says ICE raids have had a devastating impact on his bottom line.

RONNIE CAVAZOS, SOUTH TEXAS BUILDERS ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT: It's been a one, two, three uppercut type of punch, right, ever since the administration came in. We had to deal with tariffs, and that put a big blow in our system or in the industry. And then right after that, we had ICE raids that were, you know, officials were actually going on site and tapping guys on the shoulder while pouring concrete and picking them up.

And then if they were still legal, they'd bring them back or let them go. If not, they'd deport them. And I think we all know that the construction industry is immigrant heavy.

RADDATZ: Could you replace these workers?

CAVAZOS: No. We need people to actually do the work. We need manual labor. We need labor hands. And there is nobody prepared to do that.

RADDATZ: Cavazos, who doesn't identify with either party, says he's backing Democrats this cycle and thinks members of his community will follow suit.

CAVAZOS: I think there's going to be a big backlash on the Trump administration. The way they handled this -- this issue, the immigration issue, was barbaric at best.

RADDATZ (voice-over): Jessica Cantu Vuittonet runs a coffee shop in San Benito. She enthusiastically voted for Trump in 2024, her first time voting. She is now profoundly regretful.

RADDATZ: You were wearing hats and “Make America Great”. Did he make America great?

JESSICA CANTU VUITTONET, SMALL BUSINESS OWNER: No, he made it worse.

RADDATZ: Why?

VUITTONET: He literally made it worse because he's heartless, and he used a lot of us people of faith to vote for him. I didn't know any better.

RADDATZ (voice-over): Vuittonet says she at first supported Trump's immigration crackdown, but then her own brother was deported.

VUITTONET: What he told us, he was going for the criminals, for those that truly do not deserve to be in our country. But the way he's doing it now, breaking up families, breaking up communities, people have died, he's heartless. If I could have him in front of me, I would tell him straight to his face, I'm not scared of him.

I feel used. I feel betrayed. He doesn't have any compassion for what he's doing.

RADDATZ (voice-over): She is so disillusioned she says she's not going to vote at all this cycle.

VUITTONET: These are tears not of sadness. These are tears of anger, of the betrayal.

RADDATZ (voice-over): The Republicans and President Trump still have major support in the state, but if Latino voters like Jessica Vuittonet stay home or like Ronnie Cavazos turn to the Democrats, the Lone Star State's red wall may come tumbling down.

For “This Week”, Martha Raddatz, ABC News, in the Rio Grande Valley.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

STEPHANOPOULOS: Thanks to Martha for that. And while Democrats are cautiously optimistic on Texas, Republicans are hoping they can flip a Senate seat in Michigan.

Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed is starting to unify his party after a bitter primary, but Republican Mike Rogers faces the challenge of distancing himself from President Trump.

Jonathan Karl was there “This Week”.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

JONATHAN KARL, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR (voice-over): The showdown between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan may be the only Senate race where Democrats are playing defense, trying to save one of their own seats.

ABDUL EL-SAYED, (D) MICHIGAN SENATE NOMINEE: It’s getting hot here, no? Are we fired up? We’re fired up.

MIKE ROGERS, (R) MICHIGAN SENATE NOMINEE: We have a state to save. Let's get busy, Michigan!

KARL (voice-over): Rogers is trying to put some distance between himself and Trump, especially on Iran.

ROGERS: My argument is, and I made this to the administration, time to wrap this up.

KARL (voice-over): And when Trump launched his latest trade war with Canada, Rogers ran an ad where he talked up Canadian trade and Canadian beer.

ROGERS: Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that.

KARL: The president says this is an A-plus, plus, plus, plus, plus economy. Is that the way you see it here in Michigan?

ROGERS: We have some improvement to do. You know, that’s why you have different teachers with different grades.

KARL: Yeah. So, what’s your grade?

ROGERS: So there are some fundamentals -- well, I don’t -- I’m not going to do the grade --

grade thing.

KARL (voice over): While the economy is the dominant issue here, Michigan’s Senate race could hinge on three key groups, black voters, Jewish voters and Arab Americans.

Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly made false and unfounded attacks against El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim ever to serve in the U.S. Senate, going so far as to call him a jihadist and a terrorist.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: If you’re black or if you’re Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you’re crazy.

KARL (voice over): I asked Rogers, who has also accused El-Sayed of extremist ties, if the president’s attacks go too far.

ROGERS: I have never called him any of those things. And in a campaign, you should see the things that they’re talking about us. And so --

KARL: So, you think that does go too far?

ROGERS: Well, listen, I’ve never used it. And this campaign is about how I purport myself to the Michigan voters. I’m not saying those words.

KARL (voice over): Hassan Nehme is a Muslim and a Republican state house candidate who worked hard to get Arab Americans and Muslim voters to vote for Trump in 2024. The effort paid off. Trump actually beat Kamala Harris in Dearborn, Michigan, home to one of the largest Arab American communities in the U.S. Hassan is still a Republican, but he says he feels betrayed. Like the attacks on El-Sayed are attacks on all Muslims.

HASSAN NEHME, (R) STATE REPRESENTATIVE CANDIDATE: Before Trump, you know, flipped on his promises to our community. I was working very closely with the campaign. I mean, I went to the RNC. I was on the RNC national convention floor as a Muslim, you know? And now you look at it, and I'm being told, get out of this country. I’m a veteran as well, and I’m being told, get out of this country. You don’t belong here. No foreigners.

KARL (voice over): He says the Republicans are trying to use scare tactics to motivate voters, and it will ultimately backfire.

NEHME: Yes, you’re going to get out some of the crazy extremists to vote, but you’re closing the door on a lot of people, and it’s turning a lot of people off because our nation is found on diversity. It’s found on the freedom of religion.

KARL (voice over): But El-Sayed has struggled to win over Jewish voters. His opponent in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens, has criticized him for refusing to condemn an ad by an outside group.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.

STEPHANOPOULOS: OK, then let's get the final forecast from everybody, House and Senate.

MCCARTHY: I think the Democrats will win the House, and I think the Senate's up for a toss-up.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Do you have a number?

MCCARTHY: I think they're going to do quite well.

MCCARTHY: I think they can reach up to 230.

BRAZILE: Spill it out. Come on.

CHRISTIE: I'll say 234 in the House for the Democrats, 52 in the Senate for the Democrats. And for the first time in 16 years, and this one really hurts me, 27 Democratic governors.

STEPHANOPOULOS: 27 Democratic governors?

CHRISTIE: 27 Democratic governors.

STEPHANOPOULOS: They haven't won the majority of governors since 2010 (ph).

CHRISTIE: 2010.

BRAZILE: 18 new governors across the country, I agree with you. We're going to see Democratic governors in all of the key battleground states in 2028. I predict that the Democrats will pull between 225 and 234 in the House, and I think the Senate's going to be 52/48. And I'm not liquored up yet.

CHRISTIE: 225 to 234.

BRAZILE: Come on, boy.

CHRISTIE: Why don't we say 200 to 250?

CHRISTIE: Come on. It's not a prediction. We're supposed to be experts here.

(CROSSTALK)

HEITKAMP: OK, OK. I'm going to be the outlier. I think you're going to be closer to 240 than you are to 230, and I think that we're going to win the Senate seats by 54.

MCCARTHY: I think Republicans beat the Senate. (Inaudible) 50/50, we're the majority. Watch Maine, Michigan, and Alaska.

(CROSSTALK)

MCCARTHY: If Republicans win those, Democrats do not have a chance.

(CROSSTALK)

HEITKAMP: Huge.

STEPHANOPOULOS: We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

STEPHANOPOULOS: That is all for us today. Thanks for sharing part of your Sunday with us. Check out "World News Tonight," and I'll see you tomorrow on GMA.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

news.title: Michigan MI-7 Election 2026: Republican incumbent Tom Barrett is up against Democrat William Lawrence in key US House battle
news.text:
ReutersTom Barrett

The November 3 election in Michigan's 7th Congressional District will put Republican incumbent Tom Barrett against Democratic challenger William Lawrence and Green Party candidate Shane Dedrick. The contest is among the closely watched House races in the US midterm elections, with its outcome potentially affecting the balance of power in Congress. Barrett is seeking another term by highlighting his military background and record in office, while Lawrence is campaigning on healthcare, housing, workers' rights and childcare. Major race forecasters had rated the contest as either Lean Democratic or a Toss-up as of September 2026.Key candidatesTom Barrett (Republican): Barrett, who represents Michigan's 7th district, served in the US Army during Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom as a helicopter pilot with the Michigan Army National Guard. Before entering Congress, he served in the Michigan House of Representatives and the state Senate.His campaign is focused on affordability, taxes and housing. In a campaign advertisement, Barrett said, "I'll always put Michigan ahead of political party to make raising a family a little more affordable, stopping Wall Street from buying our family homes, and lowering your taxes." He has received endorsements from President Donald Trump, Club for Growth PAC and Americans for Prosperity Action.William Lawrence (Democrat): Lawrence brings an activist and organising background to the race. He co-founded the Sunrise Movement, the Michigan Rent Is Too Damn High Coalition and the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center.Live EventsHis campaign is centred on universal healthcare, workers' rights, affordable housing and access to childcare and senior care. In a campaign advertisement, Lawrence said he supported "[u]niversal healthcare that covers us regardless of our job. The right to form a union, so we and our coworkers can have each other's backs. Truly affordable housing where we can build a lasting home with our families. And child and senior care so we can support our families in life's most vulnerable and precious moments."He has received endorsements from US Senator Bernie Sanders, Michigan AFL-CIO and the United Auto Workers.Shane Dedrick (Green Party): Dedrick is also contesting the general election as the Green Party candidate. He secured the party's nomination at its convention on April 25, 2026.What to watchThe contest brings two different campaign approaches into focus. Barrett is seeking to defend his record as an elected representative and draw on his military service, while Lawrence is highlighting his work with grassroots organisations and issues affecting households and workers.Campaign funding is another factor to watch. As of July 15, 2026, Barrett had raised $6.3 million and spent $3.5 million. Lawrence had raised $1.2 million and spent $736,000.The candidates' ability to connect their campaigns with voters' concerns over the cost of living, housing, healthcare and employment will be closely watched.The Democratic primary also offered an indication of the contest within the party. Lawrence secured 42.4% of the vote, defeating Bridget Brink, who received 29.1%, and Matt Maasdam, who secured 28.5%. Barrett advanced unopposed in the Republican primary, receiving all 72,459 votes.What happened in the last election?The district was closely contested in 2024. Barrett defeated Democratic candidate Curtis Hertel with 50.3% of the vote against Hertel's 46.6%.The presidential contest in the district was even tighter. Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris by 49.9% to 48.6%.The results underline the narrow margins in the district and the competitive nature of its congressional contest. Barrett's previous victory came with a relatively small lead, making the 2026 election an important test of his support among voters.The wider stakesThe Michigan contest is part of a larger battle for control of the US House of Representatives. All 435 seats are up for election in November, and the result in the 7th district could contribute to determining which party controls the chamber in the 120th Congress.Republicans currently hold a 219-214 majority, with two vacancies. This leaves the party with a narrow margin, making competitive districts such as Michigan's 7th important to both parties.The New York Times' Catie Edmondson has described the contest as "not only one of the most competitive in the country but also a test of the standard playbook for candidates running in battleground districts."Beyond the individual candidates, the result will offer a measure of how voters in a closely divided district respond to campaigns centred on affordability, economic concerns, public services and political experience.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: North Carolina NC-11 Election 2026: Democrat Jamie Ager faces Republican Jennifer Balkcom in race for US House seat
news.text:
APRepublican Jennifer Balkcom

The November 3 election in North Carolina's 11th Congressional District will see Democrat Jamie Ager take on Republican Jennifer Balkcom and Libertarian Travis Groo. The race took a turn after incumbent Republican Chuck Edwards suspended his re-election campaign on August 5, 2026, following a House Ethics Committee recommendation that the full House censure him over allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards female staffers. Balkcom was subsequently selected as the Republican nominee.Jamie Ager vs Jennifer BalkcomJamie Ager (Democrat): Ager owns and operates Hickory Nut Gap, a meat producer that he describes as sustainable. His campaign has focused on rising costs, healthcare, Medicaid and the impact of extreme weather on communities. He won the Democratic primary with 64.7% of the vote, defeating four challengers.In a campaign advertisement, Ager said, "Rising costs hurt our businesses and our families. Medicaid insures my neighbors and my friends and now it's being ripped away. And the weather that batters us is only getting worse."Jennifer Balkcom (Republican): Balkcom is a mortgage loan officer and was elected to the North Carolina House of Representatives in 2022. Her campaign has highlighted protecting family farms and preventing foreign adversaries from acquiring American farmland.Live EventsIn a campaign advertisement, she said, "Protecting family farms is personal to me. That's why I led the effort in Raleigh to stop China and other enemies from owning or buying our farmland."She replaced Edwards as the Republican nominee after his withdrawal. Edwards had won the Republican primary with 70.1% of the vote.Travis Groo (Libertarian): Groo is the Libertarian Party candidate and advanced without appearing on the ballot after the party cancelled its primary.What to watchEdwards' withdrawal has changed the Republican campaign, with Balkcom taking over as the party's nominee after he had already secured the primary victory.The race is also drawing attention because of its competing assessments from election forecasters. As of September 2026, ratings ranged from Lean Republican to Toss-up. Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball rated it Lean Republican, while Decision Desk and Inside Elections classified it as a Toss-up.What happened in the last election?In 2024, Edwards defeated Democratic candidate Caleb Rudow with 56.8% of the vote against 43.2%.Donald Trump also won the district in the presidential election, defeating Kamala Harris by 54.2% to 44.7%.The district boundaries remained unchanged ahead of the 2026 election, despite North Carolina redrawing its congressional map in October 2025.Why is the NC-11 race important in the 2026 US Midterm Elections?The contest is part of the broader battle for control of the US House of Representatives. Republicans currently hold a 219-214 majority, with two vacancies. All 435 House seats are up for election on November 3.The outcome in North Carolina's 11th district could contribute to determining the partisan balance in the 120th Congress. The race will also test how voters respond to the change in Republican leadership following Edwards' withdrawal and the competing campaigns on healthcare, economic pressures and farmland protection.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!
