news.title: Midterm Election Watch Guide: When GOP Will Know If It’s Time To Hit Panic Button Or Reach For Champagne
news.text:
Several key races on Tuesday will determine if Republicans were able to beat expectations after trailing Democrats in the polls. 

The elections appeared grim for Republicans in both the House and Senate races, particularly as voters remained dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy. The races in deep-red states and districts, such as Ohio, Kansas and Texas, as well as in battleground states like Michigan, will be the most anticipated matchups to watch Tuesday night. 

Alaska Senate 

The Alaska Senate race has been embroiled in legal woes and investigations after The New York Times reported that former Democratic Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola’s campaign and aides with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) coordinated to recruit other Republican candidates to run against Republican Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan. Former schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan entered the race in June and will appear on the ballot, which could confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan. 

Aides with the DSCC introduced Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz to former members of Peltola’s team, who informed them he was in contact with another Sullivan from Petersburg. He attempted to recruit other Alaskans to run as Republicans by traveling to several communities and meeting different individuals in casual settings. (RELATED: Secret Scheme To Sabotage GOP Senator Revealed After Democrat Denied Involvement: REPORT)

Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage told the Times that he got a call from an unfamiliar number with an Ohio area code. The person, who identified himself as Zane, met with him at a pub and urged him to run for Senate. When the Times showed Salisbury a photograph of Kurtz, Salisbury confirmed that Kurtz was the person in question.

Alaska’s open voting system made this scheme possible, given that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves, according to the Times. Republicans backed an effort to help a candite serving time in a New York prison stay on the ballot when Peltola ran for reelection to the House in 2024.

The Department of Justice subpoenaed over three dozen individuals as part of its investigation into the Democrats’ scheme. Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the scheme violated any laws. 

Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates—including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator—to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes. The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings. I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The evidence will determine what happens next. Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support. Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.— Governor Mike Dunleavy (@GovDunleavy) October 29, 2026

Peltola led by an average of 1.2 points as of Friday, though it remains to be seen how the Times’ report will impact her chances. 

The other Sullivan’s candidacy prompted legal action to be taken over the summer. Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher informed Sullivan in an Aug. 26 letter that his declaration of candidacy “was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy,” but rather to confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan. After Sullivan appealed the ruling, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled he could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary.

The Alaska Supreme Court overturned that ruling in a June 30 decision and allowed the other Sullivan to be on the ballot. The DSCC and Peltola’s campaign celebrated the high court’s decision, according to the Times.

The other Sullivan changed his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated on Wednesday. 

Democratic strategist Amber Lee authored a press release announcing the other Sullivan’s candidacy, metadata reviewed by the DCNF showed. Lee told The Hill in January that she believed there was a good chance Peltola could defeat Sullivan and previously hoped Peltola would run for governor.

Michigan Senate race 

Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers face a tight competition to replace Democratic Michigan Sen. Gary Peters. El-Sayed, a political newcomer who ran as the anti-establishment candidate, defeated Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens by one point in the Democratic primary after receiving endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Democratic Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib. 

The race will determine whether an anti-establishment Democrat can defeat an establishment, traditional Republican in a battleground state that President Donald Trump won by one point in 2024. El-Sayed would have to win over enough non-college educated, non-white and lower income voters to win, although he struggled with these voters during August’s Democratic primary. 

Stevens won more than 50% of the vote in counties where less than 30% had a college education, while El-Sayed won nearly 60% of the vote in counties where at least 30% of residents held a bachelor’s degree, according to Politico. He also won in areas with universities while further-left candidates performed well with young voters and underperformed with black voters. 

The Michigan Democrat held a 3.2-point lead against Rogers as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. El-Sayed centered his campaign around affordability, fighting corporate money in politics and opposing the political establishment. He also supported cutting off aid to Israel and condemned the Iran war. 

Rogers received an endorsement from Trump, although he broke with Trump during the general election cycle on the Iran war and Canadian tariffs. Rogers’ campaign released an advertisement on Oct. 8 that called for an end to a “tariff war” with Canada to help lower prices for consumers in the state, given that the state’s economy is strongly tied to the neighboring country.

Trump announced in July that 50% tariffs would be imposed on various Canadian goods, including wood and large motorcycles, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, to force trade concessions. He implemented bans on specific Canadian alcohol, dairy and motorcycle products that went into effect on Sept. 29. 

Rogers backed the tariffs in an Aug. 29 statement, stating they were “necessary” for Michigan’s economy. 

“President Trump is right to put America First - and tariffs are necessary, but are not a size-fits-all solution,” Rogers said. “Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters are missing in action. Michigan deserves a Senator who will work with President Trump to broker a trade deal with Canada that supports our farmers and gets the best deal for Michigan autoworkers and manufacturers.”

Rogers flip-flopped on the Iran war, stating in a Sept. 21 ad that it needed to end to bring costs down. He previously described Iran as an “imminent threat” and called U.S. military action a “win-win-win” for the nation.

Democratic voters largely voted out establishment incumbents and replaced them with further-left candidates, such as El-Sayed. Many in the Democratic coalition have increasingly become opposed to aiding Israel, which appeared evident when over 100 Democratic representatives voted for Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s amendment that would have slashed $3.3 billion in foreign aid to Israel. 

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent $30.6 million during the primary season, spending over $20 million opposing El-Sayed and over $10 million supporting Stevens, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings. Rogers’ allies told AIPAC in August not to advertise on his behalf after El-Sayed won, although he said during an Oct. 9 debate that he welcomed support from AIPAC and anyone else who wanted to help his campaign. 

AIPAC reportedly planned to give up to $9 million to a pro-Rogers super PAC, the Great Lakes Conservative Fund, in late October, anonymous sources told The New York Times. The spending was deliberately timed for after the Oct. 14 deadline so it would not appear on FEC filings before Election Day. 

Current FEC filings do not show any contribution from AIPAC or UDP going to Rogers’ super PAC. UDP spent $95,000 on mailers to oppose El-Sayed on Oct. 9. 

Texas Senate 

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico remains tight, despite Texas being a traditionally red state. 

Republicans spent over $300 million to help Paxton defeat Talarico. Texas has not had a Democratic senator since 1993, and Republicans control the state Legislature, attorney general’s and governor’s offices. 

Talarico led Paxton by an average of 1.8 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. The tight race has made Democrats hopeful they could flip a Senate seat blue for the first time in over three decades, prompting them to spend over $130 million in ad spending. 

Corruption became a top issue for voters in the final stretch before the election, which likely hurt Paxton’s candidacy. The Republican-controlled Texas state Legislature impeached Paxton in 2023 on bribery and abuse of power charges, although the state Senate acquitted him.

Paxton was accused of misusing the office of the attorney general to protect and assist Austin real estate developer and political donor Nate Paul, who faced federal investigations. He allegedly intervened in lawsuits, issued favorable legal opinions to protect Paul’s properties from foreclosure and hired a special prosecutor to investigate claims helpful to Paul. 

Paul allegedly paid for expensive renovations to Paxton’s home and employed a woman with whom Paxton had an extramarital affair. Paxton denied all wrongdoing.

Talarico repeatedly accused Paxton of being a corrupt politician who has used his power to get richer. Paxton’s net worth rose from $174,000 when he first entered the state Legislature in 2003 to an estimated $13 million currently, according to Forbes.

An October University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found voters trusted Talarico more on handling corruption than Paxton by ten percentage points.

Talarico stated in 2021 that God was “non-binary” and that transgender children were made in His image. He claimed that the biblical account of Jesus’ conception justified abortion and also said on a May 2023 podcast that he loved transgender kids when asked to name something he loved other than his family and friends.

Paxton argued on the campaign trail that Talarico is too liberal for Texas. 

The Texas Democrat left the campaign trail for nine days during the first week of October, claiming he had a “nasty case of the flu.” 

Paxton defeated Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn by a 28-point margin in May after Trump endorsed him last-minute. During the Republican primary, Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn and his allies referred to Paxton as “Crooked Ken” and called him “corrupt to the core” in one ad. Talarico and his allies released attack ads calling out Paxton’s alleged corruption.

Ohio Senate & Governor’s races 

Democrats are eyeing Ohio as a potential win against Republicans, who control the state Legislature and governor’s office. Former Democratic Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton held slight leads in the polls against Republican Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. 

Brown led Husted by an average of 2.6 points, according to RealClearPolling. Trump won Ohio by a twelve-point margin, 55.2% to 43.9%. Husted assumed office in January 2025 to replace Vice President J.D. Vance. 

Acton led Ramaswamy by an average of 4.3 points as of Friday, according to RealClearPolling. Ramaswamy faced backlash after an advertisement featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, telling voters not to vote for her. 

Acton and her mother have been estranged since 1978, when she was 12 years old. She and her younger brother were removed from Arthur’s custody after her husband was charged with sexually abusing Acton. 

Ramaswamy’s poll numbers dropped six points Thursday after the ad aired, according to Truthout. 

Maine Senate race

Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough challenge against Democratic Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who entered the race late in the game. Heating fuel prices became a top issue for Maine voters since the Iran war began, which could give Democrats an advantage in the deep blue state. 

Jackson held a slight lead over Collins in the deep-blue state, holding a 1.4 point average lead, according to RealClearPolling. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by a 52.4% to 45.5% margin in the 2024 election. Maine Democrats control the governor’s office, attorney general’s office and the state Legislature. 

Despite Maine being a blue state, Collins has won five Senate races since 1996. 

The two candidates both campaigned on the high cost of living, particularly the high-heating costs in Maine. The average statewide heating fuel prices rose to $6.05 per gallon as of Oct. 26. Roughly half of the population in Maine rely on heating oil as their principal energy source in the winter, meaning they could face an increase of thousands of dollars in heating. 

The Iran war caused heating fuel prices to soar, given that the Strait of Hormuz handles roughly 20% to 25% of the world’s seaborne oil and petroleum product flow. Collins voted to extend U.S. military operations in Iran five times since February. 

Collins and independent Maine Sen. Angus King urged the Trump administration to tap into the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to help lower costs before the elections. She joined a bipartisan push to expedite the release of over $38 million in federal home heating assistance for Maine households. 

Collins initially ran against former Democratic Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after a woman accused him of rape. 

Kansas Senate 

Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall is trailing Democratic Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton by an average of 2.6 points. A Democratic victory would be a major upset, given that Kansas has not had a Democratic senator since 1939. 

The Republican senator sued 700 of his patients for outstanding debts during his time as an OB-GYN, which led to 81 arrests, The New York Times reported. Some facing lawsuits were mothers with outstanding bills from their deliveries, and many patients lacked insurance. One mother had a nine-month-old baby when her bank account was garnished. 

Marshall paid a bakery $1,300 after its owner, Holly Thomas, accused his 2020 campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years. The senator said on X that he paid the bill and apologized to the bakery, claiming he had “no idea” how the bill went unpaid for six years.

RealClearPolling averages showed Marshall and Hamilton in a tie in mid-October. 

The close race caused the Senate Leadership Fund, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, to spend $14 million to support Marshall. 

The Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats’ Senate campaign arm, launched a $5 million statewide television advertising campaign that plans to run through Election Day, indicating that Democrats were increasingly confident they could flip the seat, Politico reported. One ad attacked Marshall for voting against an amendment that would require the Department of Justice (DOJ) to release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The PAC’s research found that Epstein ads can sway elections three to six points in the Democrats’ direction.

The economy remained a top issue for Kansas voters, according to an Emerson College poll from Thursday. Diesel prices averaged $6.03 per gallon in Kansas, which Marshall largely attributed to the war in Ukraine. Hamilton pinned the high Diesel prices on Trump and the Iran war, which has likely resonated with farmers across the state. 

House races 

Elections forecasters projected that Democrats would retake the House in the next Congress. Republicans redrew several districts to give themselves an advantage in November, but many Republican-held seats are still at risk of flipping for Democrats. 

Republicans hoped to flip Democratic Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz’s seat in Florida’s 25th district. The state redrew the district with hopes that a Republican could pick up the seat, although Cook Political Report moved the race from the “Toss Up” column to “Lean Democratic.” 

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House super PAC, slashed $6 million in ad spending in the district to oppose Moskowitz, who is running against former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC backed by MAGA Inc., planned to spend $6.3 million in the district. 

The super PAC also slashed $3 million from Texas’ 28th district, which was redrawn to help Republicans oust Democratic Texas Rep. Henry Cuellar. Trump won the district by seven percentage points in 2024.

Cook Political Report shifted the races in Arizona’s sixth district, Colorado’s eighth district, Virginia’s second district and Wisconsin’s third district into the “Lean Democratic” column less than two weeks before Election Day. Republican Reps. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Gabe Evans of Colorado, Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin currently hold those seats.

Eight Republican-held seats shifted in Democrats’ favor, including Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick’s seat in Pennsylvania’s first district and Republican Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz’s seat in Indiana’s fifth district, according to Cook Political Report. The projection would give Democrats up to 240 seats in the House in the next Congress if they flip between 12 and 25 seats.

Republican Ohio Rep. Max Miller could lose to Democratic Ohio congressional nominee Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, where Trump won by 10.6 percentage points in 2024. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, accused him of domestic abuse, which Miller repeatedly denied. 

Miller refused to drop out of the race when some in his party called on him to drop out. Among those who called on him to drop out included Husted and Miller’s ex-father-in-law, Republican Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller did not exit the race by the necessary deadline for Ohio’s Republican party to replace him, meaning Poindexter would have remained uncontested if Miller had exited the race. 

Poindexter out-raised Miller by a wide margin in the third quarter. The Democrat reported $2.47 million in receipts and $1.72 million in spending between July 1 and September 30, while Miller raised $1.14 million and ended September with about $944,000 on hand. 

Republican New York Rep. Mike Lawler faces a competitive reelection bid against Democratic New York congressional nominee Cait Conley in New York’s 17th district. He is one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents since Harris won his district in the 2024 election by less than one point, although former President Joe Biden won it by ten points in 2020. 

The candidates were neck-and-neck as of Friday. A McLaughlin & Associates survey from late September showed Lawler leading by three points, while an Emerson College poll showed Conley leading by two points. 

Lawler painted Conley as a radical socialist on the campaign trail, while Conley tied Lawler to Trump. The district is one of the most centrist in the U.S.

Democratic New York Rep. Tom Suozzi is defending his seat in New York’s third district against former Republican New York state Assemblyman Michael LiPetri. Suozzi, who replaced former Republican New York Rep. George Santos after he was expelled from Congress, narrowly won his seat in 2024 by a three-point margin. The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC tied to Trump’s political organization MAGA Inc., spent nearly $8 million to support LiPetri, which included $5.7 million in ad spending to attack Suozzi. 

Republican New York congressional nominee Anthony Constantino and Democratic New York congressional nominee Blake Gendebien are running for an open seat in New York’s 21st district after Republican New York Rep. Elise Stefanik decided not to run. While traditionally a Republican district, the candidates are neck-and-neck while tariffs, the economy and relations with Canada remained top issues. 

A Public Policy Polling survey from mid-October found Constantino leading by two points, while a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Gendebien leading by four points. 

Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Rob Bresnahan is defending his seat against Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti in Pennsylvania’s 8th district. The cost of living remained the top issue in the district, prompting Bresnahan to call on the Iran war to come to an immediate end. About two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, which is expected to cost many Republicans House seats. 

An Emerson College poll showed Cognetti leading 52% to 48%, while A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll found her ahead by a 51% to 46% margin. 

Republican Michigan Rep. Tom Barrett is facing off with Democratic Michigan congressional nominee William Lawrence, a further-left political activist, in Michigan’s seventh district. Lawrence co-founded the Sunrise Movement, an organization that advocates for action on climate change. 

Recent polls showed Lawrence leading Barrett, including an Emerson College poll where Lawrence led by eight points.

news.title: LA LA land goes Lal? After NYC, an Indian-origin socialist takes aim at Los Angeles
news.text: TOI Correspondent from Washington: For all the attention that the 2026 midterm elections in the US are attracting over control of the House, Senate, and governorships, a municipal contest in California with strong political and electoral ties to India is challenging the Golden State -- and America’s -- reputation as a bastion of capitalism.The Mayoral election in Los Angeles, whose $ 15 billion budget matches that of Costa Rica or Chhattisgarh, pits incumbent Karen Bass, 73, against Nithya Raman, 45, an India-born socialist councilwoman whose challenge has turned into one of the more intriguing political contests of the election season. Polls show the race currently tied, with Bass, a Democrat backed by the establishment, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris, and Nancy Pelosi, clawing back from a ten-point deficit in September.If however Raman wins on Nov 3, LA will join New York City, now led by Zohran Mamdani, in having a mayor of Indian ancestry identified with democratic socialism. It would underscore the irony of two of America's most economically powerful, globally influential and famously expensive cities being governed by politicians from a movement that Trump and his political allies routinely portray as an existential threat to American capitalism.Raman's story has a typical Indian middle class template. Born in Kerala, she moved to the U.S at the age of six and grew up in Louisiana and Massachusetts, going to become an accomplished urban planner after graduating from Harvard and MIT. She moved back to India in 2009, establishing Transparent Chennai, an urban research and advocacy initiative, and worked on sanitation and water access in the city. Returning to LA in 2013, she became involved in neighborhood activism, particularly around homelessness anf affordability. She is married to Vali Chandrasekaran, a Hollywood tv screenwriter, whose credits include episodes for hit sitcoms 30 Rock and Modern Family.In 2020, Raman defeated an incumbent to become the first Indian elected to the LA City Council and went on to build a reputation for activism on affordable housing, tenant protections, and climate policy, eventually identifying herself as a Democratic Socialist. Her Mayoral campaign centers around a simple proposition: LA is a spectacularly wealthy city that is somehow lousy at providing basic services to its residents. She promises more affordable housing, better public infrastructure and a more accountable homelessness program, pointing to a nearly 50% reduction in street homelessness in her council district, even as the city's overall numbers have increased -- a jab at Bass whose term is dogged by rising living costs, infrastructure gridlock and persistent homelessness in the City of Angels.There is, incidentally, an interesting Indian historical footnote to LA’s -- and for that matter California’s and America’s -- flirtation with socialism. Long before Mamdani and Raman began making their mark in American municipal politics, several prominent Indian nationalists and intellectuals had encountered the country's radical political traditions first hand.Lala Lajpat Rai spent five years in the U.S between 1914 and 1919, establishing the India Home Rule League and publishing the journal Young India in New York. The radical humanist MN Roy arrived in the US in 1916 as a global itinerant, encountered American radicals and began studying socialism, subsequently moving to Mexico City, where he founded the Communist Party of Mexico in 1919. He later played a foundational role in establishing the Communist Party of India in 1920.B.R. Ambedkar, meanwhile, studied at Columbia University in NYC, encountering some of America's leading liberal and progressive intellectuals, including philosopher John Dewey. And Jayaprakash Narayan spent seven years in America (1922-1929), studying at Berkeley, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where he encountered Marxism and returned to India a committed socialist.All this was at a time socialism was enjoying considerable electoral popularity. In 1912, Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes, then about 6% of the national total. Socialists also held hundreds of municipal offices, including mayoralties. In fact, in the early 1950s Donald Trump’s father Fred Trump clashed with the folk singer Woody Guthrie, an avowed socialist, over racial segregation and housing discrimination in Brooklyn, causing him to write a song -- a scalding takedown of a predatory landlord -- titled “Old Man Trump" who stirred up racial hatred "in the bloodsport of the human heart."The subsequent “Red Scare” and the association of socialism with communism marginalized the movement, but almost a century later “the times they are a-changing.” Of course, Mamdani and Raman represent a different generation and a more modern version of democratic socialism. Neither is proposing to abolish private property or install a Soviet-style command economy; their politics revolve around housing affordability, public services, redistribution, workers' rights and making the wealthy contribute more towards the common good.For Trump, who has made fighting socialism a defining feature of his political identity, the prospect of New York and Los Angeles being governed by two such politicians, that too of “foreign” origin, might be particularly galling. For India, meanwhile, there is something deliciously ironic about the possibility that two of America's most influential cities could be led by activists with Indian roots, carrying forward a political tradition that some of India's own intellectual giants first encountered on American soil.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Trump’s socialist nightmare has an Indian accent

news.title: Gen Z voters feel betrayed by Trump. It's time to show it
news.text:
Gen Z voters like myself are back in the conversation for the 2026 midterm elections – and while the political class may not be putting their faith in us the way they did two years ago, there's still a chance that we can make a difference in what happens on Nov. 3.

Nearly 50 million 18- to 29-year-olds can vote in these elections. While it's wishful thinking to assume that all will vote, many are feeling motivated to show up at the polls because of economic factors, social issues and hope for the democracy that they want our country to be.

According to Leela Strong, the Newhouse Director of the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University, 56% of young people say are "extremely likely to vote" in the midterms.

 "That's not a prediction, but it's an opportunity," Strong told me in a recent interview.

The opportunity lies in the Democrats' hands. A recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed that 70% of likely voters ages 18-29 identify as or lean Democrat, up from 55% in 2024. President Donald Trump is also deeply unpopular – the same poll showed him with a 16% approval rating among this age demographic, the lowest of any age group.

Two years on from the bratification of Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris' campaign, it seems as though the party has learned a hard truth – it takes more than vertical video and memes to keep young voters engaged. In fact, we have many of the same concerns as older voters.

Democrats made several campaign errors with Gen Z in 2024

The Democratic Party's 2024 strategy was rife with errors in strategy – from the unheard concerns about President Joe Biden's ability to lead the country for a second term to the overreliance on Gen Z to push Harris over the finish line.

While the Harris presidential campaign was going viral on social media and the vice president was spending her time speaking with Alex Cooper from the "Call Her Daddy" podcast, there wasn't a solid game plan for keeping those Gen Z voters with policy proposals that spoke to them.

"There was this overhyping of brat summer and the digital game," Santiago Mayer, the founder and executive director of the progressive Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told me. "Do not get me wrong, the digital game was absolutely incredible. But you don't win young voters by making funny TikToks. You win young voters by promising them a vision as to what their future will look like if you win."

Meanwhile, Trump spent the months leading up to the 2024 election speaking with "manosphere" podcasters like Joe Rogan and Theo Von. The right poured $1.2 billion into targeting young voters that cycle, ultimately pulling young men away from the Democratic Party.

But this year is different. Trump failed to keep his promises from the campaign trail by letting the economy suffer and plunging us into a war with Iran. The Republican Party has failed to make the case for their candidates. A September Cygnal poll shows that men ages 18-30 most determined to vote are more likely to side with the Democrats.

"I think a lot of young people voted for Biden, then Trump, under this idea that they would make life work better for them, and then they just didn't see those results," Mayer told me.

Voters of Tomorrow is one of the groups that seem to be meeting voters where they're at by having conversations with them through phone banking.

"I think that right now we are seeing a very angry response, not just because things aren't working, but because this time around, they feel used and they feel betrayed," Mayer said.

So what do young voters care about in 2026?

Strong's research and Mayer's outreach have shown that young people are incredibly motivated by several factors.

It's also clear that young people – like all voters – are affected by rising costs. CIRCLE found that 60% of young people say they sometimes or often have trouble meeting basic financial needs, with Black and Latino youth being more likely to struggle financially. This can also affect their decision to go vote – it's hard to feel like civic engagement makes a difference when your material life is seemingly unaffected.

"Young people who are struggling are less likely to participate and to understand that their voice and their vote matter," Strong said.

According to a recent Harvard Youth Poll, the most pressing issue for young people is the cost of living, followed by government corruption. Mayer said Democrats have done a good job focusing on these issues.

But there are still 43% of young people who don't belong to any political party, according to CIRCLE. Strong told me that we care more about the individual candidates, particularly those who speak with "authenticity and belonging."

"That tends to resonate across the board far more specifically than a transactional conversation where you show up every two to four years and say, ‘Oh, I want your vote,' " she said.

This is where the Democrats should invest if they want to turn young people into consistent Democratic voters after these elections. They must put their resources behind campus outreach and other programs that foster community among people.

Ultimately, polling and anecdotes show a positive turn for the Democratic Party. To keep up the momentum going into 2028, Democratic leaders must find candidates who generate enthusiasm and focus on issues that affect all voters – not just niche interests catered to particular demographics.

Follow USA TODAY columnist Sara Pequeño on Bluesky: @sarapequeno.bsky.social

news.title: ‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump
news.text:
That could have been awkward. Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.

“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,” he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”

It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have actively shrugged off their party labels, eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.

Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems that Democrats do.

“Yes, we can!” chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence of an Obama 2008 campaign that now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.

With days to go before midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump’s second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign’s closing days.

America’s first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump’s autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.

“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said in Georgia. “It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it.”

For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign’s closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.

David Litt, a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: “What you’re seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you’re a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters.”

The former president possesses a rare currency in modern US politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.

“Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days,” he continued. “The other thing is he continues to live in Trump’s head rent-free. Donald Trump is out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he’s relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can’t help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president.”

That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obama observed that Trump’s gold-encrusted renovations have left the White House looking as if “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.

The comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.

Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf, accused Obama of snobbery and said: “Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I’m not that choosy.” He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion “deteriorated”.

Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager, even staged a photo-op outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging “the Martha’s Vineyard set” to sample the chain’s multi-page menu.

To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”

For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. “This is a party that spent years complaining, ‘Oh, you’re not allowed to say anything offensive any more,’” he said. “It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can’t cross.”

In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama’s remarks as elite condescension toward working people.

He said: “They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You’ve got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There’s no accountability. You’re reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we’re bombing more places.”

Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-president Bill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly, who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.

In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obama opened his presidential centre in Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.

Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama’s legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.

Norman Solomon, a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: “It’s like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it’s not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama’s record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody’s lifetime – it does not look so great.

“Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity.”

Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama’s tactical value is undeniable. “Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. In Michigan, where there’s been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it’s helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what’s at stake.”

Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.

Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign, said: “Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it’s strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.

“But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement’s momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn’t radical – it’s mainstream. It’s an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become.”

Geevarghese also highlighted Obama’s ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. “Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition’s ‘othering’ – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream.”

Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories with Zohran Mamdani in New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.

Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the DSA, said: “Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are.”

Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength. Nina Turner, a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: “President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement.”

“He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base,” she added. “Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has ‘that thing.’ He’s a force.”

“The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn’t make a whole lot of change,” said Turner. “People were hopeful, though, and it’s the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations.”
news.summary:
Former president has given series of blistering speeches to help candidates in key races – and deployment has proved a hit with party’s progressive wing

That could have been awkward. Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.

“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,” he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”

 Continue reading...

news.title: Honolulu expecting election day surge of in-person voting
news.text:
With early returns of mail-in ballots from Oahu voters continuing to lag by about 20% compared to the same point in the last midterm general election in 2022, Honolulu elections officials are bracing for a last-minute surge in-person voting Tuesday, which could once again delay the release of election results statewide.

The County Elections Division last week warned voters in a text alert that, “Long lines and delays are expected on Election Day. Vote early to avoid the wait! If you haven’t returned your ballot, do so immediately or vote in person at a Voter Service Center today.”

By law, Hawaii voters must be allowed to vote — and even register to vote — on Election Day as long as they are in line by the 7 p.m. end of voting. A holdup at even one polling site anywhere in the state delays the release of all election results.

Just as in every midterm and presidential general election since Hawaii adopted mail-in voting in 2020, Rex Quidilla, administrator for the Honolulu Office of Elections, again expects election results to be late Tuesday night despite a relatively pedestrian election season with few exciting statewide races to inspire a large turnout of voters.

This year there are no major challengers running against Gov. Josh Green or U.S. Rep. Ed Case, and U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda is facing a long-shot challenge from Republican state Sen. Brenton Awa (R, Kaneohe-Laie--Mokuleia).

Neither U.S. Sens. Brian Schatz nor Mazie Hirono are up for reelection.

Green is widely expected to win a second term Tuesday, joined by his new lieutenant governor running mate, outgoing Kauai Mayor Derek Kawakami. They are being challenged by lesser-known Republican candidates Gary Cordery for governor and Daniel Anthony for lieutenant governor.

“The bulk of our votes come through the United States Postal Service,” Quidilla said. “But we’ve had a peak of activity on the last day of every general election that we’ve run under the vote-by-mail election model. Every last day of voting has seen a spike in participation.”

The Hawaii Republican Party continues to urge voters to vote in person on Election Day as President Donald Trump continues to question the security of America’s voting system, especially regarding mail-in ballots. Notably, Trump and first lady Melania Trump voted early and in person Oct. 24 in West Palm Beach, Fla.

In one of his latest efforts to sow distrust, Trump’s Justice Department last week continued preemptive attempts to disrupt voting in Alaska and California.

The Justice Department twice attempted to separate 20,000 mail-in ballots in California it alleges were cast by noncitizens. A federal judge ruled against the effort last week and a divided federal appeals court agreed Friday.

A day earlier, on Thursday, the New York Times cited unnamed sources who said the Justice Department had also issued federal grand jury subpoenas to at least two employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office as part of the administration’s efforts to portray elections in Democratic-leaning states as rigged against Republicans.

The low turnout so far in Hawaii runs contrary to reports from parts of the mainland that have seen a surge of early mail-in and in-person voting from tens of millions of voters concerned that Trump will take further steps to suppress turnout.

Trump and the head of the U.S. Postal Service earlier this year tried to ban the delivery of mail-in ballots in states such as Hawaii that did not turn over their voter roles to the federal government. The U.S. Constitution leaves responsibility for elections up to individual states, not the federal government.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 14 upheld a lower court ruling that prevented the threat of holding up mail-in ballots from going into effect, at least for this year’s elections.

Low turnout expected 

Trump’s threats against states dominated by Democrats may be part of the reason Hawaii voters are not mailing in their ballots as usual, said Colin Moore, who teaches public policy at the University of Hawaii.

As of Friday, ballots arriving by mail — the overwhelming way that people on Oahu and across the state prefer to vote — were down 28% across Honolulu compared with the same point in 2022.

Voters dropping their ballots at remote drop boxes and voter service centers across Oahu were up 33.6%, but not enough to offset the decline in ballots arriving by mail, according to Quidilla.

Overall, the number of ballots arriving to Honolulu elections officials through drop boxes and by mail was down 21% Friday compared with the same point in 2022, he said.

Statewide, as of Friday, 210,309 people had voted, including 205,830 who voted by mail or through drop boxes.

It’s the first year that elections officials are tracking vote counts each day, so there is no comparable data to compare to previous election years.

When the 2022 midterm general election was finished, 419,363 people had voted, including 402,674 by mail, which added up to a turnout of 48.7% of all registered voters.

So Moore also expects to see voters lining up Tuesday to cast their ballots in person at Honolulu Hale or Kapolei Hale on Oahu and across the state for different political reasons.

“You’re seeing this happening on the left and the right this time,” Moore said. “For conservatives, they’ve always been suspicious of mail-in voting. But for Democrats, they’re concerned about some sort of meddling in the election or something happening with the Post Office. So it’s coming from both sides this time.”

Even if voters pack voter service centers across the state Tuesday, the overall turnout is expected to result in another year of low participation.

Voter turnout typically rises in presidential general elections, and 60.7% of all Hawaii registered voters — or 522,236 people — cast ballots in the 2024 general election race that saw Trump defeat Vice President Kamala Harris.

Charter amendments 

Honolulu ballots this year include 20 proposed amendments to the city charter that could further extend the time that voters spend in the voting booth Tuesday, Quidilla noted.

“With 20 charter amendments and two constitutional amendments, you could help yourself as well as your fellow voters by doing your homework and being prepared to vote,” he said.

Since mail-in ballots must arrive at county elections centers by 7 p.m. Tuesday to be counted, it’s now too late to ensure mailed ballots will arrive in time. So Quidilla recommends voters study their ballots at home and place them in drop box locations or drop box sites at Kapolei Hale and Honolulu Hale by 7 p.m. Tuesday to ensure they will be counted — and to avoid standing in line to vote in person.

“So that’s easy and you can take as long as you want to consider each and every question,” he said.

Of Oahu’s 20 proposed charter amendments, one of the biggest election changes could happen if Honolulu voters approve an amendment calling for ranked-choice voting for the nonpartisan offices of mayor, City Council and prosecutor.

If supported by Oahu voters and ultimately approved by the Legislature, beginning in 2032, Honolulu voters would rank up to five candidates in the order they prefer. Primary election candidates who receive more than 50% of the first-choice votes would still win outright.

If no one receives more than 50%, the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes would be eliminated and their votes would then be redistributed to their voters’ second-ranked preference — a process that would be repeated until one candidate receives a majority.

The change would likely require an extensive education campaign to get Oahu voters prepared.

Ranked choice voting is supported by Hawaii’s Democratic Party and opposed by the state’s Republican Party

Kauai, Maui races 

Not to be overlooked, there are competitive high-profile races for Kauai and Maui County mayors.

On Kauai, Kawakami’s successor after two terms comes down to either former Mayor Bernard Carvalho Jr., who serves on the Kauai County Council, or Council Chair Mel Rapozo.

Carvalho served as mayor from 2008 to 2018 and has been on the Council since 2020. Rapozo’s separate terms on the Council spanned 2002-2008, 2010-2018 and since 2022

In Maui County, Mayor Richard Bissen faces a reelection challenge from Yuki Lei Sugimura, who has represented Upcountry Maui on the County Council since 2016.

She opposed Bissen’s controversial Bill 9 to require 6,208 vacation rentals in West and South Maui to convert to long-term housing for local residents following the Aug. 8, 2023, Maui wildfires that killed 102 people and destroyed an estimated 5,500 housing units, which helped drive up rental prices on the island.

Sugimura’s support includes endorsements from unions including the powerful Hawaii Carpenters Union. Its political action committee continues to run commercials supporting Sugimura, along with commercials backing the Green-Kawakami ticket.

Bissen retired as chief judge of Maui’s Circuit Court and, as mayor, steered the Valley Isle through America’s deadliest wildfire in over a century.

West Maui voters could make history in the race to represent the District 14 House seat that has incumbent Rep. Elle Cochran running as a Republican after she switched from the Democratic Party midway through the 2026 legislative session.

Cochran is being challenged by Democrat Sne Patel, president of the LahainaTown Action Committee, and Pa‘ele Kiakona, a high-profile member of the grassroots Lahaina Strong, who’s running as a Green Party candidate with the support of labor unions.

Kiakona was one of the Lahaina Strong leaders who sat down with Green and Bissen after the wildfires and help come up with the idea that became Bill 9 to address vacation rentals on the so-called Minatoya list that were zoned as condominium apartments and had no guarantee they could be used as vacation rentals.

No third-party candidate has ever been elected to the state Legislature, so a victory by Kiakona would be a first in Hawaii politics.
news.summary: With early returns of mail-in ballots from Oahu voters continuing to lag by about 20% compared to the same point in the last midterm general election in 2022, Honolulu elections officials are bracing for a last-minute surge in-person voting Tuesday, which could once again delay the release of election results statewide.
news.author: Dan Nakaso

news.title: What Do Voters Really Think? We Asked Them.
news.text:
National polls and many pundits predict a sweeping loss for Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

That would not be unheard of, as the party of the sitting president has lost congressional seats in nearly every midterm for decades.

Yet polling has never fully accounted for the Trump factor.

In each of the past three presidential elections, polling underestimated the share of votes gained by Republicans relative to Democrats.

To get beyond statistical data, The Epoch Times invited six voters—three who voted for Republicans in 2024 and three who voted for Democrats—to join us for in-depth conversations.

The voters talked about their issues, hopes, fears, and expectations. Some were upbeat about the direction of the country. Others, not so much.

All were thoughtful, engaged, and eager for the country and its people to prosper.

We heard a lot about familiar issues—the economy, immigration, the war with Iran, Washington dysfunction—and about some we didn’t expect.

And, yes, we heard a lot about President Donald Trump.

“I voted for Trump!” Erin Mazzoni said with an excitement Tennesseans normally reserve for Memphis barbecue.

The 47-year-old wife and mother of three was drawn into politics by Trump in 2016. For her, the midterms are an opportunity to solidify the progress of the president’s second term.

“To have two years where he’s a lame duck, essentially, would just be debilitating,” Mazzoni said.

She summed up the current state of the country in a single word: “Wonderful.”

Control of the border, toppling the Maduro regime in Venezuela, cleaning out the deep state, and greater freedom of expression are all positives, she said.

Some of Mazzoni’s conservative friends aren’t quite as happy, partly because of high gas prices.

She said that’s shortsighted. Her political ideology is shaped by the differences she sees in how conservative and liberal policies affect communities.

Mazzoni described the racial tension she faced as a small business owner just outside Philadelphia and the way COVID-19 policies divided her Bucks County community.

An independent film series, Bucks County, USA, documented the health policy debate that exploded into larger battles, dividing neighbors over education, identity, parenting, and civic life.

The emotion is still fresh as Mazzoni speaks. “That was a war for about three years.”

Her family pulled up stakes and moved to Franklin, Tennessee, a Republican stronghold.

“I might have to pay a little more for gas now,” she said, acknowledging rising fuel prices. “But when I go back to Pennsylvania and see how much it costs there versus here, the differences are pretty staggering.”

Mazzoni’s enthusiasm for Trump doesn’t extend to all Republican officeholders or candidates.

She described frustration with RINOs, Republicans in name only.

Even so, she said she’ll cheerfully support the ticket in November. To her, there’s simply no alternative. She said she can reason with Republican officials about fiscal policy, local development, and water issues.

“But what am I going to talk about with a leftist?”

On her way to the polls, Mazzoni aims to influence others to show up and support the Trump agenda.

“I’m showing up to vote, and I’m dragging every single person I know,” she said with a laugh.

“I don’t care how you feel about me. You are coming to the vote!”

Ashleigh Ewald approaches politics with a seriousness that belies her 24 years.

That knowledge motivated her to begin working on political campaigns at age 14. Ewald is now a graduate student and research assistant at Georgia Tech in Atlanta.

Although she campaigned for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, she doesn’t call herself a staunch Democrat.

“I don’t like political parties,” she said. “I think they are very divisive, and I think there could be a better way of people focusing on the issues at hand.”

Ewald disapproves of Republicans’ handling of immigration.

“It is clear from this administration that they prefer a certain type of immigrant, and that if you don’t look like their type, then you aren’t an American,” she said.

“Even with legal immigration, they show frustration and hostility toward it.”

She said she believes that Democrats could do with some self-examination too.

“They’ve got to loosen up.”

She takes particular issue with the way some liberals treat young men.

“I think that they try to shame young men for wanting to man up,” she said.

She laments that even she must self-censor certain political views around liberals.

“On a college campus, I have to lock it up because I don’t want to get canceled.”

Ewald describes herself as a values voter. As the midterms approach, she’s focused on affordability and character.

“Going into November, I’m thinking about living expenses. Rent is going up, gas is through the roof,” Ewald said.

She also weighs a candidate’s character heavily and is wary of anyone seeking office who has had multiple failed marriages.

“It’s really hard for me to respect somebody who doesn’t take their own wife or husband seriously.”

Ewald has made her choices for Nov. 3 but will reveal only that it won’t be a straight ticket.

“I’m voting based on financial responsibility and economic growth, but I’m also voting on the social aspect of it as well.”

For Rowan Byrne, the appeal of Trumpism has faded—slowly at first, then all at once.

The 32-year-old law enforcement officer and graduate student from Marshfield, Maine, voted for Trump enthusiastically in 2016 and half-heartedly in 2024, and she has no plans to vote Republican—or at all—in 2026.

The movement that began with such promise has become a profound disappointment, she said, especially in the past two years.

But in 2016, it was still fresh.

“The things Trump was saying were resonating, not only with me but with virtually everybody I spoke to,” she said.

By 2024, Byrne described her mood as more exhausted than excited. Yet the border crisis was a pressing issue, and Kamala Harris seemed likely to involve the United States in war with Russia, Byrne said.

Given the options, Trump still seemed the better choice. Or at least not so bad.

She said she sees it differently now.

“After the first couple of months, it started to seem like actually it wasn’t the less bad option—it was the same option. And my entire framework of thinking about politics really changed.”

“I didn’t realize they could get in this deep.”

She expressed shock, and a touch of embarrassment for believing Trump was immune from those forces.

It felt like a betrayal, Byrne said, especially the Iran war.

“‘No new wars’ means no new wars. I thought the word ‘no’ meant no.”

“I vote principle rather than policy,” Byrne said. “I kind of went away from that this past election, and that’s where my upset has come in.” She paused. “The least bad option is still a bad option.”

Whatever the outcome in 2026, Byrne said she hopes it will bring some form of reckoning on the right.

“Maybe we'll get a shot at developing our alternative approach to right-wing politics,” she said, one focused on grassroots values from a conservative perspective.

Either way, she said she’s sitting this one out and waiting for better candidates to emerge.

“I want a candidate who is seeking to reclaim American sovereignty,” she said.

“What I mean is the American citizens’ sovereignty, our sovereignty from the billionaire-donor Epstein class.”

Character and principle guide Borchert in the voting booth, not party loyalty, he said.

That philosophy has led him to choose candidates from both major parties, including President Ronald Reagan and President George H.W. Bush, both Republicans, and President Barack Obama and President Joe Biden, Democrats.

“Both sides are lacking,” he said. “I’m sort of a disillusioned centrist.”

Borchert has worked in the metal casting industry for decades and laments the loss of high-paying manufacturing jobs over the past 30 years.

The Trump tariffs do seem to be helping, Borchert said, rattling off statistics for heavy manufacturing and the global supply chain.

“I’m encouraged by that.”

Other Trump policies are a mystery.

“Honestly, I don’t get the anti-Canada thing.”

One reason he’s able to put party ideology aside is the value he places on individual responsibility over government solutions.

“I can change the world I live in by being a better father, better husband, better citizen, better worker—by being responsible in my own backyard,” Borchert said. “What happens in Washington, D.C., is beyond my control.”

“I’m paying my bills,” he said. “I have no shortage of business.”

Yet he lamented the loss of civility in public life and said he misses the open exchange of political ideas he saw growing up in northern Minnesota.

“It’s very difficult, being purple."

Borchert said that he plans to review every line of the ballot—national, statewide, and local races as well as 14 ballot proposals in Colorado.

“I really am undecided,” he said. “But it will be a vote of conscience. It won’t be a vote of party.”

Luke Thompson is interested in politics. Very interested.

The 39-year-old from Winter Park, Florida, speaks as knowledgeably about elections and policy as about his work designing multimedia presentations.

He generally votes for conservatives, primarily because of their policy positions. He said he’ll vote Republican across the board on Nov. 3.

That hasn’t always been the case.

Thompson didn’t vote for Trump in 2016. He described himself as a right-leaning swing voter until the COVID-19 era.

Living in Seattle gave him a front-row seat for the implications of progressive policy, which he defines as protecting feelings rather than rights.

He recalled fitness centers being shut down despite a lack of evidence that they were COVID-19 hot spots. He recalled seeing people line up in front of restaurants to have their vaccination record checked.

“It’s like I was a second-class citizen in my own country,” Thompson said. “Not because these policies accomplished something practical that made a difference. It was just so people would feel safer.”

How does Thompson feel about Trump 2.0? “Mixed.”

He’s very happy with the border shutdown; deportations; removing diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives from the government; federal deregulation; and the push to develop artificial intelligence.

At the same time, Thompson criticizes the tariffs on U.S. allies, the slow release of the Epstein files, and the war with Iran.

Even so, he said he’ll stick with the GOP.

“What I want the country to be still has overwhelmingly more in common with the Republican direction than the Democrat direction,” Thompson said. “Although I certainly feel less enthusiastic about casting the vote I was going to cast anyway.”

Thompson’s vision is less about making America great and more about seeing Americans thriving. To him, that means setting aside big donor preference and enacting laws that actually help ordinary Americans live better lives.

“If either political party actually made that the center of their political focus, they would probably win 60 or 70 percent majorities for multiple elections to come,” Thompson said.

“Problem is, neither party actually does it.”

Joseph Antoniello said he is a “fairly traditional” Catholic who thinks deeply about how his faith affects his choices. That makes his political philosophy a bit of a contradiction.

The 39-year-old husband and father of three from Steubenville, Ohio, is used to being mislabeled.

“Somebody may say, ‘Oh, you’re a moderate because you’re pro-life but you’re also pro-government subsidies,’” Antoniello said.

“I don’t think that necessarily means I’m moderate. It just means I understand the world in a particular way.”

That understanding has led him to vote for candidates of both parties, but lately more for Democrats. That included Harris in 2024.

This year, his vote is driven by affordability, which has become a daily concern.

Antoniello was laid off from a marketing job this summer. He’s making ends meet with freelance income for now but still looking for full-time work.

“We’re a single-income family,” Antoniello said. “This year, even when that single income was coming in, it was really hard providing for five people under one roof.”

He said he thinks Republicans have downplayed the affordability problem.

“It’s very hard to reconcile my life experience now compared to what our leadership has said about affordability,” Antoniello said.

“It feels to me that they’re avoiding the question, or just seeing it as the state of the world instead of the state of American politics.”

Based on those bread-and-butter issues and on the GOP’s perceived unwillingness to challenge the Trump agenda, Antoniello pulled a single lever in the ballot box.

He voted for a straight Democrat ticket on the first day of early voting.

Antoniello said he hopes that if Democrats do make gains in this election, that may pull Republicans back toward the center rather than pushing them further right.

His hopes for change are modest. He said he looks for an end to the war in Iran, a greater check on the executive branch by Congress, and especially some progress on affordability.

“We need to make sure that wealth disparity doesn’t remain a problem, that our Congress doesn’t remain beholden to a handful of billionaires but comes back to representing the people,” Antoniello said.

“I just want people to live well.”

news.title: US midterms 2026: Early voting surpasses 50.5 million, Texas sees significant voter turnout increase
news.text: More than 50.5 million Americans have voted early ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections, nearly five million more than the total recorded during the 2022 midterms. The increase comes as both parties face closely contested races that could determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term.Data from the University of Florida's Election Lab showed that early voting had surpassed 50.5 million by Saturday morning, ahead of Tuesday's election.Among states that track voters' party affiliations, registered Democrats accounted for 10.7 million early ballots, compared with 7.8 million from registered Republicans. These figures reflect the political registration of voters who have cast ballots and do not indicate which candidates they have supported.The higher number of Democratic voters comes as Republicans face competitive contests in states that have traditionally favoured the party. Dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency and concerns about the cost of living have also become prominent issues in the campaign.Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and are seeking to retain control of the chamber. Democrats are targeting traditionally Republican-leaning states, including Texas, Alaska and Kansas, where competitive races could help them secure a majority.Texas has become a major focus of the contest, with more than seven million people having already voted early, as per the University data. This is around 1.5 million more than the number recorded in the state during the 2022 midterms.The increase is also evident in Harris County, which includes Houston. By Wednesday, 862,700 people had cast early ballots there, compared with 564,500 at the same point in the 2022 election, the Associated Press analysis has found.Harris County has consistently backed Democratic candidates in recent elections. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump in the county by nearly six percentage points in the presidential election. Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred also won the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican incumbent Ted Cruz.This year's Texas Senate contest has drawn national attention, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton facing Democratic candidate James Talarico. Republican Governor Greg Abbott is also seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.Early voting has also increased in other states with competitive Senate races. South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, has recorded an 83% rise in early voting compared with the 2022 midterms, as per AP analysis.In Kansas, where Republicans face another closely contested Senate race, early voting is up 34%. Maine has recorded a 44% increase, while Michigan has seen a rise of 32%, the AP reported.The midterm elections will determine the composition of the House of Representatives and Senate for the remaining two years of Trump's term. Rising prices of food, petrol and other essentials, the war involving Iran and concerns about government corruption have featured in the political debate ahead of the vote.Trump has held rallies across several states to support Republican candidates, including in areas that have traditionally been considered safe for the party. During his campaign appearances, he has repeatedly commented on candidates' physical appearance and dismissed concerns about rising petrol prices, pointing instead to the profits of fossil fuel companies.Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday night, Trump acknowledged the demands of his campaign schedule.“I thought this was it,” he said. “I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days of this crap in a row is a lot. It’s a lot.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
