news.title: US midterms: 2 days to go – what polls say as Trump, El-Sayed hit the trail  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily
news.text:
With two days to the United States midterm elections, Democratic and Republican leaders are making last-ditch efforts to woo voters, with the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points.

According to the latest survey, Democrats are still ahead of the Republicans, but several closely fought Senate races may decide which party ends up in control of the US Congress.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump will be campaigning in Iowa and Kansas, while Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate who has faced an increased wave of Islamophobic attacks, will be holding events in Michigan.

Here is what to know:

What do the latest US midterm polls say?

Democrats continue to lead Republicans by 51.5 percent to 43.1 percent, according to the latest RealClearPolling average.

A national THP/MM survey conducted on October 28 and 29 put Democrats ahead by 54 percent to 41 percent, while an Emerson College poll conducted from October 24 to 26 showed a 10-point Democratic lead.

Natalie Jackson, a political analyst and pollster, told Al Jazeera that the results reflected public dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy.

“Polling shows an environment that is pretty favourable to the Democrats. The president is very unpopular, Americans feel the pinch of high costs, which are partly due to tariffs and the war in Iran, and the general sentiment is that Republicans did not deliver in the last two years.”

In Kansas, a Washington Post-Schar School poll released on Friday suggested Democrat Adam Hamilton was leading against Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 52 percent to 43 percent.

But another Emerson College survey indicated a tighter race, with Hamilton ahead of Marshall by 50 percent to 47percent.

Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former communications director for the Republican National Committee, questioned the nine-point lead of the Washington Post-Schar School survey.

“I don’t know how it plays out, but, you know, we saw an outlier poll in Iowa just two years ago that caused a lot of damage to the whole polling industry,” Heye said.

He was referring to a Des Moines Register poll published days before the 2024 presidential election that showed Kamala Harris leading Trump by three percentage points in Iowa. Trump went on to win the state by about 13 points, a difference of 16 points from the poll’s margin.

“A lot of Republicans just don’t want to answer calls from pollsters,” he added.

Jackson, the political analyst, also said polling might not accurately reflect the result of individual Senate contests.

“In some individual races – particularly the close Senate races – we could see polling error that shifts the race in one direction or another,” she said.

“Pollsters have reported some potential issues with getting Republicans to answer polls. That might indicate that polls are underestimating Republicans, but we don’t know until the votes are counted.”

What happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

As the election nears, both parties are focusing their final campaign messages on the economy and the cost of living.

While Democrats have been focusing on affordability issues, Trump has been conducting telephone rallies for Republican candidates in closely contested races.

Heye said Republicans were struggling to convince voters that their economic policies would improve the situation in the country.

Asked whether Republicans had found a convincing closing message, he said: “No, they haven’t. That’s a big part of their challenge.”

The Republican strategist said candidates should focus on issues voters were raising, particularly the cost of energy, healthcare, groceries and other everyday expenses.

“Families are making very real economic decisions; you have to address to them what you’re going to do to solve those problems,” Heye said.

Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist and pollster working with El-Sayed’s campaign in Michigan, said Democrats were also facing questions about what they would deliver if they controlled Congress.

“The feelings about the Democrats are negative, too, which is very different from, say, 2018, when Democrats were positively perceived,” she said.

Lake said while many voters were seeking change, they were still unsure what either of the parties would do.

Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. The president had initially cancelled both appearances before reversing his decision on Friday.

In Iowa, in one of the contested Senate races, Trump will campaign with Republican US Representative Ashley, who faces Democrat Josh Turek. In Kansas, Senator Marshall is also looking for re-election against Democrat Adam Hamilton in a tight contest.

This state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming costs and opposition to Trump’s immigration crackdown have made this race unexpectedly competitive.

Heye said Trump should not have cancelled the appearances in the first place.

“They never should have been cancelled to begin with,” he said. “Whether they help or not, they certainly help Trump to show that I’m out there trying to do the things to get my people over the line.”

Meanwhile, El-Sayed is scheduled to campaign in Detroit and Southfield, Michigan, as he seeks to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in the Senate race.

Lake, who is working with El-Sayed’s campaign, said the candidate had made affordability key to his message.

“He’s very clear. He says, ‘Money out of politics, money in your pockets, and healthcare for all.'”

She said the Michigan race would depend heavily on voter turnout.

“I think the race is going to be really close. What we’re looking at is turnout,” she said.

How many Americans have already voted?

More than 51 million Americans have already voted, according to reports. Both parties have encouraged voters to cast their ballots using the mail-in system or make plans to vote on Tuesday.

But early-voting numbers do not show which party will win, because they do not establish how those voters voted.

Lake, the Democratic strategist, said turnout would be one of the most important factors in the elections.

“Did Trump really rally the Republicans? Did the Democrats come out in record numbers?” she asked.

She also identified young voters and the gender gap as important indicators to follow during the election.

Jackson, the political analyst, said the final two days will probably not bring major changes to the national political environment.

“It’s unlikely that anything really shifts in the national environment. We could see some local developments in some of these races, but by now things are pretty locked in.”

Can Democrats take control of Congress?

A total of 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for grabs.

Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to win the majority in both chambers.

While polling suggests Democrats are ahead, control of the Senate will depend on individual contests, including races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Alaska.

Jackson said the polling provided a clearer picture of the national political environment than the likely outcome of individual Senate races.

“We can be fairly confident that Democrats will win the House majority, but the Senate picture is unclear,” she told Al Jazeera.

Heye, the Republican strategist, also pointed to the differences between the House and Senate contests.

“The Senate is so campaign-, state- and candidate-specific. It’s a much harder read,” he said.

What happens next?

Candidates have Sunday and Monday to make their final appeals to voters before they head to the polls on Tuesday.

Polling stations will begin closing on Tuesday evening, with the first results expected shortly afterwards. However, some of the closely fought races might take longer.

Heye said he would be watching the first results in Indiana and Kentucky for indications of how the election might unfold.

“Yeah, I start with the two states that close earliest, which are Indiana and Kentucky,” he said.

But Jackson cautioned that the results in individual Senate races could differ from what the final polls suggest.

“That is always possible with polling,” she said, adding that the scale and direction of any polling errors would become clear once the votes were counted.

news.title: US midterms: 2 days to go – what polls say as Trump, El-Sayed hit the trail  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily
news.text:
With two days to the United States midterm elections, Democratic and Republican leaders are making last-ditch efforts to woo voters, with the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points.

According to the latest survey, Democrats are still ahead of the Republicans, but several closely fought Senate races may decide which party ends up in control of the US Congress.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump will be campaigning in Iowa and Kansas, while Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate who has faced an increased wave of Islamophobic attacks, will be holding events in Michigan.

Here is what to know:

What do the latest US midterm polls say?

Democrats continue to lead Republicans by 51.5 percent to 43.1 percent, according to the latest RealClearPolling average.

A national THP/MM survey conducted on October 28 and 29 put Democrats ahead by 54 percent to 41 percent, while an Emerson College poll conducted from October 24 to 26 showed a 10-point Democratic lead.

Natalie Jackson, a political analyst and pollster, told Al Jazeera that the results reflected public dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy.

“Polling shows an environment that is pretty favourable to the Democrats. The president is very unpopular, Americans feel the pinch of high costs, which are partly due to tariffs and the war in Iran, and the general sentiment is that Republicans did not deliver in the last two years.”

In Kansas, a Washington Post-Schar School poll released on Friday suggested Democrat Adam Hamilton was leading against Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 52 percent to 43 percent.

But another Emerson College survey indicated a tighter race, with Hamilton ahead of Marshall by 50 percent to 47percent.

Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former communications director for the Republican National Committee, questioned the nine-point lead of the Washington Post-Schar School survey.

“I don’t know how it plays out, but, you know, we saw an outlier poll in Iowa just two years ago that caused a lot of damage to the whole polling industry,” Heye said.

He was referring to a Des Moines Register poll published days before the 2024 presidential election that showed Kamala Harris leading Trump by three percentage points in Iowa. Trump went on to win the state by about 13 points, a difference of 16 points from the poll’s margin.

“A lot of Republicans just don’t want to answer calls from pollsters,” he added.

Jackson, the political analyst, also said polling might not accurately reflect the result of individual Senate contests.

“In some individual races – particularly the close Senate races – we could see polling error that shifts the race in one direction or another,” she said.

“Pollsters have reported some potential issues with getting Republicans to answer polls. That might indicate that polls are underestimating Republicans, but we don’t know until the votes are counted.”

What happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

As the election nears, both parties are focusing their final campaign messages on the economy and the cost of living.

While Democrats have been focusing on affordability issues, Trump has been conducting telephone rallies for Republican candidates in closely contested races.

Heye said Republicans were struggling to convince voters that their economic policies would improve the situation in the country.

Asked whether Republicans had found a convincing closing message, he said: “No, they haven’t. That’s a big part of their challenge.”

The Republican strategist said candidates should focus on issues voters were raising, particularly the cost of energy, healthcare, groceries and other everyday expenses.

“Families are making very real economic decisions; you have to address to them what you’re going to do to solve those problems,” Heye said.

Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist and pollster working with El-Sayed’s campaign in Michigan, said Democrats were also facing questions about what they would deliver if they controlled Congress.

“The feelings about the Democrats are negative, too, which is very different from, say, 2018, when Democrats were positively perceived,” she said.

Lake said while many voters were seeking change, they were still unsure what either of the parties would do.

Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. The president had initially cancelled both appearances before reversing his decision on Friday.

In Iowa, in one of the contested Senate races, Trump will campaign with Republican US Representative Ashley, who faces Democrat Josh Turek. In Kansas, Senator Marshall is also looking for re-election against Democrat Adam Hamilton in a tight contest.

This state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming costs and opposition to Trump’s immigration crackdown have made this race unexpectedly competitive.

Heye said Trump should not have cancelled the appearances in the first place.

“They never should have been cancelled to begin with,” he said. “Whether they help or not, they certainly help Trump to show that I’m out there trying to do the things to get my people over the line.”

Meanwhile, El-Sayed is scheduled to campaign in Detroit and Southfield, Michigan, as he seeks to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in the Senate race.

Lake, who is working with El-Sayed’s campaign, said the candidate had made affordability key to his message.

“He’s very clear. He says, ‘Money out of politics, money in your pockets, and healthcare for all.'”

She said the Michigan race would depend heavily on voter turnout.

“I think the race is going to be really close. What we’re looking at is turnout,” she said.

How many Americans have already voted?

More than 51 million Americans have already voted, according to reports. Both parties have encouraged voters to cast their ballots using the mail-in system or make plans to vote on Tuesday.

But early-voting numbers do not show which party will win, because they do not establish how those voters voted.

Lake, the Democratic strategist, said turnout would be one of the most important factors in the elections.

“Did Trump really rally the Republicans? Did the Democrats come out in record numbers?” she asked.

She also identified young voters and the gender gap as important indicators to follow during the election.

Jackson, the political analyst, said the final two days will probably not bring major changes to the national political environment.

“It’s unlikely that anything really shifts in the national environment. We could see some local developments in some of these races, but by now things are pretty locked in.”

Can Democrats take control of Congress?

A total of 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for grabs.

Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to win the majority in both chambers.

While polling suggests Democrats are ahead, control of the Senate will depend on individual contests, including races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Alaska.

Jackson said the polling provided a clearer picture of the national political environment than the likely outcome of individual Senate races.

“We can be fairly confident that Democrats will win the House majority, but the Senate picture is unclear,” she told Al Jazeera.

Heye, the Republican strategist, also pointed to the differences between the House and Senate contests.

“The Senate is so campaign-, state- and candidate-specific. It’s a much harder read,” he said.

What happens next?

Candidates have Sunday and Monday to make their final appeals to voters before they head to the polls on Tuesday.

Polling stations will begin closing on Tuesday evening, with the first results expected shortly afterwards. However, some of the closely fought races might take longer.

Heye said he would be watching the first results in Indiana and Kentucky for indications of how the election might unfold.

“Yeah, I start with the two states that close earliest, which are Indiana and Kentucky,” he said.

But Jackson cautioned that the results in individual Senate races could differ from what the final polls suggest.

“That is always possible with polling,” she said, adding that the scale and direction of any polling errors would become clear once the votes were counted.

news.title: Here's how to watch election night as the polls close, hour-by-hour
news.text:
Vote counting will start Tuesday night but could go on for days or even weeks.

While control of the House could become clear sooner because of bigger margins, control of the Senate could take much longer — the margins are tighter, seven states are especially competitive and two states use ranked choice voting which can prolong count time. Control of the House likely won't come down to one seat, but control of the Senate very well could.

As results are being tallied, here is a guide to watch election night as polls close across the country (all times in Eastern Time and organized by latest poll close time). 

To jump to a specific poll closing time, use the links below:7 p.m. ET | 7:30 p.m. ET | 8 p.m. ET | 8:30 p.m. ET | 9 p.m. ET | 10 p.m. ET | 11 p.m. ET | 12 a.m. ET | 1 a.m. ET

7 p.m. ET: Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Virginia, Vermont

To get things started, all eyes are on the senate and gubernatorial races in Georgia and Florida.

Georgia: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is likely to defeat Republican Rep. Mike Collins in the race for Senate. The governor's race is tighter, one of the most competitive in the south between Republican nominee, billionaire businessman Rick Jackson and Democratic candidate, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Despite delays in elections past, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has told local news that new laws require counties to report results within an hour of polls closing. 

South Carolina: This is an unexpectedly tight Senate race between Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after her brother Linsdey Graham died, and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Many national polls say the race in this heavily Republican state is a toss up, while the Cook Political Report says Republicans have the advantage.

7:30 p.m. ET: North Carolina, Ohio, West Virginia

North Carolina and Ohio have Senate and governor's races to watch.

North Carolina: Polls and pundits show North Carolina's Republican-held Senate seat is the most likely flip for the Democrats. The contest is between former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and close Trump ally. The last time Democrats won a Senate race in the state was in 2008, and the path to a Democratic majority becomes much less likely if the party loses this one. 

Ohio: This is the first of the seven tight Senate races on Tuesday night that could define control of the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown are deadlocked. Ohio used to be thought of as a swing state but in the last decade, it's become solidly Republican, so the close races have attracted attention. For governor, former state health director, Democrat Amy Acton is leading in the polls against venture capitalist, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who recently launched an attack ad against Acton featuring her estranged mother. The blowback to the ad was so significant, it could hurt Husted as well as Ramaswamy.

8 p.m.: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Washington, D.C.

Polls would now be closed in more than half the country. There is potential for calls at poll-close in governor's races in favor of Republicans in Alabama, South Dakota and Tennessee and in favor of Democrats in Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maine, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island.

Maine: Despite the late entry by the Democratic candidate, Troy Jackson, the race is tough for incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But Collins has remained resilient in face of challenges in the past. This is another seat targeted by Democrats to pick up, in the only place a Republican holds a Senate seat in a state won by Kamala Harris in 2024. 

Florida: Another former swing state that has become solidly red in recent elections, the governor's race between Republican Rep. Byron Donalds and his Democratic opponent David Jolly favors Republicans. But for Donalds to hold only a slight poll advantage follows the national trend of Republicans lagging behind in traditional strongholds. The Senate race is slightly less competitive. Incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody is poised to win over Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon. Where Florida has a lot of political consequence on election night is in its competitive House races. Florida is a state that redrew its congressional maps ahead of this election and this will be the first test. According to the Cook Political Report, seven House seats are competitive with two toss-ups.

Pennsylvania: For a significant portion of this election cycle, Pennsylvania has been the state with the most competitive House races — four, including three toss-ups. But as the map has solidified in the last month, all three toss-ups now lean toward Democrats. The last is a toss-up. Democrats could have a big night here.

New Hampshire: At one point, this race was quite close but the gap between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former Republican Sen. John Sununu has widened, giving Pappas the edge. Still, New Hampshire is a state with a popular Republican governor expected to win in the same election and Republicans see this as a potential long-shot pick up opportunity.

8:30 p.m.: Arkansas

Arkansas: The Senate race is not very competitive but if Republicans' margin is smaller than usual, that could show that Democrats got more votes than usual in places that they haven't traditionally won. Plus, there's a House race here that Republicans have poured money into in the final days. Not a state to watch closely but could give insight into the larger electorate.

9 p.m.: Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin and Wyoming

Another major hour for poll closures. At this point, polls are closed in more than 80% of the states. Eyes and energy will begin shifting to initial results out of Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas, where competitive senate races are at play that could decide control of the chamber.

Arizona: One of the most competitive gubernatorial contests is happening in this swing state. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs is hoping to fend off MAGA-aligned Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. This has tilted toward Hobbs at the end but Arizona is known for an independent streak in politics.

There are major Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas. Three of those states are reliably Republican and Democrats' ability to be neck-and-neck in those states shows the frustration voters feel about the economy and the Trump presidency.

In Texas, a Democrat hasn't won statewide since the early 1990s. Democratic nominee state Rep. James Talarico faces off against Republican nominee Ken Paxton, who has had to grapple with a scandal-riddled past. Talarico could take an early lead as early voting data and mail in ballots are counted but Paxton will probably start to gain ground as counties will start reporting their totals. While the governor's race between Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is also close, Abbott is still favored. 

Kansas Republicans are trying to keep Sen. Roger Marshall in the Senate. This seemed like a safe seat for Republicans until Democrat Adam Hamilton entered with his moderate message. Add to that, the Trump brand is not having the same impact in Kansas as it once did and we have another race that's become too close to call.

Republicans are nervous about Iowa because the open Senate race is a little too close for comfort. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is up against Democratic moderate state Rep. Josh Turek. Plus, three of the state's four Republican-held congressional seats are competitive, with two leaning toward Democrats. Democrats have their strongest chance for a pick up at governor in Iowa with state auditor Rob Sand. He's favored after running a very strong campaign, deemphasizing partisan politics.

A lot of media oxygen this election cycle focused on Michigan as the race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers unfolded. Republicans spent money running Islamophobic ads against El-Sayed who responded by leaning deeper into his personal story. Tuesday night will reveal which struck a chord with Michiganders. If El-Sayed wins, it will be a massive victory for the progressive wing of the party but this race remains a toss-up, even as the swing state's governor contest favors the Democrat, secretary of state Jocelyn Benson over Republican Rep. John James.

Then there's Minnesota, which, like New Hampshire, is a long-shot pick up target for Republicans. What's different here is that Democrats nominated progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan who has had to answer questions about fraud in state agencies that happened under her watch. Plus, Republican candidate, former NFL sportscaster Michelle Tafoya has run a solid race and been able to toe the line between distancing from Trump and backing Republican policies. Tafoya isn't expected to win but Minnesota could be too close for comfort for Democrats.

There are many competitive House races in this time block, including toss up races in Arizona, Colorado, Michigan and New York. With such a narrow majority for Republicans in the chamber, each of these races will be closely watched to see which seats Democrats are able to flip.

10 p.m. Montana, Nevada, Utah

Polls in three more mountain west states are closed. Eyes are on Montana, another reliably Republican state, that could surprise the country by sending a Democrat to Congress.

Montana: The state's closest race is the toss-up House race in the 1st Congressional District where Sam Forstag, the Democratic nominee and former smokejumper, and Republican Aaron Flint, a combat veteran, are in a competitive race. Another interesting race in Montana is the Senate contest. The independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, feels like he has a shot at winning the race against a Republican incumbent and a Democrat who is on the ballot but Republicans are favored.

Nevada: Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is fighting to keep his seat in a state that has been hit hard by economic conditions. Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford is the Democratic nominee and the race is considered a toss-up.

11 p.m.: California, Idaho, Oregon, Washington

At this point, voters in the Pacific Northwest, California and Idaho are done casting ballots. It could feel like a whole new election night has begun. 

California: The state has a new congressional map affecting the state of some House races. In 2025, voters opted to redraw the boundaries in the state in response to President Trump's redistricting battle to secure more safe Republican seats. The decision made the state less competitive for Republicans and the close races have mostly tilted toward Democrats in the final weeks. But in California's Central Valley, there is a true toss-up race. There are also tax-related propositions on California's ballot, including a billionaire tax. California is a slow counting state so races may not be called quickly.

Oregon: Despite Oregon being a solidly blue state, voters are unhappy with the Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek. She faces a closer than expected race against Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan.

12 a.m. ET: Hawaii 

1 a.m. ET: Alaska 

Alaska: The final state to finish voting on Election Day and by this point in the night (early Wednesday morning on the East Coast), people will be eagerly awaiting the first drop of results for the toss-up Senate race. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is in a race against Democratic nominee, former Rep. Mary Peltola. But there's been some drama in the contest. There are two Dan Sullivans in the ballet. A recent investigation by the New York Times alleges the Democratic party may have recruited the other Dan Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent Dan Sullivan. Peltola denies any involvement in the alleged scheme. 

The governor's race is also competitive, with three Republican candidates on the ballot and one Democrat. That Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, picked up a key endorsement from Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski. The other statewide race, Alaska's at-large congressional seat, is leaning toward Republicans but still less competitive than in past years. A note of caution: Alaska uses ranked choice voting and the results could take weeks — yes, weeks — to be finalized.
news.summary: As polls close on election night, here's a look at what to expect each hour and which midterm races are key to deciding control of Congress.
news.author: Maham Javaid

news.title: All the ways Trump could be more dangerous than ever after midterm elections
news.text:
With two days before the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress, Donald Trump’s opponents are praying for results that curb his powers. 

But the US President has shown a consistent ability to bypass checks and balances, and a wounded Trump could be more dangerous than ever, political analysts suggest.

This week former US secretary of state and Trump’s one-time presidential rival Hillary Clinton warned that Trump would become “more unhinged” if he suffered massive losses in the Senate and the House. 

“What I think people need to be prepared for is he becomes even more unhinged and sadly more dangerous, because as I have mentioned before there’s a concept in behavioral psychology where people who are in what’s called the domain of loss, they double down on risk.”

David Cay Johnston, a Pulitzer-winning investigative reporter and professor of journalism at the Rochester Institute of Technology, who has known Trump for decades and published several books about him, warns: “Donald is feral when cornered.”

Bad results for Trump’s Republicans on 3 November could make the lame-duck period, usually a time of winding down for a president and transition for their party, his most chaotic yet. 

“Once Donald Trump loses control of either chamber of Congress, he will become very dangerous and is likely to do truly erratic and dangerous things,” said Johnston.

Whatever the outcome in the House and the Senate, the President will retain broad power over the US armed forces, the ability to issue executive orders, and the motivation to target his enemies, he added.

Trump will dive back into war

Recent reports suggest a new US-Israeli assault on Iran is a case of when not if, with Trump hinting this could come after the midterms. 

The next campaign could be broader and bloodier, with Iran’s civilian energy facilities said to be likely targets, and the regime prepared to retaliate against the US and allies across the Gulf region. 

If escalation does not force Tehran to capitulate, Johnston fears that Trump could consider use of a nuclear weapon, as he has previously suggested with threats against Iran such as “a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”.

The comments alarmed nuclear experts. A US President has total authority over nuclear weapons use. 

“It is not beyond reason that he will toy with the idea of actually using nuclear weapons,” said Johnston. “He said he would annihilate Iran… and he didn’t walk it back. The hope has to be that American military officers would not follow any order to use a nuclear weapon.”

Trump himself has publicly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran, suggesting he could instead deploy the 10-tonne GBU-43 bunker buster dubbed the ‘Mother of All Bombs’. 

Beyond Iran, Trump has led a new diplomatic push to end the Ukraine war on terms favourable to Russia, including through coercive action against Kyiv. 

A new analysis from the Brookings Institution think-tank predicts Trump will follow a pattern of “avoiding direct confrontation with other major powers, notably China and Russia” after the midterms, while throwing “punches in directions where he does not fear counterpunches”.

That could be ominous for Ukraine, as well as potential targets in Latin America such as Cuba. Brookings experts also predict further attacks on fishermen in the region alleged to be drug traffickers without evidence and targeted in extrajudicial killings. 

Immigration crackdown could escalate

Much of the Trump era has been defined by immigration, from his campaign speeches attacking Mexican “rapists” to violent ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) raids across US cities. 

The issue is one of Trump’s stronger polling areas, at least from Republicans, as his ratings slide across the board, notes Dr Georgios Samaras, a US politics specialist at King’s College London, and he could still exercise powers on immigration even with Democrats holding one or both houses of Congress. 

“It is plausible he will focus on immigration because ICE is in his control, and federal tools can be used and shaped according to his own needs,” said Samaras. 

Republicans have strongly backed Trump’s immigration crackdowns, including theatrical flourishes such as night flights of Latin Americans to a notorious prison in El Salvador.

Samaras predicts the President could go further in his lame-duck period by targeting other ethnic groups, suggesting this could serve as an effective distraction from cost of living issues arising from the Iran war.

“You might have diesel prices going up, you might be paying more for groceries, but hey, Trump just tried to deport an elected congresswomen,” said Samaras, referring to the recent case of a raid on the house of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar.

The professor further predicts that the President is likely to return to one of his most cherished projects before leaving office, the Mexico border wall. 

The immigration crackdown has cost Trump with Latino voters. He trailed Kamala Harris by just three points with the group in the 2024 presidential election, but a new poll found Republicans trail Democrats by 24 points among Latinos in the upcoming midterms. 

Persecution of opponents 

The Ilhan Omar case fits a pattern of Trump seeking to use the justice system against critics and enemies. Former national security adviser John Bolton and FBI Chief James Comey have also been targeted. 

A Democrat-controlled Congress could put the President under severe pressure, with plans to subpoena records on sensitive areas such as alleged self-enrichment schemes, and possible impeachment proceedings against Trump and cabinet members such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. That could set the stage for retaliation, Samaras suggests. 

“I think the Democrats will start a crusade against him, with weekly subpoenas and investigations in the House. They will provoke him, and a provoked version of Trump might be even more unpredictable,” he said. 

The professor suggests this could take the form of arresting Democrats on politically motivated charges such as treason or sedition. “I wouldn’t be surprised if we saw arrests,” said Samaras, suggesting targets could include “politicians, activists, and people affiliated with the party”. Whether or not the charges stuck, they could be used to intimidate opponents.

The President is likely to take further steps to ensure loyalty and purge potential subversives within government, Johnston believes. 

Hegseth has reportedly blocked promotions of military officers for ideological reasons, disproportionately affecting women and black service members, while State Department officials claim that only Trump voters are considered for senior diplomatic positions. 

“Unless Hegseth is forced out, he will continue to purge the military, the intelligence community, and the diplomatic corps,” said Johnston.

Profiteering bonanza

Trump has been accused of using the presidency to make money through numerous initiatives, from selling dinners at his Mar-a-Lago estate to launching cryptocurrencies. The New York Times calculated that he “used the office of the presidency to make at least $1.4bn (£1.05bn)” in the first year of his second term. Trump’s son Eric, asked about the family’s estimated $1bn (£748m) in crypto gains, said the true figure was “probably more”.

Trump did not comment on the article but defended his deal-making in office in an interview with the same newspaper. “I found out that nobody cared. I’m allowed to,” he said, noting that he donated his presidential salary of $400,000 to charities. 

Eric and his brother Donald Jr have also earned windfalls, including through investments in defence firms that have been awarded multibillion-dollar government contracts. 

A spokesperson for the brothers told US network ABC that their “investment decisions are based solely on their independent business judgment and personal convictions and they do not seek to influence, direct, or participate in any government decision, procurement, award, regulatory action, or other governmental process.”

Analysts expect that pattern to accelerate as the window closes on his term. “I think he will try to take that to the maximum,” said Kaivan Shroff, a US political commentator. “As we’ve seen, his sons and himself have really made a profit this term.”

Shroff also expects Trump to “put his name on as many things as possible” in an effort to boost his brand, with the President seeking to personalise existing landmarks such as the Institute of Peace and the Kennedy Center, and christen new ones such as the legally contentious Trump Arch. 

Samaras predicts “significant numbers of pardons in the next two years” following allegations that people with criminal records have been able to buy presidential pardons.

Analysts suggest the association with sleaze will continue to taint America’s highest office and broader political system long after Trump has gone.
news.author: Kieron Monks

news.title: Smile More? USA Today Champions Kaitlan Collins and the Brave Anti-Trump Women of CNN
news.text:
Liberal media outlets like being aggressively liberal, and paint themselves as heroes for it. Liberal journalists are not asked to address how the non-liberal chunk of Americans feel they show obvious favoritism toward the Democrats and transparent loathing of President Trump.

USA Today TV writer Kelly Lawler profiled female CNN hosts on October 29 under the headline “How the women of CNN are taking on Trump, midterms and misinformation.” She began by underlining Trump’s apparent sexism:

 Screenshot of USA TODAY video

Almost every working woman in American has probably heard it: You should smile more. But only a few have heard it from the President of the United States.But that's exactly what happened to Kaitlan Collins, White House Correspondent from CNN and host of The Source, while trying to do her job. However, she doesn't feel alone in that highly unique experience."No woman likes to be told that," Collins, 34, tells USA TODAY. "Maybe it's not the President of the United States saying it to them in front of six television cameras, but that doesn't make the feeling of it any different. ... I don't ever want to get distracted or weighed down by stuff like that. We're just doing our jobs every day. When we get the opportunity to question the president, we will take those opportunities."…Collins, and her fellow female journalists at CNN − including Dana Bash, Kasie Hunt, Laura Coates, Pamela Brown and Erin Burnett, who all spoke with USA TODAY − are determined to keep going. They have things to do. And they are all eager to spread the gospel of journalism, truth and the "Super Bowl" of political reporting: Election night.

The “gospel of journalism” and “truth” is how they describe relentless anti-conservative tilt. None of these women had to actually deal with the idea that people think they are unfair. No, they’re honored for their commitment to doing The Work.

Dana Bash, who has been with CNN for three decades and now hosts Inside Politics and State of the Union, is not phased by the prospect of being in the public crosshairs. Her responsibilities are "the same," she says, "regardless if we're getting insults hurled at us or not. It makes me even more determined to do the job."It's the same strategy for Burnett, anchor of Erin Burnett OutFront. "I prefer not to respond to attacks on our reputation," she says. "This may not always be the right move [but] we focus on doing our jobs as best we can."That doesn't mean it's easy to weather an onslaught of negativity.

The obvious rejoinder to Lawler is that Team CNN generates a daily “onslaught of negativity” toward Trump and the Republicans. They can dish it out, but they can’t take it. Instead, the pretend the negativity is a one-way street, and they’re not negative, they’re just doing Journalism. They are "taking on misinformation," not creating it. 

The reporter could ask them about going too soft on Declinin' Biden, Kamala Harris, Mary Peltola, Ilhan Omar, et cetera. Instead it reads like a whitewash that was drafted by CNN PR. It continues: 

Hunt, the host of The Arena, admits, "I've always viewed my job pretty optimistically. My optimism has been challenged in the Trump decade. I'm not going to sugarcoat that. It has definitely gotten more difficult. But it doesn't diminish the importance of the work. The biggest challenge is making an argument to people that it still can and should matter."Laura Coates, anchor of Laura Coates Live and Chief Legal Analyst agrees, saying, "A lot of the time, people's anger and their hostility is misdirected, but … it doesn't mean that I am immune to criticism, and that some things don't hurt.""As a mom and as a human being in this world," Coates adds, "I'm very, very sensitive to the peanut gallery that rejoices in people's misery."

So anyone who criticizes CNN for an anti-Republican/pro-Democrat tilt is "rejoicing in people's misery"? 

Lawler performed the same whitewash Brave Reporter profile for NBC Meet The Press host Kristen Welker on October 26. When Trump attacks her as a terrible journalist, he couldn't possibly have a point that Welker is far tougher on Trump than on Democrats she likes, like Abdul el-Sayed. She asks everyone "tough questions," not just Trump. Riiiiight. 

Welker shakes off the incident, and any criticism Trump may throw at her. "I have covered him since 2015. It's not the first time he's taken issue with my reporting," she says. "I certainly stand by my reporting, and I try to keep my head down and just stay focused."“People have real questions about all of these issues, and to be able to help further that conversation and to ask the tough but important questions, it's just the greatest honor.”

news.title: Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
news.text:
He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.

Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”

That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.

“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”

Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.

The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.

The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.

‘Much more macro than Maga’

With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.

Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.

Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.

Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”

The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.

Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.

“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”

This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.

“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”

A ‘devastating referendum’ on Trump

For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.

But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”

Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.

Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.

Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.

“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”

Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”

This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.

Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.

Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”

A test for Democrats

While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.

In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)

In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.

Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”

However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”

In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.

‘He’ll do anything’

Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.

Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.

“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”

A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.

Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”

Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”

Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.

Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”

Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2020 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.

Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”

“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

news.title: 16 tossup House races could determine control of US Congress: Reports
news.text:
Washington [US], November 1 (ANI): With all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives set to go to the polls on November 3, as many as 16 closely contested races could prove decisive in determining which party controls the next Congress, according to ABC News.The 16 constituencies, spread across several states, have been rated as "tossups" by ABC News, indicating that the outcomes are expected to be closely fought and could come down to the wire.Democrats need to secure a net gain of at least three seats to take control of the House in the 120th Congress.According to ABC News, the competitive contests include Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, Colorado's 5th, Florida's 14th and 22nd, Iowa's 2nd, Kentucky's 6th, Michigan's 4th, 7th and 10th, Montana's 1st, New York's 17th, Ohio's 7th, Pennsylvania's 1st, Texas' 15th and 35th, and Virginia's 1st Congressional District.In Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, incumbent Democrat Shomari Figures is facing Republican state representative Rhett Marques. The district was redrawn after the US Supreme Court allowed Alabama to reinstate its 2023 congressional map, which had previously been blocked by a federal court. Figures are counting on strong turnout among Black voters, who make up about 40 per cent of the district’s voting-age population. US President Donald Trump campaigned for Marques in Mobile on October 2 and urged voters to back Marques. Trump would have carried the new district by 14 points in 2024.In Colorado's 5th District, Republican incumbent Jeff Crank is facing Democrat Jessica Killin, an Army veteran and former chief of staff to then-second gentleman Doug Emhoff. The district, which includes Colorado Springs and nearly all of El Paso County, has leaned left over the past three presidential cycles, though Trump won it by about 9 points in 2024. The Iran war has emerged as a key issue in the contest, with Crank supporting the war while maintaining that Trump should have sought congressional approval.Florida has two tossup contests. In the 14th District, 10-term Democratic incumbent Kathy Castor is challenged by Trump-endorsed Republican Mike Beltran. The seat became more competitive after Florida’s legislature redrew the district, putting Castor on the defensive, ABC News reported.In the 22nd District, which is an open seat following redistricting, Democrat Pia Dandiya faces Republican Casey Askar, a Marine Corps veteran. Both are political newcomers.Iowa's 2nd District is also an open seat, with Democrat Lindsey James, a state representative and chaplain, contesting Republican Joe Mitchell, a lobbyist and former state representative. The seat became vacant as incumbent Ashley Hinson is running for the Senate. According to ABC News, Trump won this district by 10 points in 2024, but the economic impact of the Iran war and tariffs on the agriculture-heavy district has made the contest competitive.In Kentucky's 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy JAG officer, is challenging Republican Ralph Alvarado, a physician and former state senator. The seat became vacant after Republican Andy Barr entered the race for the Senate seat held by Mitch McConnell. Redistricting in 2022 made the district friendlier to Republicans, though Barr remained a consistent Democratic target after his 2012 election, as reported by ABC News.

Michigan has three competitive contests. Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga is facing Democrat Sean McCann in the 4th District, while first-term Republican Tom Barrett is contesting the 7th District against Democrat William Lawrence. The 10th District is an open seat, with Democrat Christina Hines facing Republican Mike Bouchard after incumbent John James entered the gubernatorial race.In Michigan, Republican Bill Huizenga has the advantage of incumbency and substantially outperformed Trump in 2024, but his race appears to be tightening as many pollsters anticipate a sour environment for the president’s party. Trump has campaigned for Barrett in the swing district, which Democrat Elissa Slotkin flipped in 2018 before winning a Senate seat in 2024, while in another Michigan district Trump carried the seat by more than six points in 2024.In Montana's 1st District, Republican Aaron Flint, an Army veteran and conservative radio host, is contesting the open seat against Democrat Sam Forstag, a union leader and wildland firefighter. The seat became vacant following Republican Representative Ryan Zinke's retirement. Trump won the district covering western Montana by nearly 12 points in 2024New York's 17th District is another closely watched contest, with Republican incumbent Mike Lawler facing Democrat Cait Conley, an Army combat veteran. Lawler is among two Republicans seeking re-election in districts won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.In Ohio's 7th District, Republican incumbent Max Miller is facing Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union organiser and ironworker. Miller's re-election campaign has been affected by allegations of domestic assault made against him by his former wife, Emily Moreno. Miller has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with any crime, according to ABC News.Pennsylvania's 1st District will see Republican incumbent Brian Fitzpatrick face Democrat Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner. Fitzpatrick has established himself as a moderate Republican and has broken with Trump on several policy issues.In Texas, two contests have been rated as tossups. In the 15th District, Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz is facing Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer. The contest is being closely watched as a potential test of Trump's standing among Latino voters.The 35th District is an open seat, with Democrat Johnny Garcia, a deputy sheriff, contesting Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran and brother of Congresswoman Monica De La Cruz.In Virginia's 1st District, 10-term Republican incumbent Rob Wittman is facing Democrat Shannon Taylor, the top prosecutor of Henrico County. The district is among those where Harris outperformed former President Joe Biden's 2020 performance in the 2024 election, indicating a shift towards Democrats, according to ABC News.The outcome of these closely contested races could play a significant role in determining the balance of power in the US House of Representatives in the next Congress. (ANI)
