news.title: List of Trump's Media Lawsuits as Judge Tosses WSJ Epstein Note Case
news.text: A federal judge dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, delivering the latest setback in his broader legal campaign against major U.S. news organizations. In an order issued Saturday, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's suit against the newspaper, its parent companies and two reporters with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled in their current form. The lawsuit stemmed from a July 2025 Journal article reporting on a purported birthday letter sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump denied authoring the letter and sued the newspaper, alleging defamation. Gayles ruled that Trump failed, for a second time, to plausibly allege that the defendants acted with "actual malice," the constitutional standard public figures must meet to prevail in defamation cases. The judge repeatedly cited the landmark Supreme Court decision New York Times v. Sullivan, which established heightened protections for press coverage of public officials. "The costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit ... could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether," Gayles wrote while explaining why public figures must plausibly allege actual malice at the outset of litigation. The court also rejected Trump's argument that the Journal acted recklessly by publishing the article after he denied its central claim. "In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a 'fake,' Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story," Gayles wrote. "But that is not what the actual malice standard requires." The ruling marks one of the most significant court defeats yet for Trump's recent efforts to use defamation litigation against major media outlets. Pending: Trump's $10B Lawsuit Against BBC Trump is suing the BBC in a federal court in Miami regarding a Panorama documentary that spliced together portions of Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech. The suit seeks $5 billion in damages for each of the two counts listed—one count of defamation and one count of violating a Florida trade practices law. While the BBC apologized for the edit, the outlet denies defamation. "As we have made clear previously, we will be defending this case," a BBC spokesperson said in December 2025. Trump has been ordered to sit for a deposition by December 11, and the judge warned Trump this week that the case could be dismissed if he does not produce more relevant documents or evidence showing his legal team's search for them. Pending: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Lawsuit Three media outlets filed a First Amendment lawsuit in September after Trump banned them from the White House and escorted reporters off the White Houst grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico argued that the ban was retaliation for unfavorable coverage and violated the First Amendment and due-process protections. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, granted a temporary restraining order on September 24 and ordered the White House to restore the outlets' credentials. He said they were likely to succeed on their claim that the administration revoked access without adequate standards or due process. He converted the order to a preliminary injunction on October 14 to keep the outlets in the White House while the case proceeds. He found they were likely to prevail on both First Amendment and due-process claims. Kelly wrote that Trump's own statements suggested the ban was motivated by displeasure with the outlets' coverage, making it likely unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The outlets amended their complaint on October 28 to argue that even though White House credentials were restored, the Trump administration was excluding them from pool assignments in the Oval Office and on Air Force One. They are asking the court to restore that access as well. Pending: Trump's $15B Lawsuit Against the New York Times Trump sought $15 billion in damages from The New York Times, several of its reporters and Penguin Random House over reporting and the book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father's Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success. A federal judge dismissed the defamation lawsuit in September 2025. U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday, appointed by Republican President George H.W. Bush, said Trump's filing violated rules requiring a clear and concise explanation for relief, adding that a lawsuit is not "a public forum for vituperation and invective" or "a protected platform to rage against an adversary." "A complaint is not a megaphone for public relations or a podium for a passionate oration at a political rally or the functional equivalent of the Hyde Park Speakers' Corner," Merryday wrote. Rather than ending the case, however, Merryday allowed Trump to file an amended complaint. Trump later submitted a revised version, and the litigation remains pending. Pending: Trump's $1B Lawsuit Against Pulitzer Board Trump is seeking at least $1 billion in damages from members of the Pulitzer Prize Board over a 2022 statement defending the Pulitzer Prizes awarded to The New York Times and The Washington Post for reporting on Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump argues the statement was defamatory. The case has survived dismissal efforts and remains active in Florida, where discovery and pretrial proceedings are continuing. In December 2025, the Pulitzer Prize Board asked a Florida court to compel Trump to hand over his tax returns, financial records, and full medical and psychological files in a sweeping discovery request aimed at testing his claims of reputational and emotional harm. A spokesperson for the Pulitzer Board told Newsweek: “Just like any other plaintiff, the president must articulate and prove his claims with evidence." In August, the judge in the case was removed after the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a complaint alleging that the judge who ruled that Trump's case could proceed was being considered for a federal appointment. Settled: Trump's $10B Lawsuit Over CBS Interview The president and Paramount Global settled a lawsuit over CBS News' 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris in October 2024 for $16 million. Trump argued that the interview with Harris, who was Trump’s Democratic opponent in that year's presidential election, had been edited to her benefit. The lawsuit challenges "CBS' partisan and unlawful acts of election and voter interference through malicious, deceptive, and substantial news distortion calculated to confuse, deceive, and mislead the public," according to court documents. Trump's attorneys argued that Bill Whitaker's interview with Harris was edited to "attempt to tip the scales in favor of the Democratic Party as the heated 2024 Presidential Election—which President Trump is leading—approaches its conclusion." The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, sought $10 billion in damages. Settled: Trump's Lawsuit Against ABC News In a deal announced on December 14, 2024, ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward Trump's presidential library and issue a public apology to settle a defamation lawsuit over inaccurate statements made by anchor George Stephanopoulos during a broadcast earlier this year. The lawsuit was filed after Stephanopoulos said during a March 10 segment of ABC News' This Week while interviewing Representative Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, that Trump had been "found liable for rape." While Trump was found liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll, neither verdict involved a finding of rape as defined under New York law. In his lawsuit, Trump had accused Stephanopoulos of acting with "actual malice." Dismissed: Trump's Lawsuit Over Iowa Poll Trump sued The Des Moines Register, Gannett and veteran pollster J. Ann Selzer over a final 2024 Iowa poll that showed then-Vice President Harris leading in the state before Trump ultimately won it. The lawsuit sought substantial damages and alleged the poll was deceptive and amounted to election interference. An Iowa judge dismissed the case in September, finding the poll and related reporting were protected speech. In a written ruling on Wednesday, Judge Scott Beattie of Iowa’s Fifth Judicial District dismissed the lawsuit filed by Trump, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and former Iowa State Senator Brad Zaun. The suit was dismissed with prejudice, which means Trump cannot file the same claim again. A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said at the time that the president plans to appeal to the Iowa Supreme Court, vowing to pursue “a just and winning conclusion.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story.
news.summary: The ruling marks one of the most significant court defeats yet for Trump's efforts to use defamation litigation against the media.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed's Black Voter Support Compared to Harris and Slotkin in 2024
news.text: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing renewed criticism over his appeal to Black voters just days before the midterm election, raising questions about whether he can maintain a crucial part of the Democratic coalition in one of the country's most consequential Senate races. The stakes may extend well beyond Michigan. With Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to reclaim control of the Senate, the party cannot afford to lose the seat being vacated by retiring Senator Gary Peters. Black voters have historically been essential to Democratic victories in the midwestern battleground state, and even a modest decline in their turnout or support could prove decisive. For El-Sayed, the challenge is not only defeating Republican Mike Rogers, but also uniting a Democratic coalition that remains divided following a contentious primary. What the Data Shows About Michigan's Black Voters Recent polling suggests El-Sayed has substantial Black voter support, even if his numbers remain below those achieved by prominent Democrats in previous Michigan elections. A Data for Progress poll conducted October 23–25 found that 82 percent of Black likely voters supported El-Sayed, compared with 15 percent backing Republican Mike Rogers. That compares with the 87 percent of Black Michigan voters who supported Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, according to CNN exit polling. Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin received 85 percent of the Black vote in her successful 2024 campaign against Rogers. While Harris lost at the top of the ticket, Slotkin narrowly won her race despite the slightly lower Black support. Four years earlier, Joe Biden secured 92 percent of Black voters in Michigan during his successful presidential campaign, while Democratic Senator Gary Peters received 90 percent in his narrow reelection victory against Republican John James, according to Edison Research exit polling published by The Washington Post. The comparisons suggest El-Sayed could receive a smaller share of Black votes than Democrats in recent statewide elections. However, the Data for Progress poll also found El-Sayed performing slightly better among Black voters than Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, who received 79 percent support. Abdul El-Sayed's Black Voter Support Compared to Other Democrats in Michigan Share of Black voters supporting each candidate Joe Biden (2020)92% Gary Peters (2020)90% Kamala Harris (2024)87% Elissa Slotkin (2024)85% Abdul El-Sayed (2026)82% Sources: Michigan election exit polls (2020, 2024); Data for Progress (October 2026). El-Sayed's 82% is pre-election polling, not a final election result. His Black-voter subgroup comprised 67 weighted respondents. Why Black Voters Matter in Michigan Approximately 1.4 million Michigan residents are Black, representing 13.9 percent of the state's population of roughly 10.1 million, according to Michigan's official 2025 population estimates. Black voters have historically formed a critical part of the Democratic coalition, particularly in Detroit and surrounding Wayne County, as well as cities including Flint, Pontiac and Saginaw. Their turnout can be decisive in a state that frequently produces extremely close elections. Trump carried Michigan by approximately 10,700 votes in 2016, before Biden flipped the state by roughly 154,000 votes in 2020. Trump reclaimed Michigan in 2024, defeating Harris by approximately 80,000 votes. Black voters represented roughly 11 percent of Michigan's electorate in 2024, according to exit polling. Even relatively small changes in turnout or partisan preferences among this demographic could influence a close statewide race. Democratic Divisions Over El-Sayed El-Sayed's relationship with Black voters has attracted scrutiny since his narrow victory over Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan's August Democratic Senate primary. Stevens performed particularly well among Black voters and won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by approximately 51 percent to El-Sayed's 45 percent. Speaking to CNN last Sunday, Stevens said she had encouraged El-Sayed to deliver a speech directly addressing concerns among Black voters, but that it had not happened. Stevens has repeatedly said she intends to vote for El-Sayed, although tensions between the former rivals have continued over his positions on Israel and campaign messaging. Some Democratic leaders have expressed concern that voters who supported Stevens in the primary might be less enthusiastic about participating in November. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director and progressive backed by Senator Bernie Sanders, has emphasized healthcare affordability, economic inequality and opposition to Trump's agenda. He has also sought support from prominent Black Democrats. Former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside him in Detroit on October 24, while Harris joined El-Sayed for a discussion focused on Black maternal healthcare. Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock and other prominent Black Democratic figures have also supported his campaign efforts. El-Sayed has spent much of the closing stretch campaigning in Detroit and other communities with substantial Black populations, while his campaign has emphasized healthcare access and economic opportunities. Rogers has likewise targeted Black voters, highlighting proposals addressing housing construction, employment opportunities and food access in Detroit. El-Sayed has dismissed suggestions that Rogers can make substantial inroads with these voters, arguing that the Republican would support Trump's policies in Washington. Likely voters, October 2026. Figures rounded. What the Latest Michigan Senate Polls Show Despite the concerns about Black voter enthusiasm, all three recent major polls show El-Sayed leading Rogers statewide. A CNN/SSRS survey conducted October 20–27 found El-Sayed ahead by seven points, 49 percent to 42 percent, among likely voters. Data for Progress found El-Sayed leading 50 percent to 46 percent in its October 23–25 survey. A Marist poll conducted October 15–18 showed a narrower contest, with El-Sayed receiving 50 percent support to Rogers' 48 percent among likely voters. The differences highlight uncertainty about the size of El-Sayed's advantage, although all three surveys place him in the lead. CNN also found that 95 percent of Democratic likely voters supported El-Sayed, suggesting the party's electorate had largely consolidated behind its nominee following the divisive primary. Why Michigan Could Decide Senate Control Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to reclaim the chamber in November's elections. Michigan is currently represented by Peters, a Democrat who is retiring. Losing his seat would force Democrats to compensate by winning an additional Republican-held seat, complicating their path to a majority. Democratic opportunities elsewhere, including Maine, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, have become more competitive amid dissatisfaction with Trump, but those races remain uncertain. For El-Sayed, the immediate challenge is ensuring that voters who traditionally support Democrats turn out in sufficient numbers. His recent polling suggests he retains overwhelming support among Black voters. Whether that support translates into the turnout necessary to win Michigan could help determine not only his political future, but which party controls the Senate. news.summary: Black voters have historically been essential to Democratic victories in the midwestern battleground state.
news.author: Jason Lemon

news.title: Joe Rogan Sounds Alarm on Trump's ICE 'Snatching Up' US Citizens
news.text: Podcaster Joe Rogan criticized President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies on Saturday, warning that masked federal agents were "snatching up" people, including American citizens, and setting dangerous precedents that could be exploited by future administrations. Speaking with British comedians and political commentators Francis Foster and Konstantin Kisin, co-hosts of the popular politics and culture podcast TRIGGERnometry, Rogan argued that Americans should be concerned about the expansion of federal law enforcement powers, even if they support Trump's efforts to crack down on illegal immigration. Rogan, who endorsed Trump in the 2024 presidential election, has become increasingly critical of some of the administration's policies, particularly its aggressive immigration enforcement tactics and war with Iran. The podcaster is seen to have significant influence over young male voters, a demographic Trump successfully courted in 2024, and his remarks come just days before the November 3 midterm elections, with Republicans trailing Democrats in national congressional polling. What Joe Rogan Said About ICE "Most people in this country don't like the idea of a militarized police force with no identification, just pulling people over," Rogan said. "It opens up a world of problems. It sets terrible precedents." The podcast host argued that supporters of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) should consider how the same tactics could be employed by future administrations. "You're allowed to have a militarized police force with masks on, and they don't have any identification. And they're snatching up people," Rogan said. "And some of them happen to be American citizens." Rogan suggested that Americans who support such tactics because they believe aggressive enforcement is necessary to achieve Trump's immigration objectives could be overlooking the long-term consequences. "If you're supporting this, because I got to crack a few eggs to make an omelet. Okay, well, you just opened up the fucking hen house," he said. "If you're allowing that, and that's normalized in society, that's not good," Rogan added. However, Rogan also defended the need for immigration enforcement targeting dangerous criminals. He pointed to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua and other criminal organizations allegedly involved in kidnapping, illegal activities and cartel violence within the United States. "That's real too," Rogan said. "So like, support of ICE to go after that is pretty strong." The Trump administration has defended its immigration crackdown as necessary to remove dangerous criminals and protect public safety, while critics have raised concerns about due process, accountability and the detention of American citizens. Newsweek reached out to ICE for comment via email on Saturday. American Citizens Detained by ICE Rogan's concerns follow numerous reports of American citizens being detained during immigration enforcement operations. An investigation by ProPublica identified more than 500 U.S. citizens detained by federal immigration agents since Trump returned to office in January 2025. Leonardo García Venegas, a Florida-born American citizen, was detained during an immigration operation at an Alabama construction site in May 2025. Venegas said agents dismissed his identification as fake before releasing him hours later. The Department of Homeland Security disputed his account of an improper arrest, saying he had obstructed agents attempting to detain another individual. In September, two 17-year-old American citizens said they were assaulted and detained for approximately eight hours after stopping to record an ICE operation in Alamo, Texas. The teenagers said they had been traveling to a Marine Corps recruiting office. DHS maintained that the teenagers had interfered with the enforcement operation. Aliya Rahman, an American citizen, said federal immigration officers forcibly removed her from her vehicle in Minneapolis while she was traveling to a medical appointment. DHS has repeatedly defended its enforcement practices, maintaining that American citizens are not targeted for immigration arrests and that individuals who obstruct law enforcement can face arrest regardless of citizenship. What Joe Rogan Said About the Iran War Rogan also suggested that Trump's decision to enter the war with Iran had severely damaged his presidency. "It was the Iran decision that f***ed everything," Rogan said during the discussion. His remarks follow months of criticism of the conflict, which Rogan has argued contradicts Trump's campaign promises to avoid new foreign wars. During an October 14 conversation with actor Michael Douglas, Rogan said he believed Trump's promise of avoiding new wars had proven untrue. "What Trump stood for, some of it turned out to not be real," Rogan said, pointing specifically to the Iran conflict. Rogan's History of Breaking With Trump Despite his 2024 endorsement, Rogan has repeatedly criticized the administration's immigration policies. In January, he described the fatal shooting of Renee Nicole Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis as a "terrible tragedy" and questioned whether aggressive immigration enforcement risked resembling the tactics of the Gestapo. During a May podcast, Rogan similarly warned that heavily armed immigration agents wearing masks and lacking visible identification represented a dangerous expansion of government authority. He reiterated those concerns in October, criticizing ICE recruitment incentives and what he described as inadequate training for armed federal agents. Rogan has also opposed Trump's Iran war, questioning its benefits for the United States and warning about the consequences of prolonged military involvement. Nevertheless, the relationship between Rogan and Trump has remained more complicated than a straightforward political break. In April, Rogan appeared alongside Trump at the White House as the president signed an executive order accelerating research and regulatory review of psychedelic treatments, including ibogaine. Trump publicly acknowledged that Rogan had personally urged him to pursue the policy, while Rogan said he had exchanged text messages with the president about the potential medical benefits. Rogan's Influence and the Midterm Elections Rogan was widely viewed as an important figure in Trump's successful efforts to build support among younger men during the 2024 presidential election. Trump's nearly three-hour appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience attracted tens of millions of YouTube views, while Rogan endorsed the Republican shortly before Election Day. Following Trump's victory, UFC President Dana White publicly thanked Rogan and other influential podcasters for their support. Trump made substantial gains among young male voters in 2024, a demographic his campaign aggressively targeted through appearances on popular podcasts, such as Rogan's show. According to Edison Research exit polling, Trump won approximately 48 percent of men ages 18 to 29, roughly matching Kamala Harris and improving significantly on his 2020 performance against Joe Biden. Recent polling suggests that support has weakened considerably. An October YouGov survey across eight battleground states found young men favoring Democratic candidates over Republicans by 55 percent to 35 percent. Rogan's latest criticism comes as Republicans face a difficult political environment nationally ahead of Tuesday's midterms. The RealClearPolling average as of October 29 showed Democrats leading Republicans by approximately eight points on the generic congressional ballot. An October Pew Research Center survey also found Trump's approval rating had fallen to 30 percent. Although Rogan's comments do not indicate how his audience will vote, his warning about ICE detaining American citizens and criticism of the Iran War brings into focus the challenges Trump and Republicans faces in maintaining support among key voters who helped them win just two years ago. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story.
news.summary: The podcaster was seen as key to driving young male voters toward Trump in 2024, and Rogan's remarks come days before the midterm.
news.author: Jason Lemon

news.title: Donald Trump struggles to keep eye open at rally before blasting health concerns
news.text: Donald Trump paused a campaign rally as he struggled to keep his eye open before lashing out at critics amid claims about his health. The US President halted his midterm campaign rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday, to wipe his eye after struggling to keep it open. "Do you mind? I got a thing in my eye, watch this," Trump told the crowd . "Ah, that's so much better. "I wish I had little eye drops," the president added. Trump then lashed out at claims he cancelled rallies this weekend due to health issues. He said: "If I did, they'd say I was seriously ill, that there's something wrong with me." The 80-year-old has been on a whirlwind tour of deep-red states ahead of crucial elections on Tuesday that could derail his legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his term should Democrats win the House, Senate or both. While Trump has been keen to drive turnout among his loyal base, he pulled out of two rallies in Kansas and Iowa, where Republicans are facing strong challenges from Democrat candidates. Speculation had grown that he cancelled the events due to his ill health, though the president has insisted he felt "perfect". Trump's health has been a concern among his detractors since 2016. He surpassed Ronald Reagan as the oldest person to be named US President at his inauguration in January 2017, and bruises on his hands during his second term have generated speculation about his health. The Republican firebrand has declared he is healthy on multiple occasions. While Trump's health concerns have been subject to speculation, the majority of Americans have listed the cost of living, corruption and concern over the War against Iran as their leading issues ahead of the midterm elections. Democrats are heavily favoured to take control of the House and the race for the Senate has been rated as a toss-up by multiple polls. Republicans have found themselves playing defence in once-reliable red states where Trump won by double digits against his Democrat rival Kamala Harris in 2024. In a bid to stave off the worst outcomes, Trump opted not to challenge Democrats in their strongholds as he did when holding a rally in New York City in 2024, and instead has flown to multiple Republican held states in the southern US. But it has not been smooth for Trump, who has faced being heckled at multiple venues.
news.summary: Donald Trump has been on a whirlwind tour of deep-red states as he attempts to shore up his base ahead of crucial midterm elections that could end his legislative agenda
news.author: Anders Anglesey

news.title: Haley Stevens’ Fiancé Escalates El-Sayed Feud Days Before Midterms
news.text: Jason Turkish, the fiancé of former Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens, accused the party's Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed of escalating rhetoric that makes Jewish people unsafe, deepening an intraparty feud days before the midterms. The immediate fight centers partly on a digital advertisement produced by Rebellion PAC, an outside group supporting El-Sayed that describes itself as a movement that rejects “the corporate-driven status quo” and stands “against the establishment.” The advertisement shows a couple grocery shopping and talking about putting back a carton of eggs because “we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians,” before criticizing U.S. military assistance to Israel in its war in Gaza. Stevens, a U.S. Representative who lost to El-Sayed in the August primary, characterized the advertisement as antisemitic and called on him to condemn it. The ad was not broadcast but was shared widely on social media. A spokesperson for his Republican opponent Mike Rogers accused El-Sayed’s allies of “anti-Israel hate,” while the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) called the ad a “case study in antisemitism.” El-Sayed did not produce or approve the ad, however, and has distanced himself from it. “Abdul is focused on pushing back against Trump’s agenda that is raising prices for Michiganders. No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign,” a spokesperson previously told Newsweek. Stevens also called on El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, to apologize for his own comments connecting U.S. spending on Israel with Michigan’s affordability problems and to remove a separate campaign advertisement featuring conservative commentator Tucker Carlson “out of the same respect for Michigan’s Black community.” “Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens said in a statement. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.” Despite the public dispute, Stevens continues to support El-Sayed and has said she intends to vote for him over Rogers. However, Turkish said he's voting for the Republican. “Like a lot of households across America, we're a household divided,” the congresswoman said on CNN. “I still very much want our Democratic nominee, his name is Abdul, to win this race, there's so much on the line. I want our Democrats to win; I want to see Abdul do the right thing here.” Meanwhile, El-Sayed's campaign has reportedly asked Stevens not to attend his remaining campaign events, according to two sources familiar with the matter who spoke to Politico. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's campaign by email Saturday for comment. What Jason Turkish Said During an interview appearance on Fox & Friends on Saturday, Turkish, who is Jewish and a civil rights attorney, said his fiancé "has made it clear to anyone who will listen that she remains on Team Dem,” adding that Stevens' "only ask, small ask, was to say that we not blame all of society’s high costs on one group of people.” “We spend only a few billion dollars a year, and I say that in quotes, on support for a very strategic ally in the Middle East,” Turkish said. “If we chose not to do that tomorrow, that's not enough money to solve hunger in America, or healthcare in America or rebuild our schools in America. But yet, Abdul tells folks that that's what stands in our way.” Turkish also accused the Senate hopeful of using rhetoric that endangers Jewish people. “And it puts Jews at risk,” he said. “And my phone has just rung off the hook for days and days now with Jewish friends and family members in Michigan and beyond, around the world, just besides themselves, that it has come to this.” Earlier this week, Turkish told The Detroit News that he had seen what he described as “an escalation” in El-Sayed’s rhetoric since the primary and argued that it was making Jewish residents less safe. He added: “Every time he talks about genocide [in Gaza], Jews get death threats.” Turkish also told the newspaper that he would vote for Rogers in what he described as a decision to put “country before party.” El-Sayed has rejected suggestions that his criticism of Israel is antisemitic, saying his “commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own kids.” Jewish Opposition to Abdul El-Sayed May Not Matter in Michigan Race The Muslim voter advocacy group Emgage estimates that there are more than 200,000 registered Muslim voters in Michigan. By comparison, Michigan is home to roughly 105,000 Jewish adults, about 1.4 percent of the state's electorate, according to the American Jewish Population Project at Brandeis University. Republican-aligned estimates run higher, up to 130,000. "It is important to remember that no state has a higher percentage of Arab-American residents in the U.S. than Michigan. The Jewish population is less than half that of the Arab-American population there," Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, previously told Newsweek. Turnout narrows the gap, Kessler warned. Jewish voters participate at high rates, while Muslim turnout has historically lagged. In the 2018 midterms, 50 percent of registered Muslim voters in Michigan cast ballots, according to Emgage. In 2024, a Council on American-Islamic Relations exit poll of Michigan Muslim voters found that Green Party nominee Jill Stein received 59 percent support, President Donald Trump 22 percent and former Vice President Kamala Harris 14 percent. Trump won more than 42 percent of the vote in Dearborn, where more than 55 percent of residents are of Middle Eastern descent, up from 30 percent four years earlier. Many others sat out. Early voting turnout was 25 percent in Dearborn and 24 percent in Hamtramck, against 44 percent statewide. Those voters already delivered for El-Sayed once. In the August primary, he received 16,265 more votes than Stevens across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights alone, more than his statewide margin over her of a little more than 14,000 votes, in unofficial results. Mike Rogers vs. Abdul El-Sayed: What the Polls Show The feud is erupting at a critical moment in Michigan’s Senate race, one of the contests that could help determine control of the chamber. Republicans have sought to capitalize on Democratic divisions in Michigan, with Rogers seeking support from centrist voters who backed Stevens during the Democratic primary. El-Sayed has led every major public poll released in the last two weeks, mostly by margins inside the error range. His best number came from Glengariff Group, which surveyed 600 likely voters for The Detroit News and WDIV-TV from October 19-22 and found him ahead 51 percent to 45 percent. Four percent were undecided. Independents moved, too. For the first time this cycle, Glengariff had El-Sayed winning them, 45.5 percent to 40 percent. Other polls are closer. Marist University had the race at 50 percent for El-Sayed to Rogers' 48 percent among 1,185 likely voters polled October 15-18. InsiderAdvantage, surveying 1,200 likely voters October 21-22, found El-Sayed up by a point, 47 percent to 46 percent, with four minor-party candidates at 1 percent apiece. A Michigan State University Institute for Public Policy and Social Research survey conducted with YouGov over a longer window, October 2-19, showed El-Sayed up 48 percent to 46 percent among 836 likely voters. Why Is the Michigan Senate Race Important in the 2026 Midterms? Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate, where Republicans hold 53. The Cook Political Report rates Michigan a toss-up, the only Democratic-held seat with that rating, which makes it the likeliest place for Republicans to make up ground lost elsewhere. Election Day is November 3. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Steve Mollman.
news.summary: The feud comes at a critical moment in Michigan’s Senate race, one of the contests that could determine control of the chamber.
news.author: Hollie Silverman

news.title: Final 2026 Midterm Prediction: It’s Time to Die With Your Boots On!
news.text:
Experiment time: I fill a glass to the midway point with a clear liquid and put it on the table. What do you see?

An optimist sees it as half full. A pessimist sees it as half empty.

A contrarian sidesteps the premise and says something goofy and unexpected, such as “Ackshhhully, the glass is too big.” That’s their biggest weakness: Contrarians fixate on wildcard variables, which kneecaps their “real world” utility. (But on the other hand, they’re fantastic on podcasts.) 

A delusional optimist assumes the clear liquid in the glass is top-shelf Russian vodka, and warms up his liver. Za zdorovye! A delusional pessimist figures it’s probably poison, calls the cops, and grabs his gun.

We’re reached the apex of election season 2026, and the optimists, pessimists, contrarians, and delusional optimists/pessimists are making so much flippin’ noise, nobody knows what’s real anymore. They all have massive media megaphones — and Lord Almighty, they’re using ‘em!

Because they all have an ecosystem to feed.

So we’re seeing scores of articles about how the polls are all wrong, and Republicans will defy the naysayers yet again. Plus plenty of articles about the imminent Blue Wave, President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings, and the all-but-certain death of the MAGA movement.

But both stories can’t be true.

Since people tend to consume media that reinforces their beliefs, it creates an echo chamber. But echo chambers aren’t just a consumer-driven problem: Journalists, whose compensation model relies on clicks, are incentivized to report the rosiest plausible scenario — because that’s what their consumers yearn to read.

(Plus, of course, the occasional doomer piece. Every so often, a good, timely horror movie becomes a box office hit. But your bread and butter is comfort food.)

Which leads to a distorted worldview: It’s how echo chambers lose sight of reality.

Because what we really need is realism.

Hey, I love fan fiction as much as the next guy, but we’re down to brass tacks. Da-da-da, da-da-da: It’s the Final Countdown. 

The midterm election is in just three days!

And the universe of persuadable undecideds is rapidly dwindling. At this point, there ain’t a ton of ‘em left.

Which is why the emphasis is now on turnout — and getting enough likeminded, sympathetic voters off their [BLEEP] and out to vote.

That’s a critical, ride-or-die variable, but notoriously difficult to assess beforehand. Some Get Out the Vote (GOTV) plans look great on paper (and cost a fortune), but collapse on Election Day. Others fly completely under the radar, yet hit a bullseye.

I’ll just say this: The GOP has been sitting on a sky-high mountain of money for months now, so there’s simply no excuse for not having a winning GOTV plan.

If we botch this, heads should roll.

As for the Democrats’ GOTV plan, who knows? There’s overlap between voter intensity and turnout (which seems to favor the Dems), but it’s also true that DSA candidates have badly underperformed in elections. That seems to indicate holes in their GOTV game.

Probable advantage: Republicans.

(Or, instead of a bad GOTV plan, it could just be bad polls: Maybe the DSA’s popularity is, was, and continues to be wildly overreported. Can’t rule it out, since DSA success has mostly been limited to bright-blue districts and college towns. But we’ll return to polling problems in a sec.)

If you want to terrify your Republican guests at tonight’s Halloween party, the two most under-discussed, under-publicized reasons for GOP pessimism are Fox News’ ratings plummeting, and the near-total absence of mainstream media stories about Democratic operatives throwing each other — and/or the voters — under the bus.

Fox News still dominates the news ratings, but it suffered its largest year-to-year ratings drop in the month before an election in a decade: FNC’s primetime ratings fell by 28%. 

Meanwhile, CNN and MS NOW both had double-digit gains.

That’s partly a commentary on FNC’s current lineup of primetime hosts. It’s partly because of cord-cutting. And it at least partially reflects the Democrats’ edge in enthusiasm.

Probable advantage: Democrats.

The lack of Democratic operatives throwing each other under the bus is awfully revealing, too. Back in 2024, mainstream media outlets were writing about “misogyny” costing Kamala Harris the election, and how the media set her up to fail more than a week before Halloween (!) — because the writing was on the wall.

So the Dems got ahead of the story by blaming the American people for being bigoted. They blamed the media, too. And then the campaign staff blamed each other for being unprepared and wasting money.

This article from the Guardian — “Harris Campaign’s Record $1B Funds Fail to Translate Into Swing State Advantage” — from Oct. 10, 2024 (!) is a good example:

[T]here are fears that Harris’s fundraising success may lead to cash drying up when it matters most, by dampening the enthusiasm of donors to give the extra funds that strategists believe might be necessary to get her over the line in a tightening race.“There have never been so many electoral college votes in play so late in the cycle, which means that our strong fundraising and volunteer enthusiasm are not guaranteed to be enough to fully reach voters everywhere they are,” the Washington Post quoted an unnamed Harris campaign staff member as saying.Obama’s appearance on the campaign trail follows evidence that Harris is failing to connect with key components of the Democrats’ constituency, including Black men.Politico reported that Democratic operatives were worried about apathy among Black men in Detroit, Michigan’s biggest city, even as Harris’s campaign has dispatched several high-profile African American surrogates to the state, including the basketball legend Magic Johnson and the party elder James Clyburn.“I am worried about turnout in Detroit,” Jamal Simmons, a former communications director for Harris, told the site. “Do they have the machine to turn people out?”“We continue to have this widening apathy in cities like Detroit … [Harris] hasn’t done anything to change that,” added Scott Holiday, executive director of Detroit Action, a voter mobilisation group. [emphasis added]

That’s five negative leaks in six paragraphs! The good ship Harris was leaking like a sieve!

Yet we’re not seeing these stories in the run-up to the 2026 midterms. (Except in Michigan, where Democratic dysfunction is a legitimate problem.) Instead, CNN is writing puff pieces about the Democrats’ ambitious plans after winning the midterms — and the telltale signs the Dems will win in a landslide. Far-left publications such as the Daily Beast are throwing about the “landslide” word, too.

This doesn’t mean a Republican defeat is inevitable. But it reveals the Democrats’ staggering level of confidence — which is lightyears ahead of where it was in 2024.

And a big reason for their confidence is the polls. Over and over again, the polls have projected a Democratic tsunami so ginormous, it will even swallow ruby-red strongholds such as Kansas, Mississippi, Montana, South Carolina, Texas, and Iowa.

Which we see it in the predictive markets: According to Kalshi, there’s now a 94% chance the Dems will win the House; a 72% chance the Dems win the Senate.

Probable advantage: Democrats.

It’s “probable” because the polls have been wrong more than right. According to CNN’s Harry Enten, during the Trump era, polls in swing states have exaggerated Democratic support by an average of 4.1 points.

If the polls are off by 4.1 points in 2026, the Republicans will keep the Senate, pick up a few blue seats, and the House will be close.

Of course, there’s a chance the polls have recalibrated, self-corrected, and won’t make the same mistake again. The pollsters, after all, claim they’ve reweighted their polls to ensure greater accuracy. 

If so, the GOP is in deep, deep doo-doo.

But there’s also a chance that the underlying mechanisms that produce these polling errors still haven’t been addressed — and if anything, they’ve probably accelerated. Hey, when pollsters must call 140 people to get a single response, they’re not getting a realistic snapshot of public sentiment.

Because they’re talking near-exclusively with lonely weirdos with nothing better to do than yak with pollsters. And even without the weirdo-factor, Democrats respond to polls at a much higher rate than Republicans anyway.

Polls tell us what people who take polls think. Anything beyond that is a mystery. Furthermore, if only one out of 140 people is willing to answer a poll, it’s unclear if the “science” of polling is even salvageable.

Probable advantage: Republicans.

Finally, there’s the historic headwinds. The party in power almost always takes it on the chin in midterm elections. Since 1934, the president’s party has lost an average of 27 House seats and 3.4 Senate seats.

History isn’t destiny, and just because something happened in the past doesn’t mean it’ll happen in the future. As the Gipper said, “We were meant to be masters of destiny, not victims of fate.”

Until last week, the history books said the Milwaukee Brewers couldn’t win the World Series, either.

But historical trends usually exist for a reason. Unfortunately for Republicans, the midterm trend makes sense, because it matches the movement of the political pendulum.

Advantage: Democrats.

Bottom line?

The 2026 midterm races will be like a gigantic slot machine — with different combinations spinning nonstop. A handful of combinations let the Republicans thread the needle and pull off the upset.

Because a ton of critical races are still in the margin of error: If Republicans close strong and dominate the GOTV game, we could ABSOLTELY win ‘em all.

Most of the combinations give the Democrats control of the House. It’s more probable than improbable.

A smaller number of combinations also give the Dems control of the Senate. It’s certainly within striking distance.

And a minority of combinations show the Dems running the table, winning every close race from Texas through Michigan, and delivering a real, undeniable Blue Wave. That’s not the most probable outcome, but it’s a very real possibility.

So I’ll make two predictions. The first is, Republicans lose the House — not in a landslide, but the Dems will have a good night. Control of the Senate will be a nailbiter, with a sprinkling of GOP upsets and razor-thin finishes. Some high-profile Democrats will go down in flames. Donkey hearts will be broken.

But it’ll be an uphill battle for the GOP to hold onto the Senate. Could finish 49-51.

And then, all eyes will be on John Fetterman: Will he jump ship and join the GOP — or stay a Democrat? 

It’ll probably depend which on Dems lose and which ones win. If Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan, for example, the probability of Fetterman jumping increases. If El-Sayed is defeated and Chuck Schumer promises him a plum committee role, he’ll likely stay.

My second prediction: It doesn’t really matter what I write, what pollsters predict, or what the experts say.

Get. Out. And. Vote!

Because it’s not about being an optimist, a pessimist, or anything in between. Not anymore. We’re beyond all that. 

It’s about what we’re willing to do about it.

And I’ll close with poetry from Dickinson (Bruce, not Emily) about the folly of “expert” predictions:

Thirteen, The Beast, is risingThe Frenchman [Nostradamaus] did surmiseThrough earthquakes and starvationThe warlord will ariseTerror, death, destructionPour from the Eastern sandsBut the truth of all predictionsIs always in your handsIron Maiden, “Die With Your Boots On”

Folks, if you don’t like a prediction, go do something about it!

Now. Today. While there’s still time.

Because there’s not much time left.

One Last Thing: 2026 will reach a crescendo with the midterm elections. Nothing less than the future of our country teeters in the balance.

Never before have the political battle lines been so clearly defined. Blue wave or red wall, the 2026 midterms will be a gamechanger.

That means: More stories, more videos, more content, more fun, more conservatism, more EVERYTHING!

We visited five of America's key midterm bellwethers. This is what they predict for November 3

Which US president are YOU? Take Daily Mail's quiz and find out 
 By NICK ALLEN, US NEWS EDITOR (POLITICS) and NIKKI SCHWAB, CHIEF CAMPAIGN CORRESPONDENT and ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER and PHILLIP NIETO, US POLITICAL REPORTER and JON MICHAEL RAASCH, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT
 Published:15:34 GMT, 31 October 2026 |Updated:16:43 GMT, 31 October 2026 

'The Republican Party has basically sold their soul to the devil,' declared truck driver Greg Florence.
Formerly a Republican, Florence, 65, chose to cast his vote for Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton in Sedgwick County, Kansas.
Diesel is 'freaking ridiculously high,' and there's one person to blame, he fumed.
Donald Trump.
Nearly 700 miles south in Jefferson County, Texas, that explanation for soaring fuel prices did not fly with Karan Berman, 63, an administrator.
'Our gas fluctuates, Trump's going to take care of that,' she said emphatically. 'I'm 100 percent convinced we're going to come out the other side smelling like a rose.'
And, for good measure, the Democratic Senate candidate in her state, James Talarico, was a 'little weirdo,' she said.
Florence and Berman are just two of the more than 100 million people likely to cast ballots in this year's midterm elections. With nearly all reputable experts forecasting that the House will be captured by the Democrats, the focus is on control of the Senate, which will be decided by a handful of states. And within each state sit crucial bellwether counties. 
The Daily Mail visited five of them; Sedgwick County, Kansas; Jefferson County, Texas; Macomb County, Michigan; Montgomery County, Ohio and Waldo County, Maine. 

For good measure, the Democratic Senate candidate in her state, James Talarico, was a 'little weirdo,' said Karan Berman, 63, an administrator
In conversations with dozens of voters, several things became abundantly clear.
First, while Trump's name is not on the ballot, it might as well be. Voters in these counties are largely treating these races as a referendum on his leadership.
Second, Republican candidates in the toss-up Senate races are walking a political tightrope. They must avoid alienating independent voters by showing too much fealty to Trump, particularly over the Iran war, while also drafting him to maximize MAGA turnout.
And lastly, both sides are fighting an enthusiasm war. Democratic voters are riding high on polls showing them competitive in unexpected places but Republicans believe the numbers are wrong and that there is a hidden vote that will speak out loudly on November 3, as it has for Trump in the past. 
The Lone Star State 

 Which midterm races should YOU be watching? Enter your zip code in our exclusive election calculator 
Jefferson County, Texas is perhaps the best place to see which way the wind is blowing in the state. 
It is the only 'pivot county' in Texas - one of the 206 US counties, out of more than 3,000, that voted for Obama in 2008 and 2012 and then Trump in 2016.
In 2018, it backed Democrat Beto O'Rourke in his unsuccessful Senate run against Ted Cruz. But then, it went for Trump in 2020 and 2024.
Outside the Jefferson County courthouse Patsy Foret, 73, a retired schoolteacher, handed out materials for local Democratic judicial candidate John Stevens, who is her neighbor.
But she is a Republican who supports Trump and voted for Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Unlike her neighbor John Stevens, Talarico had not persuaded her to switch her vote, mainly due to his previous statements on transgender issues.
'I don't understand why he said there's six genders. According to the Bible, there's only two. You can't walk that back,' she said.
Foret was also under the impression - a myth perpetuated by Trump at a Texas rally - that Talarico doesn't, or hadn't in the past, eaten meat.
'He was vegetarian, he said, or whatever they call it, now he eats meat,' she said. Talarico has never been a vegetarian, nor a vegan, his campaign has stated.
As the polls opened for early voting in Jefferson County, the Rogers Park Community Center buzzed with lines out of the building.
The Daily Mail found about an even number of Republicans and Democrats heading in, with not one Republican saying they planned to cross party lines for Talarico. One independent said they would vote for him.
Democrats, however, claimed Republicans were shifting – in secret. 'In this county, it is very unlikely that a Republican will publicly admit they are supporting Talarico,' said Shawn Webb, a real estate company owner in her 40s.
'It is happening, I can tell you that for sure. It's kind of a smaller tight-knit community here, they want to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, but it's happening.'
Some Republicans had been motivated to vote early, not by enthusiasm for Paxton, but out of 'fear' of what they believe Talarico represents.
'Paxton is not my favorite Republican but James Talarico scares me to death. I don't want somebody like him in office, any office,' said Jim Gentry, 84.
Your browser does not support iframes.

Others said Talarico was a 'socialist' or 'communist,' and that he was trying to 'steal' Republican votes by appealing to Christians.
America's Heartland
In Kansas, the prospect of a Democrat winning a Senate seat (it hasn't happened since 1932) has actually energized supporters of both parties.
Trump won here in a landslide in 2016, 2020 and 2024, but his approval rating in the state is down to 40 percent.
Money is pouring into this race, with nearly $60 million spent so far, and the negative advertising is plumbing the political depths.
Republicans are accusing the Democrat, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, of 'protecting a pedophile,' over a church abuse scandal 20 years ago. 
Democrats, for their part, are running an ad accusing Republican incumbent Roger Marshall of 'protecting child abusers and rapists' because he voted against releasing the Epstein Files.

The most crucial factor in the Kansas election may be whether MAGA voters, who turned out for Trump in presidential elections, get out to the polls for Marshall.
Republicans need to run up the score in rural West Kansas as Democrats are expected to do so in the suburbs of Kansas City in the east.
The south-central area of the state, purple Sedgwick County, which includes the 400,000-strong city of Wichita, is expected to be key. 
'This is our chance to get rid of the corruption and, certainly, send a message to the White House - that we don't like him (Trump),' said lifelong Democrat Mike Sullivan, 66, a bookseller.
'We don't use Donald Trump's name around our house. He's just 'that man,' you know, that man started a war we didn't need to start. He is morally reprehensible, too.'
The Daily Mail spoke to several early voters who had been Republicans and were switching to Democrat.
Jeff Mohr, 65, a retired accountant, said he had voted Republican most of his life, but he was going Democrat this time around.
'Mostly, it's Trump's demeanor,' he said. 'And the Republicans won't stand their ground. I want checks from Congress on the Defense Secretary and DHS.'
Lynn Ferguson, 62, a registered Republican who works in a quilt shop, said she was now 'leaning Democrat' because Marshall backed Trump over the January 6 riot.
However, when Trump arrived for a rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Wichita on October 19, the crowd was enormous, a clear sign of Republican enthusiasm.
Michael Green, 66, dressed head to toe in stars and stripes, was in line eight hours early.
'I would like to think the silent majority, in this case, is a conservative Republican, will win this for Roger Marshall,' he said.
But in the final days a curious decision came out of the White House, Initially, it scrapped Trump's final rally in Kansas on Saturday. It was later reinstated on Sunday.
Motor City showdown 
In Macomb County, Michigan, the battle between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is also on a knife edge.
The county, which includes blue collar suburbs of Detroit and is famously the birthplace of 'Reagan Democrats,' voted twice for Barack Obama, but Trump flipped it in 2016, won again in 2020, and by 13 points in 2024.
Voters told the Daily Mail this election is going to be close.
'I'm stuck, and I know I have very, very little time before I have to go [and vote],' said Stacy Perry, a local restaurant owner. 'Everything has tripled [in price].'
Jeff Borja, a retired history teacher, and an Independent, said: 'I've voted Red, I've voted Blue. I vote policy and I vote who's going to impact me in a positive way.'

Supporters of Abdul El-Sayed before a rally in late October 

He said of Rogers that he hadn't 'seen him here in Michigan [in] a long, long, long time, and now he's here.' But El-Sayed was appealing to a lot of people, he said. 'I think he's speaking about things that really impact people's situations... I think he's talking people first.'
Borja said he had voted for Trump in 2016 but had been 'disappointed,' by the President's tariff policy and particularly by January 6, which was 'embarrassing.' 
'We learned a long time ago that the only people that suffer from tariffs are the citizens of this country that are imposing the tariffs,' he said.
Watch Macomb County as a test of whether Trump's blue-collar coalition turns out when he isn't on the ballot.
The Buckeye State 
Polls show Ohio Democrats on the cusp of wins in both the US Senate race and campaign for governor, which would make for a head-snapping reversal of decade-long electoral trend toward Trump.
In Montgomery County, which includes the manufacturing city of Dayton, it was the economy stupid. 
The county narrowly voted for Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, but then swung for Trump in 2016 by less than a point. It then went for Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024 but by only 0.5 percent over Trump. 
It's a true swing area - competitive for both parties - and is one to keep an eye on this year. 
Voters here told the Daily Mail that they too are impacted by the high cost of living. 
'I'm a factory worker and been working factory for 30 something years,' said Darnell. 'The cost of living right now, the gas prices, I mean, all the prices are just too high. I don't care for JD Vance. I don't care for Donald Trump.'
Another man called Kyle added: 'Cost of groceries. Cost of gas. Cost of everything. It's bad.'

Join the discussion

What do YOU predict for November 3?What's your view?

Voters in Ohio told the Daily Mail that they are turned off by the high cost of living

Vacationland 
In Waldo County, Maine, former McDonald's worker Kevin, an independent, voted for Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, but said he had supported Republicans previously.
'That was in the past when he [Trump] wasn't doing what he's doing, you know, insulting everybody, and I don't like that.'
Another voter, Tim, said he wasn't enthused by Jackson or his opponent Senator Susan Collins.
'I don't like either one of them,' he said. 'My number one issue is the prices of everything. It's gone ridiculous. Electricity is through the roof. I'm not a big fan of Susan Collins. She's a liar. I guess all politicians are anyway.

Susan Collins faces a tough re-election battle against Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine
'But the Democrats, we can't have that. We're going to be a bunch of communists before it's all over. I don't trust any of them. I'm gonna go with Collins only because we don't have enough choice.'
Collins will need Biden voters to survive another cycle. And those voters could come from Waldo County. 
The county backed Hillary Clinton over Trump by just 62 votes in 2016. 
And while voters in the area backed Biden in 2020 - they still handed Collins, a Republican, an 11-point re-election victory that year.
'Everything's just more expensive,' James Cox, 38, stated plainly to the Daily Mail. 
'Daily life is just like twice the cost as it was just four or five months ago.' 
That is the crack in the Republican wall. The price of a war, paid at the pump.
And the voters in these bellwether counties will determine on Tuesday whether they've had enough.

news.title: Why the Ilhan Omar saga isn't going away
news.text: President Donald Trump has his favorite riffs during campaign rallies. He’s recently complimented the physique of Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. He still calls out former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris. But in recent weeks, the president spun Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., into heavy rotation on his playlist. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department are now probing Omar for alleged immigration fraud and financial disclosure reports. TRUMP SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD GO TO JAIL OR BE DEPORTED, CALLS HER ‘A DISGRACE TO OUR COUNTRY’ "What she did was use a fake name and other things that are fake," the president groused about Omar. "She used the fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately resign from Congress." Trump argued that Democrats "just conceded her seat." They didn’t. And the president declared that "she will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body of politicians." Not accurate. The president doesn’t decide who gets to sit in Congress. Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution grants that power to the House and Senate. It charges both bodies with authority to "be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members." The Constitution goes on to say that the House and Senate may "punish its Members for Disorderly Behavior; and, with the Concurrence of two thirds, expel a Member." We bring up those responsibilities because it’s possible that the House may need to tangle with the "qualifications" of Omar. Especially since the New York Times reported that the Minnesota Democrat faced scrutiny by the Obama-era Justice Department in 2016. Moreover, that inquiry says the feds found evidence that she may have entered into a fraudulent marriage. If that’s the case, there could be questions about Omar’s citizenship. And thus, whether she’s even permitted to serve in Congress. Especially if it’s found she was naturalized as a citizen via bogus means. Republicans have been after Omar for years. Across the aisle, Democrats are concerned this could be a distracting headache. Especially if they seize control of the House after the midterms next week. THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS The inquiry into Omar began in 2016 when she ran for the state legislature. Former President Barack Obama was in office. The investigation continued into the Biden administration. The feds terminated the inquiry in 2021. After the Trump administration raided Omar’s home in October — seizing electronics and documents — Obama defended the congresswoman. "It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say," the former president said. "But that’s exactly what the Trump administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar." Obama said the current inquiry flipped her life "upside down" and characterized it as an effort to "intimidate someone." Controversial influencer and livestreamer Hasan Piker asked Omar about how her week was going amid the investigation. "It tracks for me," replied Omar. "That’s kind of what I’m used to." A spokeswoman for Omar said that she "has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory." But indications that Omar faced scrutiny ten years ago make it harder to characterize this as wild, right-wing conjecture emanating from the blogosphere. "Who ordered [the investigation] closed?" asked Fox contributor Paul Mauro. "Reportedly, both administrations had opened cases into this. We now know how much smoke there is." Omar campaigned for the state legislature in 2016. Her campaign released a letter from the U.S. attorney saying it "wasn’t investigating" nor requesting an inquiry into Omar. So was she cleared? Or does word of the old probe pour petrol on the flames? "Omar will talk about and say, ‘They've looked into this. Nothing came about it,’" said University of Minnesota political science professor Kathryn Pearson. "But I think it's also a talking point that Republicans will use. So I think sort of both sides will try to use that to their advantage." John Nagel is Omar’s Republican opponent on the ballot next week. Nagel views the new investigation as a political wedge. "With the raid on her home, people should keep this in mind. It's a very serious accusation," Nagel said. "As far as I'm concerned, Somalia comes first in her life. And we are nothing more than a piggy bank for her." TRUMP PUSH TO OUST OMAR FACES HISTORIC SUPREME COURT TEST, BUT LEGAL EXPERTS SEE ‘UNCHARTED’ TWIST At least one Republican is ready to bounce Omar from the House. "If the evidence shows that she is not an American, she has to be removed immediately and probably put in prison," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "I think the idea that a foreigner might be actually serving in Congress should be terrifying to Americans." But another House Republican urges caution. "We just need all the facts," said Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J. "I hope that the investigation is thorough, fair, and absolutely aboveboard." And then there is the question of due process. "The Ethics Committee should commence an investigation. It takes two-thirds of the House to expel a sitting Member. I would highly doubt the Democrats would agree. And certainly not without findings," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox. "I think at a minimum, the Ethics Committee should move forward with an investigation immediately upon our return." This could develop into a real hornet’s nest for the House when lawmakers descend on Washington after the midterms. That’s to say nothing of questions about seating Omar when the new Congress starts in January. If Democrats win the House, would House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. — perhaps as speaker — be forced to grapple with the question of seating Omar if Republicans move to exclude her? In fact, such a motion to exclude comes right before the new speaker swears in the entire House on Jan. 3. The speaker would swear in 434 members. Then takes votes related to the potential member in question. If Democrats win the House, new, moderate House Democrats might take their first formal floor vote on whether to seat Omar. Voting against Omar might be good for some of these new members, considering the political nature of their battleground districts. But would the Democratic brass pressure new members to vote with the caucus on such a nettlesome issue? Democrats who vote to seat Omar give Republicans an immediate opportunity to build a case against newly-christened members representing swing districts. A vote to exclude or expel Omar would go down as one of the most important roll calls of the entire two-year Congress. We haven’t even explored how progressives and Democratic Socialists — new to the House — might rage at moderate Democrats for not supporting their colleague. That could produce a serious schism among Democrats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This isn’t going away. Omar is a lightning rod. The GOP believes it can continue to milk this. President Trump has his favorite riffs about Omar. And it’s possible that House Republicans may as well.
news.summary: Trump claims Ilhan Omar must resign from Congress over alleged immigration fraud, but the Constitution grants that power solely to the House itself.
news.author: Chad Pergram

news.title: Kamala Harris urges a ‘too big to rig’ turnout for the midterms and tees off on Trump
news.text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Two years after Kamala Harris lost the presidential election to Donald Trump, she still delights Democratic donors and activists with jabs against him, saying the Republican is “callous, corrupt and incompetent” and calling him the “decorator in chief” for his White House renovations and gold adornments.

But the former vice president also has plenty to say about what her party, the electorate and the country should do next as she also considers whether to run again.

“This is the moment where we turn that anger into action,” Harris said more than once during a busy schedule in the final stretch of the midterm campaign.

Harris campaigned for candidates across seven states, ending with a recent two-day visit to Georgia. It was, in parts, the kind of nostalgic tour seen from Barack Obama and Bill Clinton — two-term presidents whose last campaigns are behind them — and the barnstorming from potential future contenders such as Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky or U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

As the first Black woman elected to nationwide office, Harris urged fellow Black Americans to “honor the ancestors” with their votes but she also has become unapologetically “transactional” by demanding more from politicians.

Harris, a California senator before joining Joe Biden on the 2020 ticket, also pushed fellow Democrats to govern aggressively and she called for “structural work” that she said was necessary to reinvigorate American democracy: U.S. Supreme Court expansion, statehood for the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, and reconsideration of the Electoral College.

“I think she’s hitting all the right notes,” said Melinda Johnson, a retired nurse who attended a Fulton County Democratic Party fundraising gala that Harris headlined in Atlanta.

Harris made it to early presidential primary states, including Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan. She also went to Mississippi, not exactly a hotbed of presidential politics, on behalf of U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom.

“The South is in play,” she said. “When Democrats invest in the South, we can win in the South.”

In Georgia, Harris delved into civil rights history as she accused the U.S. Supreme Court of “backdoor racism” with its decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and allow Republicans to redraw boundaries for congressional districts that now elect nonwhite lawmakers.

“Ruthlessness” is key, she said at the Democratic dinner in Atlanta. “Not ruthlessness in the sense of cruelty … but in our willingness to use our power to deliver on our commitments.” Democrats, she said, “can no longer let process stand in the way of progress.”

Throughout her stops, Harris nodded implicitly at her loss to Trump.

“You know we’ve been spending the last year and a half, so many of us, going through a range of emotions,” she told students. “Anger, depression, sadness, frustration, a sense of helplessness and powerlessness.”

Warning that Trump could try to meddle in Tuesday’s election, she echoed one of the president’s own mantras to encourage people to vote.

“In this case,” she said at Atlanta’s Elizabeth Baptist Church, “we just need to turn out in really large numbers that would be too big to rig.”
