news.title: U.S.-Canada tensions may not change, despite U.S. midterm results
news.text: DETROIT — Democrats are hoping Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them the power to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump — but Canadians hoping for an outcome that stabilizes the rocky bilateral relationship may be disappointed. Once-safe Republican seats are now in peril and control of Congress could flip. Trump’s poll numbers are plummeting thanks to his unpopular war in Iran, rising energy prices and inflation. Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority. The future of the Senate is less clear. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and some polling shows that is within reach. Even if Democrats gain control of both chambers, Trump will still be president, said Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont. Presidents have a lot of power over foreign policy and Trump — unhappy with being seen as a lame duck in the final stretch of his term — may be even more motivated to use it. Lebo said that could make Trump more “erratic” and “dangerous.” “It’s not clear how much the Democratic Senate will push back on him or can push back,” Lebo said. The size of the expected Democrat win will be an important factor, Lebo added. Numerous reports suggest Republicans are worried about bleeding seats as contests in places Trump dominated in 2024, like Kansas and Ohio, become competitive. Congress has control over tariffs and taxes but Republican lawmakers have largely given Trump a free hand to deploy tariffs worldwide. If the midterms demonstrate that the president has lost his hold over loyal voters, GOP members may be more inclined to break with Trump, Lebo said. But a large number of Republicans would have to join with Democrats to secure the supermajority needed to bypass presidential veto power and overturn Trump’s tariffs. And many observers question whether Democrats are looking to return to a pre-Trump era in trade policy. Trump’s first administration demonstrated how vulnerable Canada is to American whims when the president scrapped the North American Free Trade Agreement. It was replaced with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as CUSMA. Former Democrat vice-president Kamala Harris and current Democrat Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer were among the Democrats who voted against the trilateral agreement. President Joe Biden brought more stability to the Canada-U.S. relationship but not much change. He kept many of Trump’s first term tariffs in place, despite promises to reverse them, and expanded other protectionist policies. “What Canadians have learned in the last few years is we don’t trust Americans to correct course when they can in terms of the presidency,” Lebo said. While Trump’s first term rattled the bilateral relationship, his second term blew it up. Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation. Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed. Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. The trade war is deeply unpopular in states like Michigan and Maine, where tight Senate races ultimately could decide which party gains congressional control. But even if Democrats emerge triumphant next week, or win the White House in 2028, it’s not clear that Trump’s tariff wall would suddenly drop. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is considering a run for president, told CTV in August that he couldn’t guarantee Trump’s tariff policies would be reversed under Democratic leadership. One factor Democrats likely are considering is how to deal with the United States’ $40-trillion debt problem. Trump has argued tariffs bring in much-needed revenue — although they have yet to make much of a dent in the U.S. balance sheet. Democrats have not said how they plan to deal with the problem. Vermont Democrat Sen. Peter Welch, who was in Montreal this week, vowed to repeal the tariffs on Canada. Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said Democrats traditionally have been more protectionist than Republicans and he could see the party maintaining a baseline tariff wall. What that means for the future of CUSMA is not clear. The Trump administration did not renew the trilateral agreement earlier this year, triggering an annual rolling review for up to 10 years. Once that period ends, and if the partners haven’t agreed to an extension at that point, the agreement would expire. Sands said as long as the United States doesn’t walk away from CUSMA, there’s still room to negotiate. “You just want to hang on to that and hope that in a different environment, you can have a conversation about keeping it,” he said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026. Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press
news.author: The Canadian Press

news.title: Black voters were upset with James Talarico. What he did about it could decide the Senate.
news.text:
James Talarico had a problem, and he didn’t need me to tell him what it was. The unassuming state lawmaker had beaten U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett in a Democratic Senate primary that their supporters had turned nasty, even as the candidates mostly stayed above the fray.

Now here he was months later, a white man needing to endear himself to Black voters still raw over what happened on the way to Crockett’s loss. Worse, they had grown even more disenchanted by what they considered a lack of outreach from his team since he’d won. And they didn’t see his campaign spending any money to try to make it right.

Crockett gave him a lukewarm endorsement but wouldn’t give him the time of day, much less campaign with him.

The Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas had Talarico as the general election choice of 67% of the state’s 3 million Black voters. In a long-red state with 19 million registered voters, that was nowhere close to the kind of overwhelming support from that demographic it would take for him to defeat state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee.

As we walked in the middle — not at the front — of hundreds of people taking part in Opal’s Walk for Freedom, the symbolic 2.5-mile Juneteenth march that Dr. Opal Lee had turned into a Fort Worth institution, there could be no doubt about it: James Talarico had a problem.

And he could not have seemed less bothered by it, despite the rain.

Texas Senate candidate James Talarico meets voters and participates in the Opal’s Walk for Freedom event in Ft. Worth, TX on June 19, 2026.

“It’s nice to show up to things and not have to be the center of attention,” he told me. “To just be there as a supporter, as a cheerleader. Because I feel like that’s kind of the spirit we have to get back to in our politics.”

You get used to answers like that the more time you spend around or listening to Talarico. It’s a tone that often feels out of place in today’s aggressive politics. It’s the tenor of a man who has been a seminarian and a teacher.

One could argue that demeanor is one of the reasons that Talarico has the best chance in decades to do something no Democrat has done since 1988 — win a Senate seat in Texas.

By October, that same Texas Politics Project poll had him at 79% among Black voters. Overall, polling averages compiled by MS NOW partner FiftyPlusOne show him with a 3.5-point lead over Paxton with days to go — even better numbers, as Talarico modestly noted, than Beto O'Rourke ever managed in his ballyhooed but unsuccessful 2018 challenge to Sen. Ted Cruz.

Yet still a sign of a contest close enough that Black voters could swing it.

The story of how Talarico took his problem and met it head-on is a story of old-school pounding the pavement, modern campaigning via influencers, and yes, money. But it’s also a story of the power of that rarest of political traits: humility. It could turn out to be the story of the 2026 midterms.

A rough spring

Representative Jasmine Crockett speaks during a Texas primary election night event in Dallas, TX, on March 3, 2026.

In June what was clear was that the Black voter problem that Talarico had was not entirely of his own making.

The ugliness of the primary, most of it online, eventually bled into the real world, something rare in campaigns. Black Texans were largely behind Crockett, a two-term member who had quickly become a national figure. And the people who had gone all in for her, especially the Black women who make up the backbone of Democratic turnout in Dallas and Houston, were left feeling like it was 2024 all over again (particularly after Crockett got a last-minute endorsement from former Vice President Kamala Harris).

The day before I walked with Talarico, I sat down in a Dallas art gallery with two of the most influential political content creators in Texas, Camille McCallum and Olive Okoro, both Black women who backed Crockett in the primary. Between the two of them and the roughly 40 other online creators who had been in Crockett’s orbit, they could reach millions of followers. Both told me they would hold their noses and vote for Talarico.

Their concern was that millions of Black Texans wouldn’t be doing the same.

Olive Okoro (left) and Camille MacCallum speaking to MS NOW on June 18, 2026.

“Jasmine Crockett spoke to Black Texans,” Okoro said. “She didn’t change how she spoke. And it put a lot of people there like, ‘I can see myself being like her. I can see somebody who looks like me on the political floor, who’s talking the way I am.’”

McCallum’s frustration was more specific. She had been on the bus Crockett organized to take people from Dallas to Austin to testify against the new congressional maps Republicans drew up at President Donald Trump’s behest. She’d seen the fight up close.

And then she’d watched supporters of Talarico throw racist and sexist attacks online.

“There were friends of mine that were harmed in the whole stan culture with the Talarico campaign people, and that wasn’t James Talarico himself hurling insults,” she said. “But you know, even Beyoncé sometimes tells the Beyhive to calm down.”

Crockett endorsed Talarico the morning after the primary, and for Okoro and McCallum, the message they were receiving was to join the team they spent months trying to defeat. It immediately had McCallum feeling taken for granted, even knowing she was going to vote for Talarico.

“What am I going to do, get Ken Paxton elected? Definitely not,” she told me then. “But at the same time, why is no olive branch being extended?”

At this point, neither of them had heard from the Talarico campaign. Not a call, not a text, not a DM.

“No,” Okoro said. “Which is so crazy!”

It wasn’t that they wanted to be courted for its own sake. It was that they read the silence as strategy. McCallum laid it out as plainly as anyone about the Democratic Party’s simmering Black voter issue:

“From where I am sitting, it feels very much like ‘we have our Democrat core, and then we’re going to get these flip people, the people who may flip-flop in elections, Republicans who are not MAGA,’” she said. “And in that strategy, Black people get lost. As kind of a nonpriority, or kind of like a safe bet. Like, ‘Well, the Black folks that been voting since 1965, they’re still going to be voting in 2026.’”

For Talarico, she had one message: “Make me feel like a priority. Because I was going to show up for you anyway, but I’m trying to help you.”

I showed Talarico the message McCallum had for him at a Black-owned coffee shop in Fort Worth, after the walk and still a little damp. He watched the whole thing. First, he made the point that it’s a false choice between mobilizing disillusioned voters and peeling off Republicans, and that he had done both when he flipped a Trump district for the state House.

But he also conceded her premise: “I think Black Texans have felt that they’ve been taken advantage of by the Democratic Party.”

Is it a feeling, or is it an actual fact?

“That feeling reflects a truth,” he said. “The Democratic Party, certainly nationally, has just assumed that Black people are a part of the Democratic base. You hear that all the time, right? And a base implies those are people who will never leave you. And that is such a harmful way to think about voters.

“And I will tell you, as someone who has been in tough elections, it is the fastest way to lose an election, is to take voters for granted. To assume Black folks are going to show up and vote for you because you have a D by your name. We have to stop doing that. We have to start treating Black voters as swing voters.”

So what was he doing to put his words into action, specifically, right then, in June? “We are building it by the day,” he said. Faith leaders, visits to historically Black colleges and universities, a volunteer army of 45,000 and growing.

On Crockett, he said they had exchanged messages in March and April, and that he’d left her a voicemail a few weeks earlier inviting her to deliver the keynote at the state convention. She told the Dallas Morning News around the same time that she hadn’t returned the call or listened to the message, and that she had “no idea” whether she would campaign for him.

I told him that I had been told over and over, by pollsters and by Black Texans, that it was hard to see a path for him without an active Crockett on the trail.

“I feel like what’s happening in Texas is so much bigger than any one politician, including me,” he said. “I honestly don’t think it depends on me or any politician. It’s really going to come down to the people of Texas.”

However, he acknowledged, “As the nominee, this is on me to bring the coalition back together.”

A month later, an event in Houston would test exactly how much he meant it.

Hot temps in Houston

Voters wait to ask questions of Talarico at Kingdom Builders Center in Houston on July 19, 2026.

On July 19, Talarico walked into the Kingdom Builders’ Center in Houston for a town hall that was, by design, a room full of Black voters who had hard questions. Crockett’s home turf is Dallas but the primary wounds were just as raw in Houston, with its half-million Black residents. And a Houston state representative, Jolanda Jones, had been publicly saying he wouldn't return her calls.

The questions came fast. Voting rights, Black farmers, diversity initiatives, Black campaign staffers, downballot Black candidates. About 45 minutes in, his staff tried to cut it off at one more question. That’s when Kandice Webber stood up.

“You cannot win without us,” she told Talarico, her voice raised. “So you stay here and you answer our questions, or you suffer the consequences!”

He stayed, for about 20 more minutes. Another woman, Juli McShay, asked him to rebuke the supporters who had harassed Crockett and other Black influencers online, and he did it right there in the room.

“Please keep Congresswoman Crockett’s name out of your mouth,” Talarico said, and demanded that his people treat his former opponent with respect.

It was that Beyhive moment McCallum was looking for.

That night, Talarico pledged to spend $25 million on Black voter outreach, something his campaign called the largest such investment in modern Texas history. “I’m committing to you here that we will be putting resources where our mouth is,” he said.

Spending money and showing up

Talarico shakes hands with people on the sideline during the first half of the State Fair Classic at the State Fair of Texas on Sept. 26, 2026, in Dallas.

By September the campaign was spending the money earnestly. It hired three veteran Black Texas operatives to run the outreach program. It brought on Black-owned firms. It bought ads in legacy Black media like Dallas Weekly and The Houston Defender and joined podcasts that younger Black Texans actually listen to. And he received the endorsement of the powerful Congressional Black Caucus.

When I went back to Texas on the last weekend of September, the state fair had just opened and Talarico walked onto the field at the State Fair Classic. It’s an annual football game between Prairie View A&M and Grambling State, in front of more than 50,000 people. Two HBCUs, two serious Southern marching bands and the Divine Nine Greek organizations in full regalia.

The candidate was announced as a special guest. A man in the stands gave him a bear hug and told him he had his vote. A woman leaned over the railing and asked him what he was going to do about Black schools that keep getting shut down. He told her he was a former teacher and he was working on district takeovers.

The reception was warm, including from McCallum, who had begun to volunteer for the campaign.

“Mr. James Talarico! You have been invited to the cookout,” she said into a tiny handheld mic as she stood in front of the “Talarico for Texas” bus. “What did you think?”

Camille MacCallum films a social video with Talarico at the State Fair of Texas on Sept. 26, 2026.

“The energy out here is great. The food is right. The music is right. So I’m honored to be here,” he answered.

On Sunday we went to church. Concord Church in Dallas is one of the biggest Black congregations in the state, and its pastor, Bryan Carter, has been in the pulpit there for 23 years. Every Sunday since the summer, Carter told me, they had been registering voters in the lobby.

“Voting is a moral obligation,” he said. “Your vote is your voice.”

Pastor Bryan Carter of Concord Church in Dallas, on Sept. 27, 2026.

Carter is careful, the way Black pastors who have been doing this for a long time are careful. He didn’t tell his congregation who to vote for. But when he introduced Talarico, he called him “a man of conviction, a man of faith, a champion for justice,” as the room stood up and applauded.

Talarico, the grandson of a Baptist preacher, is comfortable in church. He’s able to connect the political and spiritual.

“When Jesus healed the sick, he didn’t ask for a deductible. So when I fight for universal healthcare, I’m doing it on biblical grounds,” he said from the pulpit. “And when the Hebrew prophets saw corruption in high places, they spoke truth to power. So when I take on the politicians who are serving themselves and not the people, I am doing it on biblical grounds.”

Carter said Talarico strikes a note that others who have come courting Black votes struggle with. “He’s been unique in that he has been able to blend both an agenda that supports justice, that cares for the poor, the marginalized and oppressed while at the same time leveraging that as motivation for public service,” the pastor said of the former seminarian.

Talarico speaks at Concord Church in Dallas on Sept. 27, 2026.

I sat down with Talarico one more time in a side room at Concord. We had been talking about Black voters for months at that point. I wanted to know what he had learned.

He said he hadn’t understood, when the campaign began, the size of the funding gap between HBCUs and other schools. He said he learned on the trail that Harris County, anchored by Houston, is the deadliest place in America for a Black woman to give birth. He said he’d figured out that younger Black Texans aren’t in the pews on Sunday morning the way their parents are, which is why the campaign was at Sunday Funday brunches in Houston and tailgating on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard before the Classic.

“If we really want to reach those voters, showing up at a Black church is not going to suffice,” he said. “We’ve got to be out where they are.”

The long game

A volunteer helps to register voters at the Concord Church in Dallas on Sept. 27, 2026.

One of the things about courting Black voters in Texas these days, though, is that it’s not only about persuading them. It’s also about whether they will actually be able to vote.

At the end of August, Tarrant County, home to Fort Worth, moved to close 92 Election Day polling sites, from 316 in the last midterm to 224. The Legal Defense Fund, the American Civil Liberties Union and the Campaign Legal Center sent a letter warning that the cuts fell hardest on Black, Latino and Asian American neighborhoods.

“Voter suppression is powerful, I don’t want to sugarcoat it. Big money is powerful,” Talarico told me in that side room at the church. “But none of that can compare to people power. I’m putting my faith in people power every day of the week and twice on Sunday.”

The hill Talarico has to climb to win in Texas is huge. His campaign thinks it’s made a lot of headway on the Black voter issue with its investments, though it’s impossible to know whether all is forgiven until Tuesday.

It’s possible those investments won’t pay off this time around. I asked Talarico about the long game, the way the other side has been playing it for decades. He looked to the Civil Rights Movement.

It’s a balance of an inherent conflict between “urgency and patience. We can’t get discouraged after one election,” he said. “We can’t give up after one victory or one Supreme Court case. We have to maintain that urgency over decades. And I think Black Texans have obviously shown us how to do that, because it’s a necessity.”

James Talarico had a problem, but he saw it differently. Where Black voters saw a lack of his talking to them, he saw a need to listen. Where they saw a lack of investment, he saw a need to make sure he would have the money for it. Where almost the entire Democratic Party saw a desperate need for him to win, he saw beyond November.

MS NOW producer Shawn Killebrew contributed.

news.title: 82% disapprove of Trump. So why are fewer Indian Americans identifying as Democrats?
news.text: At an Indian restaurant in Irving, near Dallas, Democratic US Senate candidate James Talarico tried his hand at making a masala dosa, spreading batter on a hot pan and filling it with spiced potatoes. In Connecticut, Governor Ned Lamont joined Diwali celebrations, while Republican Congressman John James visited a Swaminarayan temple in Michigan. From dosas to Diwali and temple visits, politicians from both parties are making symbolic overtures to Indian-American voters ahead of the November 3 midterms. But the community’s political allegiances are not as straightforward as those campaign gestures might suggest.At the national level, Republicans are fighting hard to retain control of both chambers of Congress. And the odds, at least in prediction markets, are not in their favour. As of October 30, betting website Kalshi gave Democrats a 92% chance of taking control of the House of Representatives and a 69% chance of winning the Senate. Polymarket's corresponding figures were 94% and 72%.A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on October 26 also found Democrats leading Republicans 47% to 36% among registered voters. Losing control of either chamber, or in the worst case both, could severely hamper US President Donald Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his presidency. So the stakes couldn't be higher.With the Trump administration pursuing what many see as anti-immigration policies, the stakes are also fairly high for the 5.2 million people of Indian origin living in the US. However, there is an interesting paradox between their voting patterns and declared political affiliations. While most are strongly anti-Trump, many don't identify as Democrats. The party's perceived leftward tilt appears to be one source of discomfort among some Indian-Americans.An AP-NORC and AAPI Data survey released on October 19 found that 82% of Indian-American respondents disapprove of Trump's job performance. Yet four in ten held an unfavourable opinion of the Democrats. A separate series of surveys by the Carnegie Endowment earlier in the year suggests that fewer Indian-Americans identify as Democrats than they did six years ago, while more describe themselves as independents.Together, the surveys challenge the idea of Indian-Americans as a politically uniform community. They reveal differences across age, education, income and other factors that shape political affiliation.A clear Democratic leadThe AP-NORC/AAPI Data survey, conducted from September 8 to 15, found Trump's handling of the economy similarly unpopular: 81% disapproved and 18% approved. On immigration, 70% disapproved of his performance.Almost in lockstep, the Republican Party was viewed favourably by only 19%, while 70% held an unfavourable opinion of it. Democrats were in a substantially stronger position, with 51% viewing the party favourably.That advantage also appears in surveys measuring voting intentions. The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey, conducted by AAPI Data and APIAVote between June and July, found that 66% of Indian-American registered voters preferred Democratic candidates for the House of Representatives, against 18% favouring Republicans. Democratic Senate candidates also attracted 66%, compared with 22% for Republicans.Fewer are calling themselves DemocratsAccording to the Carnegie Endowment's 2026 Indian-American Attitudes Survey, conducted between November 2025 and January 2026, the share of Indian-American adults identifying as Democrats declined from 52% in 2020 to 48% in 2024 and 46% in 2026. Over the same period, Republican identification rose from 15% to 19%, while independent identification increased from 23% to 29%.Republicans' gains came between 2020 and 2024; between 2024 and 2026, their share of party identifiers remained unchanged at 19%. The independent share, meanwhile, rose four percentage points. The two-point dip in Democratic identification during this period is small relative to the survey's margin of error.Being independent, however, does not mean being undecided, particularly given the two-party nature of US politics. Carnegie found that the independent share dropped from 29% to 17% when respondents were offered the option of leaning towards one of the two parties.The ideological picture offers another clue. Carnegie found that 32% of Indian-Americans identified as moderates in 2026, up from 28% in 2024. The share selecting the specific label 'liberal' declined from 25% to 21%. But when those identifying as slightly liberal and extremely liberal are included, the broader liberal segment has changed little over the past six years. Rather than indicating a conservative shift, Carnegie describes the community as broadly centrist, with a left-of-centre tilt.On a scale of zero to 100, the Democratic Party's average rating in Carnegie's survey fell from 60 in 2024 to 53 in 2026. The Republican Party's rating also dropped, from 41 to 34. The decline extended to leading political figures. Kamala Harris's average rating fell from 62 to 52, while Trump's dropped from 40 to 32.Exhausted, but engagedThere is another striking finding from the AAPI Voter Survey. Although 92% of Indian-American registered voters said they planned to vote in November, 66% said they always (29%) or often (37%) felt exhausted when thinking about politics.At the same time, 43% described themselves as more enthusiastic than usual about voting in the midterms, compared with 22% who were less enthusiastic, perhaps because a lot more is at stake now.Three-quarters of respondents said they had discussed politics with family or friends in the previous year. Another 25% had discussed politics or community issues through group messaging platforms such as WhatsApp, while 24% had posted about politics on social media.But direct party outreach tells a different story. Forty percent of Indian-American registered voters reported receiving no contact from the Democratic Party over the preceding year, while 56% said the same of Republicans.The Democratic drift is not uniformCarnegie's findings also challenge the idea that younger Indian-Americans are necessarily moving away from Democrats. Among respondents aged 18 to 29, Democratic identification increased from 51% in 2024 to 56% in 2026. Among those aged 50 and above, however, it declined from 47% to 39%.Education produced another divide. Democratic identification among respondents without a college degree fell from 48% to 35%, while remaining broadly unchanged among college graduates, at 49%. Income revealed a similar split. Among Indian-Americans in households earning between $50,000 and $99,999 annually, Democratic identification declined from 54% to 44%. Among those in households earning at least $100,000, it increased from 46% to 51%.Gender differences were also visible. Democratic identification among men fell from 46% to 40%, while among women it rose slightly, from 50% to 52%. So older Indian-Americans appear to be moving away from identifying as card-carrying Democrats, although the trend among the well-off is different.Economy remains the big issueIn the September AP-NORC/AAPI Data poll, 87% of Indian-American respondents identified the economy as one of the most important election issues. Cost of living followed at 84%, while 76% said the same of healthcare.Despite weaker party identification, Democrats enjoyed sizeable advantages on these issues. Fifty-three percent trusted Democrats more to handle the economy, compared with 12% who trusted Republicans. On the cost of living, the corresponding figures were 52% and 8%. On healthcare, Democrats held an even larger advantage, with 60% trusting them more, against just 6% for Republicans.But these preferences did not amount to universal confidence in the party. On the economy, 20% trusted neither party. On the cost of living, the proportion was 25%.Democrats also had an advantage on immigration in the September survey, with 50% trusting them more, against 18% who preferred Republicans. On crime, however, the numerical gap was narrower: 29% trusted Democrats more and 19% Republicans, while 28% trusted neither.India ties not a major concernInflation and prices were the single most important policy issue for 21% of respondents in Carnegie's survey, followed by jobs and the economy at 17%. Healthcare ranked next at 13%, followed by immigration at 11%. Only 2% named US–India relations as their top concern.That is perhaps along expected lines, though many in India probably view Indian-Americans' political behaviour through the prism of the India–US bilateral relationship. For most desis living in the US, it is not the top concern.The finding does not mean that Indian-Americans are indifferent to relations between Washington and New Delhi. It means that domestic issues, particularly economic concerns, matter more when respondents are asked to identify their single most important policy priority.Is the Democratic Party's leftward tilt a problem?Carnegie asked respondents who did not identify as Democrats to rank their top two objections to the party. The most frequently cited reason, at 19%, was the perception that Democrats were too influenced by their left wing.Concerns about the party's approach to illegal immigration and disagreements with its economic policies followed at 17% each. Another 16% cited perceptions that Democrats were too soft on crime, while an equal share objected to what they considered excessive emphasis on identity politics. These issues overlap with broader conservative criticism of what is often called liberal or 'woke' politics. The findings suggest that the Democratic Party's perceived leftward tilt makes it harder for some Indian-Americans to identify with the party.But there is another side to this argument.The same Carnegie survey found that 68% of Indian-Americans who were familiar with Zohran Mamdani were enthusiastic about his election as New York City mayor, while 22% were unenthusiastic. Among those enthusiastic about his victory, 44% cited the expectation that he would govern as a liberal or progressive. Among those unenthusiastic, 36% said he was too liberal or progressive. Even among Indian-Americans identifying as Republicans, enthusiasm and opposition to Mamdani's victory were almost evenly divided, at 44% and 45%, respectively.That makes the political picture more complicated. Some Indian-Americans regard the Democratic Party as too influenced by its left wing, while others welcome the rise of progressive politicians such as Mamdani.The question beyond November 3There are important limitations to these findings. The relatively small ethnic subgroups surveyed carry greater statistical uncertainty than the surveys' overall samples. Carnegie's historical survey waves also involved different respondents and changes in sampling methods, so the reported shifts do not establish that individual voters have switched party allegiance.What the surveys do show is a distinction between candidate preference and party identity. Democratic candidates continue to enjoy a large advantage. Trump's job performance is viewed negatively by a substantial majority. Beyond the midterms, the challenge for Democrats will be to sustain their electoral support among Indian-Americans while addressing the concerns of those who no longer identify strongly with the party.Attention will eventually turn to the nomination contests ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The continuing influence of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, and the ideological direction of the Democrats, will be among the factors shaping the political choices facing Indian-Americans. For now, though, the polling suggests that many desis would like to give Trump the electoral blues.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Ahead of the November 3 US midterms, fresh polling shows Indian-Americans strongly favour Democrats on the economy and in congressional races. But a six-year decline in Democratic identification, growing political exhaustion and dissatisfaction with both parties suggest a more complicated relationship with the party.

 By JON MICHAEL RAASCH, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTand HARRIET ALEXANDER, US SENIOR FEATURES WRITER

By the time James Cox was first permitted to enter the polling station, Susan Collins had been his senator for a decade.
Cox, now 38, voted for the veteran Republican several times – swayed by her pledge to fight for the rights of her Maine constituents.
He is thinking of doing so again.
'Susan Collins is more of a familiar face to me,' he told the Daily Mail, standing in his flannel jacket in the windswept street of Bangor – tiny Maine's third-largest city, with a mere 32,000 residents.
But he's heard word of a 'new' kid on the block.
'It was brought to my attention that Troy Jackson's actually been involved in the Senate and politics for over 20 years,' he said.
Does he know enough about him to trust him with his vote? Probably not.
Cox's comments, with a week to go until the midterms, will sink like a stone in the Jackson camp.

View gallery

GOP incumbent Senator Susan Collins is running for a sixth consecutive term against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and longtime local Maine lawmaker 

View gallery

James Cox, 38, a Bangor resident, told the Daily Mail he supports Collins because she's a familiar face and he does not know much about Jackson, although his top concern was ending the US war in Iran

View gallery

The Daily Mail interviewed half a dozen Bangor residents the week before Election Day. Voters in the area consistently gravitated towards Collins over Jackson, sighting their unfamiliarity with the Democrat whose run a truncated campaign after his predecessor dropped out

Jackson, the 58-year-old Democrat logger-turned-politician, is hoping to unseat 73-year-old Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history.

EXCLUSIVE Leaked Pentagon group chat reveals vulgar nickname for Trump-pick Army chief 
Collins, campaigning for her sixth term, is hoping that the majority of Mainers feel, like Cox, that she is a safe, well-known bet.
Jackson's team, meanwhile, are wracked by concerns that his late entry to the race has hobbled him – especially because, in running against such a well-known politician, he needed all the time possible to get his name on everyone's lips.
'Jackson served six years as the head of the state Senate, but he's not terribly well known by a lot of Maine voters, especially in the southern part of the state,' said Ronald Schmidt, professor of political science at the University of Southern Maine. 'He needed every opportunity he could to introduce himself - before Senator Collins and the PACs supporting her began to do that introduction on their own.'
Jackson was not confirmed as the Democrat candidate until July 25, after the previous nominee, Graham Platner, was forced to pull out amid allegations of sexual misconduct.
Platner had launched his election bid in August 2025, meaning that Jackson effectively lost a year of campaign time.
'There was a lag in terms of organizing and in terms of finding the right tone,' said Schmidt. 'That being said, I think he still has a decent chance of winning, in part because of exhaustion with the Trump administration and the Republicans in Washington.
'But in terms of the strengths of his campaign, that slow start definitely did hurt.'

View gallery

Graham Platner, 42, was the Democratic candidate for Maine's Senate race until July. He dropped out after being the subject of rape and sexual misconduct accusations. He has denied all wrongdoing

View gallery

Platner faced intense scrutiny after reports revealed an active profile on the anonymous messaging app Kik and a scandal involving extramarital and sexually explicit texts. Platner's Kik profile picture, viewed by the Daily Mail, showed the Democratic candidate posing shirtless and in only a towel

View gallery

After Platner dropped out, Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, 58, a former logger and president of the Maine state Senate launched his campaign in late July
For some Maine Democrats, it's all agonizingly familiar.
Like Kamala Harris's supporters in 2024, Jackson's fans feel he has not been given time to establish himself.

 Which midterm races should YOU be watching? Enter your zip code in our exclusive election calculator 
And, with the crucial contest currently too close to call, Jackson needed all the help he could get.
Certainly, he has the Maine bona fides.
Born in the far north of the state to a 16-year-old teacher and her logger husband, Jackson's parents did not want their son to follow his father, grandfather and great-grandfather into logging.
But age 11, in 1981, he went with his father to support striking loggers, only to see them forced to return to work or be fired and replaced by Canadians. It had a profound impact on the youngster, who vividly recalled earlier this year the powerlessness his father Joe felt.
'He couldn’t say anything,' said Jackson, speaking to a reporter before meeting with electricians at their union building in Lewiston. 'You lose your sense of pride, your sense of dignity.'
By the age of 19, Jackson was working full time as a logger – waking at 2am for 18-hour days in the woods, and leading protests for better working conditions. When the protests failed, he entered politics – initially as a Republican, knowing that the Bush family had ties to the state, before switching in 2004 to run as a Democrat.

View gallery

A statue of the legendary North American lumberjack Paul Bunyan stands proudly in Bangor. The area has deep ties to the logging industry 

View gallery

Jackson camapaigned alongside Senator Elizabeth Warren on Monday in Waterville, Maine. At the event he spoke out about growing corporate power undermining working class families and noted how he is against 'for-profit' higher education, two progressive platforms
Your browser does not support iframes.

 In a state which prides itself as fiercely independent – one-third of voters refuse to declare themselves a member of either party – his switching sides has not concerned people.
And indeed, independence is something his Republican rival is desperate to play up.
Donald Trump's approval ratings are at record lows, and so Collins is now doing her utmost to distance herself from her party's leader. She voted to impeach him in January 2021, and voted against some of his Cabinet members in both terms – notably Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel. But she did vote to confirm Robert F Kennedy Jr, and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.
She supported Trump's policies 95 percent of the time in 2025, according to CQ Roll Call analysis, and voted to advance the Big Beautiful Bill in the Senate, but then rejected it in the final vote – a classic, performative Collins move, her critics say. Her campaign insists it shows her independent streak.
Is it working?
'That's a great question, and in many ways the answer to it might be the biggest driver of the outcome,' said Professor Mark Brewer, chair of the University of Maine's department of political science.
'Collins has done a pretty good job of making the case, as she always does, for the benefits she brings to the state.
'Jackson has made a relatively strong case that Collins has changed over time, that she's become less bipartisan and less moderate.

View gallery

Along Maine's coast in Bar Harbor, many residents were more supportive of Jackson. Voters along the coastal regions interviewed by the Daily Mail expressed more interest in Democrats than Republicans

Read more: US Midterm Elections 2026

A Blue Tsunami? My poll reveals a very different scenario: POLLSTER BRENT BUCHANAN
I'm the founder and CEO of the top private polling firm in the US, as recognized by The New York Times for the accuracy of our 5,000 polls conducted across all 50 states.

MAUREEN CALLAHAN: Obama's new low has tipped the race

Inside America's 'Arab Capital' where families are divided as state that flipped for Trump could now snub one of their own

Fake polls are threatening the midterms. We must act now to stop it

'On the question of whether she's Trump's lackey, as Jackson wants to claim, or whether, as Collins claims, she's an independent voice who sometimes votes with the president when it's good for Maine and against him when it isn't, I don't know who's been more credible. But the answer to that would go a long way towards telling us who wins.'
Collins agreed to an unusual four debates with Jackson, in the hope that she could press home her independence, and stress her track record of using her powerful Senate appropriations committee position to help her constituents.
But her October 6 debate against Jackson saw her hand him perhaps the most powerful campaign slogan of the season.
'I have been strongly voting against the tariffs with Canada, but I've also been working behind the scenes,' said Collins. 'Troy mocked it, but I was successful in getting concrete pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list and if you ask towns in Northern Maine and Eastern Maine, they get all of their road salt from Canada.'
Jackson retorted: 'We can't eat road salt.'
His supporters have taken to wearing T-shirts emblazoned with the line.
So does the ghost of Graham Platner haunt Jackson's campaign? Or is it simply a referendum on Collins's five terms, and Trump's two?
Mike Hurley has lived in central Maine's Waldo County, a stone's throw from Platner's Blue Hill hometown, for over 50 years.

View gallery

A man fills his ballot during early midterm voting in the town hall in Bangor, Maine, on October 16, 2026
Your browser does not support iframes.

He told the Daily Mail that Platner's forced departure was 'painful' – but he was still supporting the Democrats.
'Susan Collins is on Team Trump,' he said, adding that he disagreed with the administration on 'a plethora of issues'.
Maine, sharing a 600-mile border with Canada, is hard hit by tariffs: only Alaska and Michigan share a longer landline with the northern neighbor.
Furthermore, it is a state strongly dependent on heating oil for homes – and the Iran war has sent costs rocketing. This time last year an average Mainer would spend $907 to fill their tank for the winter; today, the cost is $1,660.
'The tariffs and the war with Iran are huge issues for me,' said Hurley. 'And Trump turning on Ukraine is a terrible, terrible thing - and I don't hear Susan Collins saying anything about it. The country is going in the wrong direction, and I hope this turns it back.'

View gallery

Mike Hurley has lived in central Maine's Waldo County, a stone's throw from Platner's Blue Hill hometown, for over 50 years. He is backing Jackson and admits Platner's dropping out was a 'painful' process 
Steve, a 40-year-old chef who has lived in the picturesque Bar Harbor area for ten years, is also voting Jackson, but is infuriated by the missteps that led to Platner's ouster.
'The Democrats are always trying to do the right thing, but they keep shooting themselves in the foot,' said Steve, dressed for work in his black chef's 'whites'.
He said he was dismayed by the 'clown show' of the Trump administration and Republican party, adding: 'These guys shouldn't be hard to beat.'
Indeed, this race is widely seen as the toughest of Collins's 30-year political career, and gives the Democrats their biggest chance in a generation of at long last turning New England entirely blue.
Collins is the last Republican standing in the region: the other 11 are all Democrat, except for the independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine.
And yet Collins has, time and time again, proved herself to be remarkably resilient.

'But this president is the least popular any president has been going into a midterm in almost a century. It is really hard to run in that environment, even for someone like Susan Collins.'

news.title: Gas Attack: Blue States Have the Highest Prices at the Pump
news.text:
Democrats can't seem to decide whether they want higher or lower gas prices. On the one hand, they're promising that if they win a majority in Congress, they will work to bring down prices at the pump. On the other hand, they can't bring down prices in their own blue states.

 We at Unleash Prosperity recently analyzed gas and diesel prices in the 50 states. Here's what we found: The more Democratic a state, the higher the price of gas. For each additional percentage point of the state's vote that went to former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, gas prices are about 2 cents higher.

 On average, deep-blue states pay about 25 cents a gallon more for gas than deep-red states. Yes, we know correlation is not causation (umbrellas don't cause rain), but it does suggest that relying on Democrats to lower gas prices is probably a fool's errand.

 Take California, where gas now costs more than $6 a gallon. That's because of climate change policies and taxes that reach up to 75 cents a gallon. All told, Californians pay about $1.25 a gallon more than the average state. Yet California Gov. Gavin Newsom is considered a frontrunner for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

 Eight of the 10 states with the highest gas prices are run by Democrats. And eight of the 10 states with the lowest gas prices are run by Republicans.

 This isn't a coincidence. Democrats are so deeply in bed with the radical climate change lobby that they have done everything they can to strangle the industry. Let's not forget that one of former President Joe Biden's first actions in office was killing the Keystone XL pipeline.

 That was followed by a plan that his "climate justice agency" promoted, the goal of which was to stop all new production of fossil fuels. The plan was even opposed to nuclear power and aimed to curtail highway spending to discourage Americans from driving -- unless they were in an electric vehicle.

 New pipelines were to be banned.

 Meanwhile, several Democratic state attorneys general are suing the oil and gas companies for climate change costs. None of this is increasing our supply of oil.

 When President Donald Trump announced a "drill, baby, drill" energy dominance strategy, Democrats in Congress nearly had a cardiac arrest. Trump's energy policy has led to an all-time high U.S. output of oil and natural gas. How high would gas prices be today if we weren't now the world's leader in oil and gas? Anyone remember that former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi was in favor of natural gas until someone had to remind her that natural gas is a fossil fuel?

 America still gets the majority of its energy from the fossil fuels that the left hates: oil, gas and coal. To power the energy needed for the next tech revolution, we will need to double or triple our energy production, and it's a fantasy to think we can do that with windmills.

 As for gas prices, you can't in one breath talk about "net zero" carbon emissions and a war on our oil and gas producers and in the other breath promise lower gas prices at the pump.

 You don't send an arsonist to put out a fire.

 Stephen Moore is a former Trump senior economic adviser and the cofounder of Unleash Prosperity, which advocates for education freedom for all children.

news.title: Melania hijacked the Pope’s ceasefire as Catholic support for Trump craters
news.text:
Wall Street Journal national security reporter Alex Ward says First Lady Melania Trump essentially stole credit for Pope Leo XIV’s hard work to broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia.

Hundreds of people from an occupied city of Oleshky, in southern Ukraine, were evacuated on Friday under a ceasefire agreement allegedly negotiated by Melania Trump, according to the White House. But Ward told “Today, Explained” co-host Sean Rameswaram that it was really the Pope who built the bones of the agreement.

“It’s possible she had a role. I’m going to personally, without too much reporting, say that it was probably more Pope Leo,” said Ward.

“Melania stole Pope Leo’s ceasefire?” asked Rameswaram.

“I think a little bit. … The Russians are very much saying, ‘look at Melania Trump, look at how important she was to all this.’ And if I’m the Russians, I would love to be saying things like that because then President Trump feels like the Russians are being very generous towards my wife and to my family, and therefore I side with them.”

“It feels very convenient that the Russians are pumping that up and that even the White House is pumping up Melania Trump’s influence,” said Ward, while adding that he did not want to fully discredit her. “I’m sure she did work on this.”

Ward added that while it’s “totally possible” that the First Lady is the driving force behind the ceasefire, he said “there’s just a lot of skepticism out there about whether Kyiv and Moscow were brought to the table and browbeaten by the First Lady.”

“Again, very possible, but both sides, being Ukraine and Russia, have an incentive to play up her role,” said Ward.

Meanwhile, Trump’s catholic approval has collapsed to 30 percent before the midterms, as Trump continues to square off against Leo and impose the White House’s will over the Hole See.

“Donald Trump won the Catholic vote in 2024 by twelve points, 55 percent to Kamala Harris’s 43 percent, reports Catholic Church correspondent Christopher Hale. And four years earlier, the same group had split almost evenly.

However, six days before the midterms, Pew now finds that only 30 percent of American Catholics approve of the job Trump is doing.

“For most of his first year back in office, the decline came gradually. Trump’s approval among Catholics fell to 42 percent by April 2025 and bounced around the low 40s through the summer and fall; by January 2026 it sat at 39 percent,” wrote Hale. “ … Since then, Trump’s Catholic approval has fallen another nine points, from 39 percent to 30. With white Catholics the slide runs steeper: 13 points, from 52 percent to 39, nearly double what he lost with them over his entire first year.”

Pew does not explain the collapse, but Hale said the slide has everything to do with another Trump-era war: his voluntary attack on Iran.

news.title: Hear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prize | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Haters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at a recent rally. The president has also spent the greater part of a decade claiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.

But despite his many trophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, the country’s tourism board highlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”

Speaking in my capacity as Philadelphia’s Woman of the Millennium, I’ve got a modest proposal for the people of Norway. The toilet gag was excellent, but if they want to do some top-tier trolling then I think next year’s Nobel peace prize needs to go to Melania Trump.

Some people would be thrilled for their spouse to be in the spotlight, but I’m not sure that’s the case with Donald. Indeed, the president has said: “You can only have … one star in a family; it doesn’t work with two.” If Melania got Trump’s coveted Nobel peace prize, it could spark a war in the White House.

But look, I’m not just suggesting the Norwegians honour Melania because it would raise Donald’s blood pressure. No, it seems Melania has become quite the diplomat. Last week, the White House announced that the first lady had “successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, localized to the city of Oleshky”.

How on earth did she manage that? Apparently, Melania initiated discussions with Russia and Ukraine and “aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary”.

Whatever all that means, it seems to have worked: the ceasefire went into effect on Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, which has been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis. On Friday, hundreds of people were evacuated from the frontline town and emergency supplies were brought in for people who needed to stay.

Melania has been widely praised for brokering this ceasefire. Melania’s adviser has claimed she “singlehandedly” secured it, adding that no other first lady has ever achieved what Melania just pulled off, and she is “completely revamping the role of first lady … [and] saving lives.”

Perhaps. But if there is one thing that the Trumps are good at it, it is taking credit for other people’s work. So is the first lady really the great peacemaker that she’s making herself out to be?

To be fair, Melania has done some good work vis-à-vis Ukraine and certainly seems to be better at peacemaking than Jared Kushner is, who has made huge sums of money while operating as one of Trump’s top diplomatic envoys to the Middle East. Last year, for example, Melania wrote a letter to Vladimir Putin pleading for Ukrainian children seized by Russia to be returned to their families. Since then, her office has said she’s facilitated numerous rounds of family reunification.

However, despite the claim that Melania “singlehandedly” secured this ceasefire, it would appear she had a little help. Pope Leo XIV also personally appealed to Putin about the situation in Oleshky in early October. It’s unclear whether he had more or less sway than the first lady had, but the pope is certainly being rather more modest about his involvement.

So what’s next for Melania after her success in Oleshky? In an interview with Newsmax, her adviser Marc Beckman said Melania might help pave the way to “durable, everlasting peace” in Ukraine and Russia as a whole.

“She’s against war, she thinks it’s senseless … she wants to see peace all over the world,” Beckman added.

Does she indeed? In that case she might want to have a word with the president, who started a very bloody war against Iran and who is currently trying to use US taxpayer money to send 2,000lb bombs to Israel, a country accused of genocide.

Forget the Nobel peace prize. If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.

Bad news for US women trying to manage menopause symptoms

Last November, the FDA announced that menopausal hormone therapy medications would no longer require a scary “black-box” label on them, which is the highest safety-related warning a medication can have. This reassured a lot of women about the treatment and caused a surge in demand. Supply didn’t keep up, and there’s been a shortage of estrogen patches in the US all year because of an uptick in demand. Now Reuters reports that the shortage has spread beyond estrogen patches “with some injectable and vaginal estrogen products also in short supply”.

Dolores Huerta, labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96

Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which improved conditions for agricultural workers in the 1960s and 1970s. She is also credited with coining the phrase “Sí, se puede!” (yes, we can), which was UFW’s slogan and then Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign rally cry.

Kamala Harris advises Democrats not to impeach Trump if they win House and Senate

“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris said in a MeidasTouch interview. “I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there.” In other words: don’t hold your breath that Trump will face immediate accountability if the Democrats dominate the midterms.

Egypt continues crackdown on press freedom and fines editor Lina Attalah

Attalah is the editor-in-chief of Madr Masar, an independent Egyptian news site that has frequently been critical of the Egyptian president Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s government. The government recently accused her of running a website without a license, detained her, and shut down Mada Masr. The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, one expert told the Guardian.

The toxic legacy of body positivity

“We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies,” writes Hannah Marriott in the Guardian. The body positivity era is over, but “much of its social training lingers.” Thanks to the GLP-1 boom, everyone is shrinking, but it’s taboo to talk about it. “What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.”

Queer romance is dead: Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken up

You may be familiar with this viral tweet: “I’m 50. All celebrity news looks like this: ‘Curtains for Zoosha? K-smog and Batboy caught flipping a grunt.’” I am still a mere 43, but I had my own curtains for Zoosha moment this week when I saw the headlines about G Flip, which I could have sworn was a watch. If you are similarly confused, Rebecca Shaw has an explainer as to why some of the queer community are in mourning.

 Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
news.summary:
The first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some help

Haters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at a recent rally. The president has also spent the greater part of a decade claiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.

But despite his many trophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, the country’s tourism board highlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

news.title: TIM GRAHAM: Three-to-one negative coverage tells the story of network bias
news.text: Watching the broadcast news networks report on campaigns makes you think they’re not creating news as much as they’re trying to make the political weather. On every day, in every way, they labor to place the blackest clouds over the heads of President Donald Trump and the Republicans. Good news is not news. There is no balance of good and bad. Any hint of neutrality is despised as "normalizing" Trump. Nonpartisanship somehow becomes partisanship. So, resistance against Trump is the norm. A Media Research Center study of the 2024 campaign from July 21 through Oct. 25 found ABC, CBS and NBC evening newscasts punished Trump with 85% negative coverage. Meanwhile, the Democrat nominee, Kamala Harris, received 78% positive coverage. One choice sounded like doom, and the other was painted as hope and joy and "vibes." With that kind of stark difference in tone, does that sound like news, or campaign advertising? HUGH HEWITT: LEGACY MEDIA LEFT HALF OF AMERICA OUT. FOX NEWS LET THEM IN Leading the themes two years ago was the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, including Trump’s insistence that the 2020 election was rigged – 47 minutes of coverage. Another 30 minutes was spent amplifying claims that Trump is a "danger to democracy" and/or a "fascist." It's happening again in 2026. The Media Research Center just found ABC, CBS and NBC evening newscasts from Sept. 28 to Oct. 26 gave Trump and the Republicans almost 57 minutes of negative coverage on the evening news, while the Democrats received almost 19 minutes of negative coverage – a three-to-one ratio. That math could be a little misleading, since the bad scandal news for Democrats, like the immigration agents raiding the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., came wrapped in framing against the Trump administration for doing this in the closing weeks of an election. (These results came before the new eruption over "Decoy Dan" Sullivan in Alaska.) DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ It was the same pattern on the formerly taxpayer-funded "PBS News Hour." From Sept. 1 to Sept. 30, the GOP received 94% negative spin, to 6% positive. The Democrats received far more balanced coverage – 53% negative, 47% positive. No one would say the network news should avoid negative news. Consumers inherently don’t trust happy news any more than they trust gushy positive campaign commercials. Stubbornly high gas prices and a lack of a decisive victory in the Iran war aren’t positive stories. But the overwhelming tone of news coverage should force viewers to understand these broadcast network stars aren’t neutral referees, calling balls and strikes. They’re throwing beanballs at the Republicans. BROADCAST BIAS: NETWORKS SHOW FRANCE BURNING BUT HIGHLIGHT ‘PEACEFUL’ PROTESTERS Inside the broadcast network news bubble, democracy is mentally associated with the Democrats, autocracy with the Grand Old Party. If the Republicans show party unity, that’s a failing. They are weakening democracy by not weakening Trump. When the Democrats show party unity, that’s not controversial at all. In fact, the elitist media help enforce party unity. Republicans dissenting from Trump quickly draw positive media attention. "Lifelong Republicans" who endorse Democrats get promoted as the zeitgeist. Democrat dissenters would be ignored and gain no advantage. The growing radicalism of the Democrat party and its Democratic Socialists of America faction, and what they plan to do if they gain a majority in one or both houses of Congress, have not been serious topics. If the voters are casting ballots for Democrats because of the economy, do the Democrats have an actual solution? The networks weren’t focused on what happens next. Anyone perusing social media can see the Democrats salivating at more impeachments of Trump, and maybe an impeachment for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., not to mention some very aggressive hearings into how the Trump family is personally prospering in Trump’s second term. TERRY MORAN SAYS NETWORK REJECTED HIS BIDEN HEALTH STORY AFTER HE WITNESSED PRESIDENT’S FRAILTY During President Joe Biden’s presidency, the broadcast networks obsessed over the House’s Jan. 6 hearings, including incessant live coverage, even in prime time hours. In the last two years, House oversight hearings into subjects like Biden’s use of the autopen and his declining mental fitness, were largely ignored. Republican hearings aren’t news. Democrat hearings will surely be big news – again. Inside the broadcast network news bubble, democracy is mentally associated with the Democrats, autocracy with the Grand Old Party. The networks have focused most of their attention on Trump’s rallies, often noting that when he campaigns in red states, it’s a sign that Republicans are anxious about losing in states they should be winning. If former President Barack Obama campaigns in a blue state, like appearing with radical Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, that’s not painted as desperation.
